For on-ear phones, though, these aren't bad and the ear fatigue is less than many I have used.This particular set boasts an on-demand bass boost, and for me that's a huge plus. Most headphones have the bass boost baked right in and there's no way to turn it off. I don't care for heavy-handed bass (gives me headaches), so for me it is a feature I will leave turned off most of the time. However, there are times when the bass needs some help, and these deliver. When activated, there is a very noticeable increase in bass response that will certainly make some people happy.So, about the sound profile... A set of headphones isn't worth any amount of money if they sound bad. These are fairly balanced phones when the bass booster is turned off. The highs are bright and clear, the midrange is warm and the bass is present but not overwhelming. The bass becomes front and center when the boost is turned on.These connect via Bluetooth and they pair and establish connection quickly. I have no complaints.These are good on-ear phones that work well. They're reasonably comfortable, and they connect well. The most interesting feature, to me, is the on-demand bass booster which is better than having a continuous bass boost that's built in. For me, that's a major positive point and is the reason I will continue using these.  These sound good.

comment: I'm an audio guy, and care mostly about sound quality. For ten bucks shipped on Prime, these are very inexpensive and you have to adjust your expectations accordingly. I thought the build quality was pretty good, and they looked more expensive than they were. They're comfortable to wear, and are lightweight. There's no battery, no volume control, no noise-cancelling, no Bluetooth, and no microphone, but there's not supposed to be. These are simple, straightforward audio headphones. My one main gripe -- and it's a pretty big one -- is power efficiency. By that I mean the volume, when connected to a phone or a computer, is really low compared to my other headphones (I also have high end of Shure studio monitor headphones). Even at maximum volume, they're pleasant but seem to provide half to a third the volume of my other headphones. In addition, the sound is flat, kind of like you're listening through a thick blanket. So yeah, they work fine, they're very inexpensive, they're well made enough, they look good, but the audio quality is at best on par with other sub-$10 headphones - there's no bargain to be found here in that respect. If sound quality is also your priority, I think you may be disappointed.EDIT: I just lowered the rating. I think Sony's Chinese manufacturer is kind of screwing them. I think they substituted poor-quality magnets or some other component in the middle of the manufacturing run without telling anyone, including Sony. Probably the first batch of them were pretty good. But these are really annoying me for one primary reason: very low volume. Compared to nearly anything similar, they just plan too quietly. I usually have to turn the volume up to 100% on everything  I have lots of other headphones and none of them are like this, even my very expensive and inefficient studio headphones. I'd recommend looking for something else, even at this extremely low price.

date_review: Reviewed in the United States on March 4, 2024
comment: I did not need another pair of headphones, but I ran across these at a good price, and paired with a promotional credit, I figured they would be nice to keep at the office. I have a set of Bose QuietComforts that I am still in love with, and I knew these were not a direct competitor, but Sony's WH-1000XMs are. I figured for less than half the price (MSRP), if these were even decently comfortable and sounded ok, they would work great for my needs.I got the headphones out of the box and set them up with my phone yesterday. I have always had issues with Sony accounts working properly and I never got the app connected to my account. It's only necessary if you want to use the adaptive feature (adjusts ambient settings based on where you are, and your habits), saving settings, etc. Connecting the headphones to the phone via the app went smoothly, and the settings are pretty straight forward. You're kind of hit with wizard after wizard, but I guess that's just supposed to make setting them up for the first time easier. I skipped a lot of that, knowing I could easily revisit each setting in the app.To be honest, my first impressions were not very positive. The sound was ok at best with the default settings. I did the ear analysis, though I really don't understand what pictures of my ears are supposed to achieve, and I tweaked the equalizer using the "find my equalizer," and the best one still didn't sound very good. I definitely expected better than this even at a lower price point. Especially from Sony. I played around with the manual EQ, but I think I was just already in a negative headspace on these headphones. I decided I was going to return them the next day and boxed them back up.The next day, I went ahead and processed the return. Then I remembered looking at reviews for these headphones, not just here, but professional reviews as well. All reviews were pretty positive. What was I missing? So I decided to take them out of the box and play with the EQ some more. I had reset them so I had to go back through everything with the app, but it only took a minute the second time around. I went in search of a good starting point for the EQ. Reddit did not disappoint. Several people listed their settings with these headphones and the one that I found worked best for me was: +2, +3, +4, +6, +9 Clear Bass at 7. It was massively better than what I heard the previous day. I tested with my phone and laptop, and both sound really good. They are comfortable, but you do have to move them around so that the drivers aren't pressing into your ears. I have fairly flat ears, but they still lightly touch. No big deal, but could become an irritation if wearing them too long. The pads to get a little warm after a while, but I just take them off periodically and all is well. Return cancelled.The microphones seem to work fine. I've taken a few calls on my phone, as well as VOIP calls through the laptop, and everyone hears me perfectly clearly. The dual device switching works perfectly, as expected.In my work environment, the ANC works perfectly well. It definitely works in other environments as well. My boxer was going nuts playing with a ball while I was testing them at home and cycling through the settings, and his barks were noticeably muted when I would cycle the ANC on. You can still hear him, but I don't know if anybody's ANC can completely mute a hyper boxer's barks when he's right next to you.  I would have to fly with them to see how they do with droning jet engines, but I imagine they would do just fine. Maybe not as well as higher end headphones, but on a budget, these should do the trick. I think they would be better than my Samsung Buds Pro, but not as good as the Bose.I'm quite glad I decided to give these headphones another try. They will fit my needs nicely.

overview_text: Perfect for running, ear pads a bit small
comment: I run outdoors frequently and was looking for a decent pair of headphones because my area is noisy and I was tired of constantly adjusting my airpods while running. I wanted something with serviceable audio quality that I also wouldn't mind putting through the constant wear and tear of sweaty runs. I was previously wearing a more expensive pair of headphones to run, and while I do prefer those for use at home or for noise-canceling, they were too heavy and hot for running and I was worried about damaging them. The beats solo3 are a better fit for this particular use case (for me).Pros:- the apple bluetooth chip is extremely useful, it makes it so much more convenient to switch between devices! Major QOL improvement over other headphones I own- lightweight and don't make my ears hot during exercise- stay put well even with a lot of movement (I've even worn these while hanging upside down at the gym and they didn't fall off)- blocks out the perfect amount of sound for outdoor running, such that I'm not distracted by ambient noise but I still have enough situational awareness to hear a car honking at me at close range- audio quality is better than any of my in-ear headphones, which is really all I needed in this case- battery life is great, I never find myself running out of battery even though I use these quite a bitCons:- My primary reason for deducting a star: I was expecting these to be over-ear, but they're actually more like on-ear; the ear pads are a bit tight and sometimes they start to hurt my ears after wearing them for longer periods of time, usually after ~45 minutes (I'd be especially cautious if you have any cartilage piercings)- It's a bit hard to use the control buttons sometimes- the double tap to skip is a little finicky, sometimes if I press too quickly in succession or not hard enough it doesn't register. The volume controls are so much smaller and so far to the top and bottom, respectively, that I sometimes accidentally hit the center pause button instead. Still convenient to have controls there, but they have room for improvement. I also find myself wishing that I could use the controls from either side instead of just the one, but that's not a big deal.- I worry that the band might be damaging my hair a bit, as it's a pretty grippy material. It's not pulling out any hair, but I do wish it had a bit more slip since the headphones feel tight enough to stay put regardless

comment: Let me start off by saying likely the only reason I didn't give this 5 stars was because I'm coming from really nice headphones like the Sennheiser HD559 and Sony WH-1000XM4's so I've been a little bit.... spoiled in that category. Overall these headphones are pretty hard to beat for the price-- but if you shell out a little bit more you could get things like the Anker Q20 and Q30 which are pretty decent as well.Sound quality is decent on these. My first impression out of box is sometimes they sound a little tinny-- but after using them for a bit I think they've broken in a bit and aren't nearly as bad as I initially thought. I don't really listen to any high fidelity things though so take that with a grain of salt. These are on-ear headphones meaning they sit on-your-ear. They don't clamp super hard so I don't think they're great for working out or anything like that but I didn't have any issues with discomfort and I wear glasses. Some people prefer over-ears (in fact I prefer over-ears) but it's not a deal breaker. Just know that they produce a bit of heat because of that and don't 'seal' sound as well.I didn't have any issues pairing or keeping the headphones connected (I have an iPhone SE 2nd gen). In fact, one of the nice to haves that I didn't even realize I would have is my iPhone actually displays how much charge is left on the headphones as I'm using them. EDIT: IT DOES NOT DISPLAY HOW MUCH BATTERY IS LEFT, IT ALWAYS DISPLAYS 100%. NOT A DEAL BREAKER BUT IT WOULD'VE BEEN NICE TO HAVE.Now onto some of my gripes of the headphones. First thing I noticed is that the charging port is in a weird place on the inside earcup. Why? It makes it kind of weird to plug in a cable there and I can't figure out why they would want to do that. Another thing that kind of annoyed me-- the power button is located on the 'inside' of the right ear cup. I have to contort my right hand in a weird way to press the button with my thumb-- it just doesn't feel natural. I feel like a little bit of insight would've gone a long way if they just tested using the headphones for a little bit. There is also no way to disable voice commands-- my Sony headphones have them as well but you can disable them with their app which Amazon does not have. Which leads me to my next gripe which is a more nice-to-have than a necessary on headphones in this price range-- No EQ. Thankfully balance isn't the worst out of the box and I'm quite happy with the way they sound but offering the ability to change those would be nice.Would I recommend these headphones? It kind of depends. Really for the price they're not half bad and I've had good experiences using them around the house. I also have a bit of disposable income though, so I probably would've opted for (and have even opted for with my Sony's) higher end headphones with amenities like nice sound stages and active noise cancelling. But it's hard to go wrong with getting these

date_review: Reviewed in the United States on January 13, 2024
overview_text: Great Headphones, Flimsy Build Quality, Expensive Repair
comment: In June 2023 I was gifted these Sony WH1000XM4 headphones by my mother (the owner of this account). I wanted them because I noticed that I would get overwhelmed in loud environments. A friend of mine recommended them because of how good the noise canceling was and the pressure from the earpieces also helped with overstimulation.When I got these headphones, I loved them. They arrived quickly and the set up was easy. I wore them everyday and I took care of them. They were great for listening to music and they were great for keeping the outside world a little quieter when it got to be too loud.One day, in early December 2023 (a little less than 6 months after I had received the headphones) they broke. I was putting them on like normal and something snapped off and the right earpiece was left hanging by its wire.I was initially very upset and confused because I knew I had taken care of these headphones. I would store them properly, I would charge them, etc. and they just broke in my hands.I know that I’m still under warranty, so I call Sony Customer Support and they tell me that because the damage was “physical damage” they would not replace my headphones. My dad has the case escalated and they tell us the same thing.I call Customer Support again and they give me a number for the only authorized repair service in the United States. I call the number and it’s defunct, but it gives me a new number to call. I call that number and the AT&T jingle plays, the automated voice asks if I’m calling about a repair and I say yes. The system then gives me another number to call, the AT&T jingle plays again. The new automated voice asks if I’m trying to repair a receiver and I realize this is not what I’m looking for at all, so I hang up.I call Sony Customer Service again and after waiting on hold for about 20 minutes I tell them that the number they gave me doesn’t work and the associate gives me the website of the repair company that I learned is called United Radio at this point.I find United Radio’s contact and I email them telling them about what happened to my headphones and that I want them repaired. They tell me that the cost of the repair would be the part they need to use to repair the headphones + the labor cost ($90) + shipping. They also informed me that no fees would be waived even though I was under warranty because Sony would’ve just replaced the headphones if my problem was under warranty.I try looking for the part that would be needed to repair my hanging earpiece and I found it on a couple websites ranging from $15-$40, so I go ahead and and send my headphones to United Radio.About 2 weeks pass and I get a call from United Radio. The associate tells me that they found the issue and the part to fix the problem will cost $140 + the fixed $90 labor fee + shipping equaled to about $272. That’s pretty much what was paid for these headphones back in June and they were charging me for a more expensive part than what I had researched.I feel cheated by Sony. A $300 product should not break in 6 months and it should not cost the same amount to get them repaired because some flimsy piece of plastic broke. This product should have lasted years, not months.

Reviewed in the United States on December 25, 2023
overview_text: Full functionality requires monthly payments, but overall nice sound quality.
comment: TL;DR the headphones are nice but you need to pay monthly to get the full functionality of it, which dramatically impacts my review.When I first put these (or possibly the previous gen, I can't remember which but definitely a Sony WH series) on in Walmart when they were on display about 4 years ago, I wanted a set ever since. I finally made it happen this year in 2023, and I was blessed by the sweet sound of silence to the outside world, and I often just wear these without anything playing just to hear silence, as the active noise cancelling blocks out about 90% of my tinnitus and allows me to experience what I believe is true silence, which I love these for. You can link it to Google Assistant, or Alexa, or change the button to change the ambient sound mode on/off or noise cancelling on/off. To change settings and functionality of the buttons, you'll need to download their app and link the two together, there's no way to do it on the headphones themselves.These headphones are amazing for noise cancellation, battery longevity, and can fold up into a relatively compact size for portability. After using it for a while as wireless, It tried to plug it in using an aux cord and it just powers self off. Not sure if it's not compatible with aux input or if it's a user error, so I'm assuming it's only Bluetooth until I find out otherwise, but that's only a small issue. It folds up into a nice hardcase with zipper, and that's nice too. The headphones work great by themselves, but I have a bone to pick about the decision to make the optimum sound quality locked behind a paywall. Greed has eliminated the days of full functionality straight from the box, and it leaves a sour taste in my mouth, especially since this is relatively expensive, even when it is on sale. Of course you don't NEED to buy the subscription, and can get by just fine without it. However, I feel like the average person is adrift in the endless sea of 5.99/mo here, 9.99/mo there, and so on, and while the headphones are amazing even without the subscription, I am unable to overlook the lack of full functionality without a subscription to allow me to fully endorse this already expensive product.

date_review: Reviewed in the United States on August 25, 2023
overview_text: Headphones do not last more than 3 years of use
comment: I have used these headphones on a near daily basis, and they were good (not great) throughout its lifetime. Below, I've included my experience throughout my 3 years with these headphones before putting them in its grave.Sound quality - 3 stars- These are great headphones for daily music use, and you won't regret the purchase if this is the only thing you're after. However, when I compared them to Bose's 700, the sound quality seemed a bit worse. However, for those of us who aren't sound engineers, these are good enough. I'd highly recommend going to a store and trying them out before purchasing. These headphones are good for answering calls in a quiet place, I would not recommend taking calls outside if it's a little windy, inside a car while driving, or anywhere that is relatively noisy.Noise cancellation - 4 stars- I can't give these 5 stars because the technology isn't there yet for total noise cancellation and honestly, they should do us a service and call them limited frequency cancelling. First, for those of us not familiar with noise cancelling headphones, they will not cancel every sound. However, these work great when on an airplane and definitely worth the price if this is a big weighting factor in your decision. Moreover, these work well for office noise, it won't totally cancel your co-worker's conversation if they are close to you, but reduces it enough to make the experience a little better.Comfort - 3.5 stars- I think the cushion starts out fine then after about a year it'll start to noticeably wear down, flatten and become uncomfortable. Maybe not a big deal if you have a replacement handy.Control - 1.5 stars- The automatic voice notifications drives me nuts and it now I essentially take off the headphones before receiving those voice notifications. These notifications are the "power on," "bluetooth connected" etc.. There's no way to disable them, and Sony has remained quiet on this despite people calling for an option to disable the voice notification. The iPhone app is atrocious at times, it won't even load and sometimes you'll have to wait a while for it to connect to the headphones. The hand gestures are decent, and infrequently hit or miss with the swipes.Reliability - 2 stars- The headphones worked great the first year. The second year was good enough since the padding started to breakdown. In the third year, the headphones began to randomly disconnect from devices from time-to-time. Finally, I now experience a frequent and unbearable high pitch sound on the right earcup and the sound quality has been degraded. I can still hear fine on the left earcup, but I'd classify these headphones as not usable anymore. For the $300+ price I paid, this was not the best investment.TL;DR - If you want durable headphones, do not buy these. If you are going to buy these, I'd highly recommend trying them out in a store before committing.

These Sony WH-CH520’s sound the best, hands down (followed by the Creative Soundblaster 2). I did initially download the Sony app out of curiosity, and there’s plenty of presets to play with. You can opt for a bloated bass boost, or a crisper sound with more treble, and everything in between, but I was most interested in the 360 audio. The music sample in the app showcasing how it sounded was pretty impressive. However, I was disappointed to discover that 360 audio requires a paid subscription. No thanks.Also, considering the privacy aspect, and the possible impact the app could have on the WH-CH520’s battery life, I decided to delete it since the stock sound was plenty good enough for me. Speaking of battery life, I get about a month, maybe more, so no hassle about having to charge the headphones every few days, but then again, I can’t use the WH-CH520’s for hours on end like I was planning. More on that below.While the build quality is much better than any of the headphones I’ve owned previously, comfort and fit is another story. The clamping pressure on these is a little tight. After about 1.5 hours of wear, my outer ears start to feel discomfort, and after 2-plus hours, my ears are screaming at me to take these off. My ears get so irritated and raw from the tightness and from the fake leather rubbing against them, I can actually see redness on the cartilage. I used to wear my Creative Soundblaster 2 on-ears, which I no longer own, practically all day with no issues whatsoever, so the fact that I can’t wear these Sony’s for more than 2 hours sucks. When the pain becomes unbearable, I swap these out for my Nord Buds 2.Lastly, though I’m disappointed about the discomfort the Sony WH-CH520 cause me (others might not have this issue), and the fact that these will be relegated to a backup role, they do sound great, have easy controls, and sport an attractive design. Just wish these were over-ears instead.

comment: I bought these for a bargain price. My Sony MDR-XB650BTs kept breaking (and while I adore the sound on those they kept going up in price). Knowing Sony’s sound quality to be good, I looked for another pair of Sony bluetooth headphones and stumbled upon these for an incredible sub $50 bargain.I apologize in advance for the constant comparison to MDR-XB650BT in my review. I’m no headphone afficiando, but the only fully experienced reference point I have to compare these to are the MDR-XB650BT which I bought these to replace.MATERIALOn the WH-CH520, the material of the pads appear to be made of synthetic leather. The issue with this is that this material absorbs moisture (oils and sweat) and wears down the fabric over time causing pilling and eventually tearing of the fabric, leaving your ear pads with a spongy hernia.Unfortunately I wasn’t aware of this until only recently and had this happen to multiple MDR-XB650BT ear pads, but I took preventative measures for my WH-CH520 by purchasing a pair of silicone ear pad covers like another reviwer had mentioned to protect them from degrading.Despite the headphones being lightweight and made of plastic they feel sturdy at the same time. They feel less fragile than the MDR-XB650BT which is definitely a plus but I haven’t had them for long enough to talk about the build quality and how long you can expect them to last. By handling them I get this feeling they’re pretty durable. The only thing I find I might be concerned about over time is the swivel.FIT AND DESIGNI have a small head and these fit me fine. The headphones are worn on-ear. They’re a snug fit but can become uncomfortable after about an hour but that’s usually because I wear them tight but I can loosen them when I please. Because of how round the design is there’s a bit of space between my head and headband when it connects to the earpeices which can look kinda goofy (see pic) but it’s nothing major and has no bearing on what I’m looking for in headphones. The good news is because of this gap you can probably wear them comfortably with glasses. The actual ear pads a little small compared to other headphones.I really enjoy the design. The WH-CH520 are minimalist, streamlined, and the matte is charming.SOUND AND SOUND QUALITYBottom line: It’s good.In comparison to other cheaply priced headphones I’ve had the experiences of trying (but not owning myself), the sound quality is good. It’s not stellar but it’s definitely good for the price.One thing that bugs me is the depth of the sound dynamics. In the app, you’re able to adjust and set your own custom EQ settings but the sound quality is slightly boxy or stuffy. I’ve tried a ton of different settings adjustments in the app’s equalizer with it and I experiment with different songs to see which settings holds up between songs, but there’s still a baseline emphasis on lower-mid frequencies in this sound of these.The EQ setting that I find sounds best ends up just being the flat default with bass turned up and 400Hz slightly cut. I do wish the equalizer options in the app were more granular.Overall I find that the WH-CH520 has less of a dynamic range than the MDR-XB650BT. An analogy to this are “blackest blacks” and “whitest whites” on a screen with a dynamic range monitor. In terms of sound this is loudness and quietness in instruments which create a feeling of depth in the music. With the WH-CH520 the actual balance of the volume of the instruments are a bit muddled compared to the MDR-XB650BT.Their noise isolation leaves something to be desired but it’s better than nothing.It’s not the end of the world and I would still recommend these for the price. When you can adjust it right to work around the low-mid oddity it’s actually pretty good.Also, everyone hears things differently and I’m quite sensitive to subleties in sound so take what I’m saying with a grain of salt if you’re not as sensitive.BATTERY LIFEI haven’t even charged them out of the box yet after using them nearly every day and they’re only at 50% battery life. Phenomenal. That’s all there really is to say.FEATURESThere’s a minor feature of these headphones that bug me. At least pairing it with my iPhone, the volume control on these is tied directly to the volume of your phone. If you click the volume up button on the headset, that’s going to use your phone’s volume. The MDR-XB650BT has a separate sound adjustment from your device. Unlike the MDR-XB650BT, with the WH-CH520 you can’t further increase the volume on your headset if the volume of the song on your phone is a tad quiet. This takes away a bit of listener flexibility.As other people have stated, the buttons are difficult to distinguish by finger.The MDR-XB650BT that I’m used to has a button that sticks out between the volume controls where you can press it inward to pause/resume the music or flick the button forward or backward to change the song in a playlist.The WH-CH520’s buttons are flat which makes it harder to distinguish and it does not have that controllability from the headset. You can pause and resume your music with the middle button (which you might mistake for the volume buttons unfortunately) but if you want to change your song to the next or previous, you’ll have to do it on your device.Despite all the negative things I have said, these points are all relative. In a vacuum, these headphones are great for the price especially if you just need a set of headphones that can get the job done while sounding pretty good. You’re probably gonna get more than you expect for the price.

If you care about noise cancellation and noise insulation (others not being able to hear what you're listening to) these aren't for you. But if you don't mind those things everything else is perfect.Notably my favorite part about these is the battery life. I've left them on for days and the battery only goes down like 25% max. The battery lasted me two weeks after the first charge when I bought them! Super good battery life. Also, the exterior design is minimalistic and fashionable. There's room to decorate with stickers if you wanna get creative with the design too. I even kind of like that these aren't noise cancelation headphones because I wear them in public spaces where I need to be aware of my surroundings, like the gym, so they're good for that.The ear pads are soft enough to not hurt when you wear it for too long, but I do have smaller ears. If you have bigger ears these may hurt after an hour or two. The headphones are also nicely adjustable to fit the desired size/length. It's worth a mention that I also use these for gaming and in-game calling, and the audio input and output are both great, so if you need a wireless mic, go get these headphones.Overall, no regrets in buying these! It's a good quality product.

comment: For a long time I just used the medium price range Sony earbuds. The best tended to be Sony WI-C200 or similar. Finally I decided to spend twice as much for Beats Flex. I'd been curious about the Beats brand since Dre started it years ago. I was pretty excited to get them but a bit bewildered by what I got.The sound of the flex is only maybe a little bit better than the Sony, but it also lacks some mids and a lot of the highs. And the flex are quieter! I think the extra power is probably going to the bass(?), which isn't even that impressive honestly. I will say though that the flex frequency range is probably slightly more comfortable to the ears when listened for long periods of time. Still I think I kinda like the Sony sound better. For anytime punky or with heavy guitars the Flex sounds too EQ scooped and hollow. For podcasts and talk the Sonys are easier to hear when in noisy places.BATTERY: But what I'm fully confused by is how terrible the flex battery is. It doesn't last even half as much as the Sony. With my Sony headphones I would listen some days, all day, and never run out of battery. I've run out of battery with the flex many times and it comes quick. When you turn on the Sony it tells you approximately how much battery power you have left! It will also warn you to plug it in when the battery power gets below a certain point. FLEX doesn't do any of that! WTF?!? The flex doesn't even tell you that it's turned on when you turn it on, it only makes a sound once you connect to bluetooth. Then it just dies with no warning. Flex feels dumbed down and dysfunctional.I also like the Sony controls a little better, though some people might find them chunky.CALLS: whereas the Sony is great for phone calls, people constantly tell me something's going on and my voice is muffled and such with the flex. It probably has something to do with the mic placement. You can hear a lot of rubbing and wrestling of the device against your body and clothes with the flex, whereas with the Sony people say my voice is clear.Neither are rated well for water, so be careful in the rain.I doubt I will be buying Flex again. I might try something higher end than the Sony headphones I usually get, but unless there's improvements, I wouldn't buy Flex again.Biggest Con: dismal Battery life.Con: doesn't tell you battery level (doesn't show up in Bluetooth controls either).Con: lower volume (quieter) than my Sony earbuds.Con: doesn't handle calls well. date_review: Reviewed in the United States on February 20, 2024
comment: These are hands-down the worst wireless earbuds I’ve ever used. I’m fortunate that I received these as a gift two months ago and didn’t spend a penny. I’ve owned dollar-store headphones with better life-span, usability, and connectivity than these. I wanted to take this chance to warn anyone else from buying these to instead consider literally any other option.Let’s start with the case. Like all wireless earbuds, you’re meant to carry these in your pocket. Any sane individual would expect it not to matter the orientation they sit for the earbuds to be charged by the case. But oh no, not these. Unless the case is sitting perfectly upright, the contact leads do not always connect and your earbuds are always out of juice. I have to make sure when I get home to sit them perfectly upright. And don’t bother charging the case unless you want them to accidentally connect to your phone. The charging port is on the bottom and you have to tilt it slightly. I have to be surgical with how I handle the case since the earbuds bounce around ever so slightly. Which leads me to my next issue with the case…You’d think the headphones would disconnect if placed inside the case and the lid is closed. NOPE! After I set the case perfectly upright, I have to raise and drop each earbud individually for them to hopefully disconnect. This takes 2 or 3 tries on each earbud. If I don’t do this carefully, one or both earbuds remain connected or trying to pair until they eventually run out of their short battery life. Sometimes I’ve given up and restored to manually disconnecting from my phone to let the things die. I frequently hear music playing out of my case. At least it resumes the last thing I was playing.As of writing this review, my left earbud is still dead because it stopped charging in the case. None of my tricks to lift and drop the earbud have worked. I’ve tried cleaning out the case of any dust or lint, making sure the contact leads are clean but no dice. The thing is only two months old! And you don’t get any noise cancelling from a dead earbud.The battery life is perfectly mediocre. They advertise 6 hours but it’s more like 4, and unless you’re using them for all that time straight you really won’t run into issues. So don’t bother using them at work. The case charges decently quick which is the only silver lining.Let’s talk about the software. Every time I pop into the app, even with the headphones paired, one of two things happen: I see two entries for the same pair of headphones or nothing at all. For the first 20 seconds after the app opens, you can’t tap on either of the two entries. Then it either corrects itself or you have to forget the Bluetooth device and repair again. If the entry doesn’t appear, you gain muscle memory for going into Bluetooth settings to reset and repair. I’ve only owned these since the end of December and had to reset the pairing three times! That’s something I’ve maybe had to do once or twice with every single other Bluetooth device I’ve owned combined.The range is just short enough that the earbuds will occasionally desync. When the left one was still working, it would usually fall a split second behind the right one. And every few minutes the music would cut out entirely for 5-10 seconds. I’ve gotten used to holding my phone in my hands during a run because I can’t keep the phone down in my pockets without disconnection issues.The settings are cool, the controls are customizable, but you can find that in every other product for this price point. This one has just been disappointment after disappointment and I’ve reached the point of getting frustrated enough to leave this review.

comment: I got these earbuds to replace a pair of Apple AirPods Pro 2nd Gen, ONE of which is lost (naturally) and doesn’t show up on FindMy because it’s out of power. Didn’t want (can’t afford) to spend $300 to replace them…Soooo … I chose these as replacements. The earbuds arrived when promised, well packaged, looked fine. Now for the details:It’s kind of annoying to have to download JBL’s app, but at least it’s free. The earbuds themselves have great sound quality, and the mic picked up my voice OK when I had to take a call in a crowded area and wanted to speak softly. Those are the pros.The cons, for my particular situation and tastes: I chose these buds for the noise cancellation feature, and guess what? The tips that support that feature are not on the buds when they arrive. The installation diagram was confusing to this late Boomer, and I didn’t want to ruin the things, but I finally figured out that … Yes, you have to pull off the tip which looks as though it’s part of the bud in order to install the noise canceling tip.That problem solved, I moved on to pairing, which went OK, although I had to do some setup both in the app and my iPhone Settings. Annoying, but acceptable.The real problem with these earbuds is this: Whenever I touch a bud to adjust the fit, or replace it after it falls out (which seemed to happen more frequently than with my AirPods), it messes up the playing of my podcast or YouTube video. Sometimes it arouses Siri. Once I get the bud(s) seated firmly again, it will sometimes play some random thing that I never heard before and don’t want to hear again. Worst of all, several times I had to re-pair the buds through Bluetooth. I attribute this issue to the earbud controls. I don’t really want to use on-bud controls. When someone calls, Siri says: “Call from Xyxyxy. Answer it?” And I can tell her yes or no or whatever. I never had to re-pair my AirPods.Someone will probably tell me there’s a way to configure the JBL app and/or my iPhone Settings to eliminate this problem, but I don’t have the patience to deal with all that stuff. These buds are going back to JBL and I am ordering a replacement pair of AirPods Pro — Used - Like New — from a seller with good ratings at a decent price point and delivery date.Overall, these earbuds are great quality for the price, and would probably be perfect for someone who actually wants and uses the earbud controls (unlike me), someone interested in music streaming or video gaming. I hope some other buyer will give them a happy home. 😸

comment: So these are going to be inevitably compared to Apple Airpods, right?When making comparisons, the JBL buds are harder to get out of their case, due to the weird geometry of the case, and my fingers keep inadvertently snapping the case shut when I try to take the earbuds out. I haven't found someone willing to have a six hour phone call with me, but I would imagine that whether or not noise cancelling is engaged, these'll last a while.In my personal opinion, the Airpods are a much better product, all things considered. overview_text: A solid alternative to pricier buds--just beware of the charging
comment: I bought my original pair of these about two years ago, and they still work, but the battery life isn't as long as it used to be, so I took advantage of holiday sales to buy a new version. There's some upgrades in the app for these since the prior version that increase the customization of them, but the one issue still remains: the charging consistency.The bottom of the earbud and the posts inside the case are very delicate, and if you don't drop your buds in precisely, you may come back later to find they're dead because they didn't charge. One might charge and the other one doesn't. Sometimes there's loss of conductivity, which is remedied by using the lead end of a pencil to gently work around the bottom conductors on the earbud and the eraser on the posts inside the case. It's literally in the official instructions for their earbuds.With that said, if you get them on sale they're an excellent deal overall. Call quality is great, noise cancellation and pass-through audio work as advertised, and the touch gestures are easy to work with. Music comes through with impressive clarity, and I hear things in songs that I never noticed before due to the custom equalizer.It'd be five stars if they change how these charge.

overview_text: Good sound quality, medium comfort, and confusing controls.
comment: I've been a user of those old school wired earbuds for a long, long time and I'm just starting to dip my toes into the wireless bluetooth market.  I've owned a different cheaper pair of bluetooth earbuds in the $30 price range that I've been using for about the past year, but those were for sound only (no call functionality) and the sound quality for music is not great.  They lacked bass and music just didn't sound pure.  I will give them credit though, the part that went into the ear is comfortable and the controls are reliable and intuitive.Fast forward to these JBL earbuds.  The sound quality difference is immediately apparent.  I'm really happy with the sound quality on these earbuds for music which is what I use earbuds for most.  There's nice bass and the music is clear.  It's night and day compared to my $30 earbuds.  I'm a little indifferent towards them as far as call quality is concerned.  The people I talk to regularly tell me that they hear wind or that it's difficult to hear me if I'm outside.  If I'm inside and in a quiet environment they work well, but they aren't a substitute for just holding the phone up to your head if you're after max sound quality as far as I'm concerned.  I've been able to hear people ok on my end with them, but they're a little quieter than I'd like.Comfort wise, these aren't as comfortable as my $30 bluetooth earbuds or my old wired earbuds.  The plastic heads seem pretty standard size and do fit into my ears, but I don't know why people want such big bulbous plastic knobs in their ears when they could just have the smaller silicone part.  Maybe it's just me?  The old school little pea sized round silicone flexible caps are comfortable - what's with the hard plastic balls on higher end earbuds these days?  I don't think this is an issue specific to these earbuds, but I don't understand why people would prefer this style.  They're not as comfortable, they don't fit snugly, they don't create as nice of a seal in your ear to block out other noise, etc.Lastly, my biggest gripe with these is something that is probably learnable or fixable with just using them more over time, but the controls are wonky at best.  There aren't any actual buttons on them, but tapping on them does "do things".  It's a learning curve.  The instructions are confusing at best about this too.  Also, if I'm using them in both ears while listening to music and then I take a call but only want one earbud in, I will put one back in the case, but then I've had trouble reconnecting music to both earbuds once I'm done with my call.Overall I think I'm going to generously give these 4 stars for now and chalk the controls up to user error and just being new to understanding how the tapping system works.  If I still struggle with the controls down the road, I think they're more of a 3 star item for me.

date_review: Reviewed in the United States on September 5, 2023
overview_text: Ridiculous bass can't compensate for sub-average features
comment: tl;dr The sound is average if the bass slider is kept to a minimum. Otherwise, they're uncomfortable, heavy, with no ANC, no LDAC, no multi-point connectivity, and they wobble if you move your head to the music.Before we begin, ears are funny things and any review of headphones or earbuds is purely subjective. To cut down on variables I use the same sound sources and test tracks for all my reviews, but what sounds great to me might not sound as good to you.I've never owned a Skullcandy product before, and was looking for some new over ear headphones to replace my venerable Sony MDR V600 so thought I'd give these a try. When they arrived there was a USB-C charging cable in a Skullcandy branded box along with the USB-C charging cable that came included in the box with the headphones. No idea why, but hey it is always good to have a spare cable on hand.In the box itself I found the headphones in an cloth bag. Unlike many headphone manufacturers Skullcandy aren't providing a padded case, even at this premium price point. There is a short 3.5mm cable but be warned it is designed for cellphone/microphone usage so if you want to plug them in to any audio equipment that uses a traditional 3.5mm stereo jack they won't work. There is also the provided USB-C charging cable.Putting them on I instantly noticed that they are heavy on my head. They adjust well and I was able to get a good seal on my ears over my big head, but the padding over the crown of my head pressed uncomfortably, becoming painful before the end of an album. The weight is evenly balanced, but is enough to feel like a pull on the top of your head and ears. worse still, they are heavy enough to wobble if you move your head to the music, an instant issue for bassheads!Connecting them to my phone was a straightforward pairing experience, but they lack the latest Bluetooth codec features so do not support aptX or LDAC for audiophile listening. They also do not support multipoint connectivity for those who want to use their laptop, phone, and console with them. All of the above are features I've come to enjoy on my daily earbuds, so missing them here felt like a big step back especially at the similar price point.I installed the Skullcandy App, which initially ahd some problems accessing the headphones. It could detect them but not connect. Installing the app is a must in my opinion as without it you only have a single band EQ in the form of the bass slider on the left headphone. However, it lurches from "a bit of bass" to "comically shaking the headphones" in the smallest of movements. With the app you get three EQ modes; Music, Podcast, and Movie. You also have the ability to create a custom profile based upon a brief test in which a series of tones are played at differing volumes to each ear and you respond as to whether you hear them. I used the headphones both without the app, with the app but without a custom profile, and with a custom profile having taken the audio test and didn't notice any significant difference across the experiences.Listening to my audio test track playlist nothing sounded "bad" as long I kept the bass slider in at almost zero. Turning up the bass rapidly drowns out the mid-bass, and the mid range in a muddy throb of bass. I explored my whole music catalog for anything that sounded worth listening to above the 50% mark on the slider, and couldn't find a thing, from huge bass drops, to epic electronic, to huge orchestras, nothing survived the crushing bass of the Skullcandy Crusher Evo. Keeping the slider in check the sound is average. The soundstage seems very cramped, with everything trapped in the closed back headphones. The sound also lacked the warmth and depth that I am used to from my old Sonys.At this price point I expected a lot more from the Skullcandy Crusher Evo. The lack of features such as Active Noise Canceling, and multi-point connectivity, and even a decent case put them at a big disadvantage in the competitive premium headphone space. This is made worse by the average sound, and lack of support for high quality streaming codecs. Add to all that the uncomfortable fit and these are definitely not the headphones I'd choose to take with me every day. So I'll give them 3 out of 5, they work but there are better options out there.

comment: I now believe the earphone jack in my computer case was bad.  I have since plugged this set into the headphone jack of the external speaker, and it works fine.  As far as being careful not to jerk it-- well, I've jerked it several times.  I do take extra precaution of passing the cable under my keyboard or mousepad for extra strain relief, but I have jerked it so hard it moved both the keyboard and the speaker!!  I finally messed up the "rachet sizing" in the headband, but the phones still fit and stay on my ears and the sound is still good.  Turns out to be very well worth the price!Product is described as lightweight, as it should be.  Actually, that's one of the things I like about it.  And for a lightweight on-the-ear headphone, the sound is not bad.  For the money, I still think this is a good buy, and I got free shipping!However, you must take care to not jerk the cord because it simply won't handle the stress.  It seems --as with most headphones -- the weak point is at the L-shaped connector that plugs into the jack.  I use mine on the computer, and I inadvertently jerked the cord two different times-- and that caused a break in the cord where it enters the L-shaped plug.  If I turn the plug so the cord hangs down (or some times a little sideways) it still works, but I suspect it will not be long before it won't work at all.  So, it's a good buy, but be aware of this issue.

overview_text: Decent, but not an upgrade from my $100 headset.
comment: I am using a G6 DAC with this and the default sound without any profiles used, etc.. sounds a bit muffled. Voices don't sound like they would in real life ( It helps to record audio from someone you know and play it back to help calibrate ).With my previous headset, I had to tune it quite a lot and get it sounding good but the sound stage on those aren't as good as this. In games you can accurately pick out locations pretty easily but I still have to do more testing to see if it justifies paying this much, especially because voices sound off, music sounds muffled, etc..Treble on these headsets is very sharp, similar to my previous headset ( which I tuned down ) but very slightly less. It is ear-piercing and hurts.I don't know why noise-cancellation is an option as these are open-back and no mic.The open-back design is nice as it expands the sound-stage.The headset is about half the weight of my previous headset so that is a plus, however the major flaw is how it sits on the head. You want the clamping force to have the pillows apply even force all the way around your ears, but these are more /o o\ rather than \o o/ or |o o| which causes sound to escape out the bottom and actually hurts the sound stage. When moving my ears I can improve the sound quality a decent amount, but holding those muscles in that position is difficult for long periods. I loosened the headband so much that the headband barely touches the top of my head to make it somewhat fit but it doesn't feel secure and the cushions still don't fit right or help the sound quality.Because this is made of plastic I can't simply adjust the headband to make it fit without breaking them.I'm giving this 3 of 5 because of the sound stage, the decent sound quality ( when I move my ears ), how lightweight they are, the oversized area for your ears and the fact that it has a removable cable.I am docking 2 points because these don't quite fit, and the sound is quite muffled even with moving my ears. I shouldn't need to use an equalizer for this headset; however, when tuning it the sound quality can be improved but moving my ears kills it and because it doesn't sit quite right it is easy to change how the sound enters the ear and ruining the immersion. The other issue is this doesn't have a removable cable on both ears, and I've owned many headsets and they typically fail when the internal cable going through the headband wears out as I tend to baby my headsets but just the motion of putting them on and taking them off causes rubbing.I am currently looking for an alternative and will likely be returning these soon, but I'm going to see if there is anything I can do to help with the issues I've had.

overview_text: Loosens over time and gets better, at first painful with glasses. Sounds great.
comment: The first thing you'll notice is that they're *very* tight on your head. For two days, I had a headache because it would press my glasses into my temporal lobe. I solved this by placing them over the cardboard box they came with for two nights, and they have been incredibly comfortable since. There is a bump in the back of each ear cup that bothered me at first, it would brush against my Ferengi lobes. I got used to this over time, and it no longer bothers me. If you have them positioned properly (I did not at first) you won't notice the bumps.I took off a star for build quality, even though I still think they're quite good. The plastic feels quite durable. They have survived the airport, I made sure to pack them carefully between clothes, and a few drops from when my dog snags the cord. No visible damage after a month.Now for the complaints: the padding on the headband seems to be sightly raised away from the plastic (picture attached). This makes sense though, as there seems to be a compliant mechanism inside that allows the plastic to be stretched. Nevertheless, what I don't like is the fact that I can clearly see adhesive where the overlap occurs.The second complaint is that the left and right swivels feel different. I notice that the right is more loose. When I place them on my head, because the right has less resistance, the do not swivel to the same degree and I have to manually adjust them. No normal person would ever notice this though.As for sound: the high impedance but also high sensitivity make this easy to drive with a laptop or smartphone. I do think it is worth finding something of quality to drive these, because of the high sensitivity.Normally it accentuates the high-middle frequencies, but it is clear all around. It is pleasant for listening, but high frequencies can sometimes get irritating.It sounds excellent by itself, but I went the extra mile. I use this with and Qudelix 5K. Using that little DAC-Amp significantly cleans up the audio signal and allows these headphones to truly shine.Do note that the sensitivity on the box says 110 dBSPL/V while software is going to ask for dBSPL/mW. That measurement is going to be 100.78 dBSPL/mV, do some research on this to verify my calculation. Impedance is 120 ohms.Since I have the Qudelix, I started playing with the parametric equalizer. I discovered these headphones can sound even better and more accurate than they do from the factory. I ended up with a customized version of Oratory1990's parametric settings for the Harmon target. I changed some of the gain levels in the upper-mids and highs to bring the headphones closer to the way they sound from factory, but to reduce the irritation and allow me to listen comfortably for longer. The preset I used definitely helps with the bass, and I left that alone.Don't get these if you're a basshead. That is not what they are meant for. The bass is clear and accurate, and just boomy enough for me.Imaging is, I would say, great, but the Philips SHP9500 beats them by a small margin. When playing video games, you can hear things in front, above, and behind you, but other headphones may be better.Overall, these are a great general-purpose pair of headphones. Combined with the Ablet Boom Microphone, they're great for gaming, and with a Qudelix 5K, they're great for music. Highly recommend. Would have been 5 stars if not for the visible glue on the headband and the sloppy swivel on the right ear cup.

date_review: Reviewed in the United States on March 22, 2023
overview_text: Among the highest sound quality headphones in its price range
comment: The Sennheiser HD 560S are a clear and revealing pair of headphones. On my other headphones and IEMs, when I apply EQ (Oratory1990 results from AutoEQ on GitHub) the effect is immediately apparent, the music seems to have greater clarity. I would liken it to the feeling of clear breathing after one has blown one's nose when waking up with clogged sinuses. The HD 560S, on my system, don't seem to need any EQ for greater clarity. You can of course EQ them to taste, specifically those who want more bass. The HD 560S have bass that go deep and sound good but they aren't boosted so those wanting a bass heavy tuning/signature may want to EQ by boosting the lows (or cutting the mids and highs depending on your approach to EQ). I find the HD 560S to be an excellent sounding pair of headphones. I use them a lot but not exclusively since I do have other headphones I also enjoy. Those looking to try a pair with that clear, revealing, linear sound should give these a listen.I generally use headphones with an amp but I've also used the the HD 560S with my Sony Xperia mobile phone and they aren't hard to drive. I have the volume at about 60% on the phone at my preferred listening level. The 560S's clarity helps here, I don't need to have the volume so high in order to hear the details I want from the music. Though compared to my other current headphones these do need the most amplification, but not by a lot. On a song that I would have my headphone amp's volume knob set at 10:30 for the Sony MDR-1AM2 or at 12:30 for the Philips Fidelio X2HR, the amp would be at 1:00 for the HD 560S (I try to volume match for vocals when listening to music).The HD 560S are comfortable enough for me to wear for extended periods. I do feel the clamping force on the sides of the head, surrounding the ear, but I don't find the pressure to be uncomfortable. The pads are large enough to fully go around the ear and deep enough so the drivers don't come into contact with the ear so no pressure is put on the ear itself. There is a little protrusion inside the cups that might touch the ears depending on how forward or back you have the headphones. I don't find them bothersome and in fact I use them to set the headphones consistently on my head by having them just barely touch the rear edge of my ears.However, these Sennheisers aren't a perfect set. For my purposes the cable is rather long. I use these at my desktop so a shorter cable would be better for me but others might be fine with the longer cable. They are open back in design so there is some sound leakage which might be an issue if you listen loud and share the room with others. Of course their open back nature is part of what gives them a less boxed in sound than the closed backed alternatives.I did encounter an issue that was easily fixed in my case. Out of the box I seemed to hear a channel imbalance. This was disappointing at first but  I also noticed that the left and right ear pads of my set were not equally soft. I then swapped the left and right ear pads and the imbalance wasn't there anymore. I'm now perfectly happy with my pair and can recommend them for their sonic qualities but buyers should be aware of possible issues. I have had other Sennheiser headphones over the years and this is the first such issue I've had with them.The build quality is good but there are less expensive headphones that have equal or better construction. At this price ($199 when purchased, it's cheaper now) it would have been nice to have extra cables and a pouch. I got my MDR-1AM2 at a similar price and it has a more premium/luxurious feel, and includes two different cables (including balanced, since the HD 560S is wired for balanced it should have come with such a cable) and has a carrying pouch. The X2HR was about $50 less and feels like a more substantial set. Each of these headphones have different sound signatures and are good for diffent use cases but even though the HD 560S has really good sound (arguably better than others if that's the sound you're after) it doesn't deliver the best value overall. Because of that (as well as the issue I encountered above) I can only rate these headphones at 4 stars. If, however, sound is all you care about then I could maybe give them 5 stars since I do enjoy using them quite a lot.

overview_text: Analytical, neutral sound, average build, easy to drive.
comment: I have previously owned the HD 600, 650, and the Phillips Fidelio X1.The Sennheiser 560s are very neutral in tonal presentation. They have better bass extension than the 600 series, and a bit more presence in the lower treble region. This adds some air which helps with detail retrieval and separation. The soundstage is larger than the 600 series as well, though still not class leading, even within its price bracket.The mid range is, as expected, organic and well presented. They do not have the thick "veil" characteristic of the 600 series, and as a result the sound feels a bit thinner, though by no means anemic.I would say it's a trade off:The 600s are very intimate and elegant, working particularly well with small ensembles, chamber music, or with music that emphasizes vocals or acoustic instruments. The lushness of the mids, and the lack of broad separation or soundstage make them unfit for orchestral music that involves many elements as these get muffled, for music that rewards spatial immersion, or for music that benefits from strong bass presence or treble energy. They are not analytical headphones, but beautifully natural or 'musical'.The 560s are in contrast much more analytical: because they don't add the characteristic veil and add some energy up top and to the bottom frequency, they reveal more detail, separate better, but as a result are more dependent on the quality of the source. If the recording or source is flawed, these will make it evident, so they can be very picky, as opposed to the 600s which smoothen everything. The upshot, as I mentioned, is that these will also allow you to position and separate instruments better, and notice details in the upper and lower regions better. They are not V-shaped by any stretch of the imagination; they are very tonally balanced.The bigger downshot is their analytical nature means that they feel a bit cold and unexciting: they don't have much in the way of dynamic slam on the bass, the mids don't have that natural timbre of the 600s, and the upper range is controlled but lack the sparkle or airiness of more V-shaped efforts. In contrast, the 560s are reasonably expansive in relation to the intimate 600 series, but I still wouldn't recommend these for music requiring spatial openness, or for music that requires exceptional separation-imaging capabilities. If you listen to orchestral music that is busy or music involve too many instruments, this will still come across a bit muffled together.With regard to drivability, these are very efficient and generally will get loud enough.  No distortion or sibilance. I have tested them with a small Aune amp/dac with marginal benefits.Overall, I think these are good headphones for analytical listening more than musical enjoyment. Their neutrality might appear to make them a jack-of-all trades, but they lack the broad soundstage, dynamics, and lushness that other headphones offer. Finally, with regard to comfort, they are a bit clamped, so if you have a big head, beware. They do get more relaxed with time.SUMMARY:Pros: Neutral sound that works for analytical listening and studio work. Easy to drive, balanced.Cons: Revealing of bad sources, a bit cold and sterile, still unexceptional soundstage and separation, lack of dynamics at the ends, lacking the natural timbre of the 600 series.

The Sennheieser 439s sounded better for music, but just felt like something that I could not describe was missing.This year, I decided I wanted to try a step up in headphone quality and get something at least at the bottom end of audiophile/reference grade headphones.  I narrowed my choices down the The Sennheiser HD 560, Sennheiser 6XX, Beyer Dynamic DT 770, and the AGK 371 (all in the 150-250 price range).  I probably would have been quite happy with any of those four options, but in the end, I watched a lot of reviews and trusted my gut to go with the HD 560 (I wanted to experience a better sound stage with a close to neutral tuning).So far, I am very happy with my choice.  Pretty much everything I have listened to on these sounds at least a little better, but in particular, Folk (Faun, Omnia, Blackmore's Night etc), Industrial (Rammstein), and electronic (VNV Nation and L'ame Immortelle) were even more of an improvement than I expected to experience.  Even some traditional metal (Jusdas Priest and Iron Maiden in particular) feel like I'm experiencing their old material in a new way (probably hearing bits the old headphones were just not good enough to pick up).My only complaint is that they now come with a 1.8M cord rather than the 3M cord, so that limits me to using them with my PC for now (I have ordered a 3M replacement cord direct from Sennheiser and look forward to being able to enjoy them in my living room after that).  The above impressions are all from my PC with no Amp or Dac - once I get a longer cord, I will be able to test how much difference an Amp/Dac makes, but even without that I can still comfortable recommend these.

If you are looking for gaming headphones, I much prefer my Steelseries Arctis 5 over these. In terms of comfort, they aren't too impressive, but the lightweight design means that you will likely not get fatigued by wearing them. Also, if you don't have an amp, you need one. These require 150 ohms to be powered correctly, so don't just plug them into a laptop. FiiO makes a cheap DAC/amp combo for only $75 that can power these perfectly fine. If you're getting into high-end listening, or just want a pair of great headphones for under 200, this is really the best option, but once again, if you like a bit more bass, I have to recommend the Meze 99 Neos. They are punchy and provide such a clear high-end, but can form a bit of a v-shape and bass intrusion can be a problem with some songs.

overview_text: Amazing sound with a few annoyances
comment: First off, the sound. These have a very flat frequency response, meaning that the headphones do not really "color" the sound much. The soundstage is not very wide and the imaging isn't perfect, but they have a good amount of detail for the price. I quite like this sound signature, but if you're used to "fun" sounding headphones, you might want to look elsewhere.Sound quality is easily 5 stars for me at $200. Comfort is very good too, given the very light materials used and the comfortable, huge pads. The pads are so deep that my ears barely touch a small bump on the back inside of the cups, and the open back design keeps my ears from getting very hot.Now the not so great stuff. While the materials are good for making the headphones light, they don't inspire much confidence in the build. The headphones themselves feel cheap. Not so much that they feel like they are just going to break, but they really don't feel like quality headphones. Aside from the thin metal grill on the sides of the earcups, they are completely plastic. At least its not any of that awful shiny stuff. 1 star off quality for the construction.Now we get to the cable. The cable is garbage. It feels cheap, has an uncommon locking end that hooks up to the headphones, and is way too long for normal desktop use. Also, for some reason, they decided that instead of giving you a cable with a 3.5 mm end and a screw-on 1/4 inch adapter, they give you a 1/4 inch cable with a big 3.5 mm adapter. I don't understand why they decided to go that direction. Maybe less adapters means better sound? I sure can't hear a difference. Thankfully replacements are cheap and because this uses the same cable as other 500 series headphones, better cables are already available here on amazon.A few final notes. In case you aren't aware, these being open backed means that sound leaks like crazy. Anyone in the same room as you is going to be able to hear what you are listening to if you have them at even just a reasonable listening volume. This also means you hear everything going on around you, so a quite room is pretty necessary. They are pretty easy to drive and can run off my MacBook's built in headphone jack just fine. I do seem to get slightly better sound out of my dedicated amp and dac, but volume wise a phone could probably power these just fine. That is, if your phone even still has a headphone jack.

date_review: Reviewed in the United States on February 17, 2021
overview_text: Excellent sound quality but comfort is just okay
comment: Let me preface this by saying this is my third pair of Sennheiser headphones - first the HD58x, then the PC38x, and now these. I will also add that I have an extremely large head, so comfort is sadly hard to come by for me. Having said that, I find these to be more than adequate in terms of comfort and the sound quality is just excellent.I won't linger too long on sound quality as you can find a lot of reviews, especially from audiophile types on YouTube, that will provide much better information than I could. It's very clear, very detailed, very neutral (flat frequency response), and the imaging is excellent. It favors music in that the sound stage is sort of in front of you as opposed to all around you, so if you play a lot of first person games, the PC38x is a better choice. But if you primarily listen to music and play 2D games, these are the overall better choice. The only thing I will disagree with people on is the bass. Some people say it's lacking compared to the HD58x or PC38x and that's simply not true. Frequency response charts back me up on that. I think what people are hearing is that there's more high end, so they turn it down a bit and thus the bass "feels" lower even though it's really not. I don't find it to be lacking at all compared to either of those; in fact, I feel like it might even have a tad more bass than those.In terms of comfort, these are not the most comfortable headphones I own but I can easily wear them for hours at a time with no issues. Like most Sennheisers, the clamp force is a bit much at first, but they break in over time. I gave up on the HD58x not because of clamp force but because the headband simply doesn't stretch flat/wide enough to fit my big head comfortably. The HD560s, by comparison, use what appears to be the exact same headband as on the PC38x, which I find to be much more comfortable overall. These also have deeper ear cups than the HD58x, though not quite as deep as the PC38x, so while my ears do touch the sides just a bit, it's not uncomfortable. My main gripe is how the headband attaches to the ear cups. As with most Sennheisers, the bottom of the ear cups can swivel out but not in. When you have a big head like I do, that means that you don't get quite enough inward swivel out of these because the headband is stretched out too wide. For most people, this won't be an issue, but I'd really love to see Sennheiser change that in the future. Otherwise, this is the most comfortable pair of Sennheisers I have owned.Finally, the cable. It is not a bad cable, though some my complain about the proprietary locking mechanism it has, but really I just don't like that it terminates in a 1/4" plug. On the one hand, I primarily use these in conjunction with an audio interface, so it's actually perfect that it has a 1/4" plug. On the other hand, if I want to use them with my phone, I have to use the clunky adapter cable that's included. I'd have much rather they include, or at least make available, a full cable that terminates in a 3.5 mm plug instead. A small complaint, but one worth considering if you don't have a bunch of audiophile or studio gear to use these with.Overall, a really great pair of headphones with excellent sound, great build quality, and reasonable comfort.

comment: These are outstanding headphones at any price, and an unbelievable value at their typical ~$150 street price. I'm a recovering headphone addict and these have been good enough to help me stay sober. I think if your budget is up to $300 and you don't want to fuss around with amps and DACs and other gear considerations, these are probably the best "plug 'em into anything" headphones I've ever owned. They're light, they're comfortable for average-sized heads (though see more below), and they sound great playing any content from any source.Highlights:- Value: I've owned a lot of headphones (including perennial darlings like the HD600+650 and Audio-Technica ATX-M50 and higher-end stuff like the Audeze LCD-X and Focal Clear) and honestly, the headphone world is a perfect case study for the Law of Diminishing Returns. In other words, you can spend $150 on the 560S and get 75% of the sound quality that's even possible, or spend $1500 to get to like 85%. For most people, this is the sane stopping point.- Weight: the all-plastic build lets these float on your head at 280g (9.9 oz). For comparison, the Hifiman Sundara (another highly regarded pair of <$300 headphones) weighs 379g (13.4 oz). Three ounces may not sound like much, but over the course of hours, you really feel every ounce that's sitting on your head.- Easy to drive: I use these plugged directly into a PS5 controller and they get plenty loud at roughly 50-60% volume. I've tried them with different combinations of amps and DACs as well, but such gadgets are totally unnecessary to get the most out of the 560S.- Perfect audio for gaming: the wide soundstage is great, as is the sharp treble for picking out things like voices, footsteps, and gunfire. These are very popular with FPS players, and I can see why. I don't play PvP games, but they've saved me from many a cheap off-camera attack with their amazing positional audio cues. The nicest surprise on these is the bass, which is meatier than you'd expect for open-backed headphones. Unfortunately, because of the proprietary cable jack, I had to buy a kooky adapter (ASIN: B07Z2MPW61) so I could use the V-Moda BoomPro mic I had lying around for voice chat. The overall setup is a bit klunky but almost certainly outperforms popular gaming headsets.- Surprising noise isolation: these are by no means going to block out the outside world like a pair of closed-back headphones, but there are enough layers of stuff inside them between the grille and your ear that you're not going to hear everything around you with them on.Lowlights:- Oddball connector: I despise proprietary connectors, and Sennheiser's 2.5mm recessed jack with a twist lock is one of the most obnoxious on the market. What they lose in compatibility with other cables is by no means gained in security—who cares if your headphones unplug at the earcup when subjected to intense force?- Not very comfortable for big heads and big ears: although the design of these is generally compared to the HD500 line, having owned the absurdly comfortable HD598SE, I can say these don't come close. They clamp kind of hard and worse, the earpad foam is thin and when it flattens out (immediately), it presses the driver units against the cartilage of my ears. Fortunately, I was able to modify these with some third-party 3d-printed adapter rings so I could use bigger, cushier pads from Brainwavz. Now I can use them for 4+ hours without major discomfort. This may not be an issue if you don't have big ears like I do. Also worth noting is that some styles of glasses will be agony with these.- Not as nice for music: the things that make them perfect for games (accentuated high frequencies) make them a riskier proposition for music. Your mileage may vary, of course, but these can be pretty spicy for certain instruments and effects.All in all, despite the added hassles and costs to make these comfortable for my anatomy, I'm still very happy with them and don't think I could do better for my use case (plugged directly into PS5 controller with an inline mic) at any price. For their usual price of $150-180, I can't see what anyone could complain about. Thanks for reading!
