date_review: Reviewed in the United States on September 21, 2023
overview_text: Hear music as it was intended to be heard
comment: I'm not an audiophile or headphone expert.  I played drums as a teenager and later took guitar lessons for 10 years, still play the guitar almost daily, and love music in general.  Hard rock has always been my favorite genre.  I use headphones with my PC while watching YouTube music videos and concerts and also while playing video games like Cyberpunk 2077, Skyrim, Diablo IV, etc.  I also have a pretty big library of old and new music on a 7th gen iPod Touch (now discontinued) and do some critical listening with that.  I had been using budget headphones like the Koss KTXPro1 and Logitech G333 gaming earbuds, but always wanted to try something considered as "audiophile" headphones.My son is somewhat of a headphone expert, so I reached out to him for buying guidance.  His ideal headphones would be completely neutral, with no emphasis on either highs or lows.  To start, he gave me a FiiO K3, which is a DAC/headphone amplifier.  I didn't know I needed one, but he insisted.  He also convinced me to download and install the open-source Equalizer APO application and its companion Peace UI component.  It's a bit daunting for a newbie to get started with the headphone amp and equalizer software, but there are plenty of YouTube tutorial walkthroughs available.In a few hours I had the headphone amp and the Peace interface working, and had separate configurations saved for the Koss and Logitech headphones.  I downloaded pre-configured settings for each pair of headphones, which are set with the preferred "Harman Curve".  I had no idea about any of this stuff previously.  By the end of that day, I had learned how to tweak and save additional configurations, and now could choose between multiple pre-sets for each pair of headphones.  For example, I created a pre-set that boosted the bass, another that boosted the highs, and one that boosted both bass and highs while leaving the middle frequencies at the standard Harman curve settings.  That allowed me to experiment and decide my own personal preferences for music listening.Just a primer - the headphone amp connects to the PC by USB, and it disables the built-in PC audio chip with a more powerful and clean signal.  Then you plug your headphones into the headphone amp instead of the PC headphone input jack.  Windows audio and volume is bypassed, so now the volume is controlled by the volume knob on the headphone amp.  (You can turn off the headphone amp to listen through PC speakers or with the standard PC headphone jack.)With the headphone amp and equalizer software, both my Koss and Logitech headphones sounded better than ever and I was hearing details that I wasn't hearing before.  I had heard of headphone amps before, but never thought they were necessary.  I couldn't imagine not using one now.Then my son lent me his AKG K702 open back headphones to try.  He likes them because they are pretty neutral.  As he puts it, "you hear the music as the producer and engineer intended it to sound."  The AKGs were the best headphones I had ever tried, hands down.  I downloaded the pre-configured parametric EQ file for them and listened for a few days.  I learned that I preferred a more bass-heavy sound, especially with the hard rock I usually listened to.  (I am currently obsessed with a band named The Warning, but like many other artists including Spiritbox, Breaking Benjamin, Band-Maid, Evanescence, Muse, and older classic rock like Deep Purple, Pink Floyd, Zeppelin, Hendrix, and Van Halen.)  Given that I liked a bit more bass emphasis, my son suggested the Sennheiser HD 560S.I love them.  With the standard EQ configuration, the low bass is a little lacking for my taste. I want the bass drum emphasized.  So I created a pre-set with the bass boosted at 52 Hz and left the rest of frequencies alone.  Perfect!  I created another pre-set with the same 52 Hz boost and an additional boost at 5K Hz.  I have some high frequency hearing loss, so this compensates for that, and allows me to hear the cymbals a little better.  Normally I listen with the bass boost pre-set only and can hear everything fine.The only minor gripe I have with the Sennheiser HD 5600S phones is the comfort level.  The ear pads are soft and comfortable, and the clamping force isn't too much.  But the headphones are somewhat bulky, especially compared to the Koss which are feather light and have almost zero clamping force.  The Logitech earbuds are another story since they weigh virtually nothing and there's no clamping force.  That said, I have used the Sennheisers for hours at a time and they're fine.  You do forget they're on once you're immersed in the music or the game.  I'll definitely choose the Sennheisers every time for critical listening.  Occasionally I will use the Logitechs or Koss when watching non-music videos like interviews or product reviews, for the improved comfort level.Here's a good website for scientifically tested objective headphone ratings:  https://www.rtings.com/headphonesDefinitely recommend the HD 560S as an entry level audiophile headphone.  They're a tier above sub-$100 headphones for sure.

date_review: Reviewed in the United States on June 3, 2021
comment: All plastic, does not feel very robust at all. Part of the headband allows the cups to rotate, and this part is thinner than a bic pen. The sound is fine as you'd expect, but they do not feel like a $50 pair of headphones, much less a $200 pair. Planned obsolescence, what a shame. I'll be returning them ASAP. They are not built to handle daily wear and tear, but unless you buy a new pair of headphones every three years, these companies don't make as much money. Personally I don't think of headphones as a "subscription service". For some reason, people seem to make light of planned obsolescence with comments like "you'll want to upgrade in a few years anyway". If my first pair of sennheisers, or first pair of grados, or first pair of sonys, or first pair of portapros, or my beats (I know. They were free.) had lasted, I would not have bothered replacing any of them. I'm not rough on my headphones either, they never leave my desk.Look at how an aviation headset is constructed. Each cup is bolted on both ends to a piece of stamped metal, which in turn is bolted to a metal headband. This is not an expensive arrangement, and it would last a long time. It's nothing more than a few pieces of stamped, flexible metal and some bolts and nuts, and it allows the cups to pivot up and down and from side to side. This is how vintage headphones were made too. Instead of this time-tested design, every headphone maker has some shoddy setup that breaks just after the warranty period runs out. Journalists and youtube reviewers fawn over these products, and people buy them in droves. Then they buy them again in three or four years, and again, and again, creating mountains of e-waste and wasting lots of hard-earned money. It's a racket.While I don't have any other working headphones on hand to compare them with, I suppose I ought to say something more about the sound quality to make this a proper review. Compared to my old Grado sr80e's which had strong, well-defined mids supported by controlled highs and lows, the midrange seems relatively muted on the 599s. I remember being much more impressed by the Grados, which were about half the price. I do not recommend the Grados either though, as the cups are allowed to freely rotate and this tends to twist up the cables over time as you take them off, set them down, and put them back on. This usually necessitates recabling, so you'd think that Grado would either 1) modify the headband design to keep the cups from twisting freely a full 360 degrees, or 2) change the cable design, or 3) make them easier to recable, right? Right? Nope, they started gluing the two pieces of each cup together, which makes them horribly difficult to take apart and recable. This is truly a shame since they sound wonderful, but neither company will earn another cent from me.And they list "lightweight" as a feature? Give me a break. If thin African girls can schlep around sacks of coffee/grain around on their heads, I'm pretty sure we could have handled a few extra ounces. I notice most of these items on amazon have good reviews and I think part of them problem is that it tends to be hard to review an item after a few years. The item listing is usually outdated or the manufacturer has updated/discontinued the product, and most of the reviews we see are people's first impressions, not long-term reviews. That and you have paid influencers who have ulterior motives, so I don't put too much stock in a 4.5 star rating or the "amazon's choice" pseudo-endorsement.

My gold standard after all these years is a pair of Sennheiser 555s, which I picked up for around $90, and remained among the most comfortable pair of headphones I've ever owned. Comfort with headphones comes from three main factors:Head clamp pressureEar breathabilityHead pressureThe 555's I owned performed as absolute champs across the board. You could wear them for days without any issue.Seeing a pair of 599's on sale for $100, which normally go for $200, I thought I'd be getting a terrific deal. Immediately out of the box though, the feeling was certainly "these do not feel like $200 headphones". There's a large amount of cheap feeling plastic. The headband cushion is the worst part, having a very thing, seeming unremoval strip, of rigid padding. After about an hour, even though these are not heavy headphones, you will start to feel pressure building up on your head. This is in spite of the ear cups themselves being fairly larger than normal, and not having much head clamp.For Amazon and Sennheiser to work together on a product, promote is heavily on Prime Day, and co-brand it with that level of comfort is actually a little embarassing. It makes me think a little less of both Amazon as well as Sennheiser products, as it honestly feels much more like a $50 headphone sold for $100 than a $200 headphone dropped to $100.If you can find it DEEPLY discounted, and have a very sturdy head, you can consider it. Anyone else who cares about comfort, give it a skip.

These will probably blow any other headphones under $100 out of the water in that category. Do not listen to anyone saying you need a $50 amp. You don't. If you turn these to 100% volume, they will easily be as loud as your computer's speakers on 40% volume without putting them on. The open back design allows for a bigger sound stage, which is nice, but also people next to you will hear whatever you're listening to.Comfort: Sure, it's an open back design, but that doesn't mean your ears won't get hot after extended use. Heck, these get hard to wear after 1-2 hours, especially because I have a big head. The padded headband starts digging into my head, and the clamp force on the sides is annoying (if you want decently adjustable headphones with no annoying clamp force for just $60 with slightly worse sound quality, try out the heavily underrated Phillips SHP9500). Still though, these headphones will fit over your ears, guaranteed. I believe the high clamp force is there so they won't slide off your ears altogether. You get the standard headband adjustment that clicks on both sides, which honestly is more comfortable than the automatic adjustment on "studio" headphones with a hard clamp force.Aesthetics: sexy as hell.Build quality: mostly plastic, but built to last with quality materials. Should you wear them for hours on end, watching a movie for example? Probably not, unless you can stand the clamp force and headband. Top quality, clear sound as always.

overview_text: Sennheiser HD 599 SE Comfortable wearing headphones...
comment: Well, I purchased the Sennheiser HD 599 SE stereo headphones here on this Amazon link over 3 months ago for a whopping 60% off the $199 retail, and it's good thing I did, or I would have returned them.. Let me explain, (since I did give it a 4 star rating!).  The headphones are very comfortable and the quality is reasonable. I literally had to set the 100 Hz bass shelf at -6 dB to approach a balanced, neutral sounding headphone. Even at that, they are a slight bit dipped at 1kHz, but have an acceptable sound signature for many listeners with that EQ. The clarity or sparkle up top that people like is there on the HD 599SE's, but not too excessive. The efficiency is good for a 55 ohm impedance headphone. I would not purchase these headphones for mixing or studio, though. They were a great deal for what I paid, and sound nice on various music programs, but with attention paid to the bass EQ.  I recently purchased AKG k240 studio's on sale for even less than I paid for these Sennheisers, and they were much more neutral, which will come in handy for me.  Note that the AKG k240 studio's were less efficient than expected for their 55 ohm impedance, but worked acceptable fine at my mixing desk. The Sennheiser HD 599 SE's may be good for you if you like excessive bass, but then, you may be better suited to the Audio Technica ATH-M50x's, which sound good too, but are not really studio headphones either, imho, but Sennheiser doesn't seem to make that claim like Audio Technica does..  Good luck to you, and thanks for taking the time to read this!

I ended up getting a set of Sennheiser HD 560S and spent an hour or so listening to both of them on the same album, replaying the tracks of the record over and over, first listening to the HD 599s then the HD 560S. The album I was listening to was Wishbone Ash on Deca Records, and recorded on 180 gram vinyl. I also listened to both sets with my equalizer set flat, no adjustments. I found the HD 599s to be lacking in detail, a bit muddy, not as clear over-all and somewhat muffled or toned down. The top end is not as clear and concise as I found the HD 560S set to be. The soundstage of the HD 560S headphones I found to be more complete, spacious and quite good. In short, the HD 599s lack the detail, clarity and soundstage of the HD 560S headphones; if you like a mellow, less punchy sound the HD 599s might be for you. For me I want to hear the same detail and clarity as I'm hearing with my Polk Audio Signature S60 tower speakers hooked up to my Rotel receiver. The HD 560S come pretty close to that sound, but they are slightly less comfortable, which is a bit hard to understand as the build is very similar to that of the HD599s, maybe they will loosen up some and become just as comfortable. Only Time will tell.This is my second try at headphones in the $150 price range, the first pair were the Audio-Technica ATH-M50XGM, which if found to be excellent as far as sound quality, but after a very short period made my ears hurt. So I returned them and after searching and reading reviews, decided to give the HD 599s a try.My suggestion would be to buy all three of these headphones and give them a try. In this price range the HD 560S are my choice. I'd like to keep trying more brands but, not too many out there have the oval ear cups that actually sit completely over the ears. My ears are very sensitive and become sore easily, so the oval cups are a must for me. If you can tolerate a round ear cup, try the Audio-Technica ATH-M50XGM vs the Sennheiser HD560S. comment: So I tested these against my reference headphones which are the HiFiMan Ananda. The Ananda's are my preference compared to these HD599s in all genres except Classical music and Metal or anything with heavy electric guitars. I just had a listening session of some Megadeth, Black Sabbath and Soundgarden and these sound pretty good for that purpose, much better than my Grado's for heavy metal. The Grado sound is my preference for "Classical" music being anything Baroque, Classical, Romantic, Modern, Post-Modern and Opera. Grado headphones are really excellent for that type of music because they can reproduce the orchestra's Forte (F) with a lot of dynamic excursion of the driver giving the listener the "jump out of your seat" moment and feeling when the orchestra hits full force. Grados can do that but the 599s and planar headphones cannot. I tested this with a few tracks from my test track playlist and these HD599s don't have that capability. They don't sound good for pop music either I actually prefer my Anandas for pop music I tested some Lady Gaga off her album Chromatica tracks and these 599s are not on the same level of sound resolution, micro-detail and bass excursion. That said -- the 599s actually have a moderately to very good tonality, although veiled moderately. This is why they probably do so well with heavy metal music or anything with electric guitars. You probably realize that I swap headphones for genres and I do do that. The 599s were a treat to listen to during my testing session on Slaves and Bulldozers by Soundgarden and Age of Reason by Black Sabbath. Although the midrange is forward on the 599s it only really becomes a issue with heavy metal when listening to the loudest sections of the track where you might experience a effect that sounds like clipping. But otherwise these 599s will be my new go-to headphone for anything like Led Zeppelin, Rock, Heavy Metal etc because planars with their lightning quick attack then release and weak guitar tonality don't do good for this type of music. I can also add that the 599s get a 10 out of 10 for comfort they are extremely comfortable and the clamp force does not bother me at all because it's only moderate and not excessive. There's really nothing like hearing Chris Cornell scream "So bleed your heart out, There's no more rides for free" and these 599s really gave me a spine tingle when listening to that part of the track. Vocals on these are not crystal clear so know that in advance. The best vocals I've ever heard are on my Anandas. Planars really have a knack at that trick. So despite me only going to be using these for a certain genre I still consider this a good buy and am happy I found a use case for them. This is my first set of Sennheisers.

date_review: Reviewed in the United States on December 17, 2019
comment: The short version: the sound is too bass-heavy for my taste, but the build quality is great and the ear cups are very comfortable.First, I should say that my go-to headphones are the Sennheiser 380, which I've had for about five years. They can do bass when necessary, but are overall flat, at least to my ear. Flat as in they don't over-emphasize any range of sound, not flat as in dull.The 599s are a different story. To me, they very much over-emphasize the low end. Everything I listened to had an odd boomy quality to it. To be fair, some music sounded good, with the extra bass. But other music didn't sound that good at all. Speech wasn't great, nor were game sounds. Basically, the sound profile isn't at all what I like in my headphones.However, the 599s are very comfortable. The 380s have leather cups that I've always liked, but the cups on the 599s are even better. The headphones themselves are light, and don't clamp as hard, letting me easily wear them for a few hours. The padded headband was also comfortable.Physically, I prefer the 599s to the 380s. The sound was my problem. I just couldn't get used to it, even after two weeks of daily use. And yes, for those who feel it matters, I ran a headphone burn-in sound file all night the second day I had these headphones. It made no difference at all for me.I'm giving these 2/5 in sound, and 5/5 in build quality. However, I can't be too harsh on the sound, because the profile is tuned differently than I like. It's not bad, just different. Sennheiser did what they set out to do, and I'm simply not the intended audience. I have to add a star in audio for that.

date_review: Reviewed in the United States on December 14, 2019

comment: First off, at $99 you aren't going to get better sounding open back headphones than these. Sound quality is pretty great on these. If you just bought these as your first mid range headphone you won't be disappointed. But, I purchased these as an "upgrade" to the cheaper SHP9500 headphones, and for me, it was actually a downgrade. SHP9500's have a wider soundstage, and a much more comfortable on my head. They have less clamp, bigger ear cups, a 3.5mm standard connector, and a more comfortable headband. Sound quality overall is about the same between the two headsets. This is just my personal preference, and they're both great headsets, and will work on basically any device, so go with whichever appeals to you more.

date_review: Reviewed in the United States on December 4, 2019
overview_text: They are Sennheisers and they are nice
comment: Definitely minimal packaging, making unboxing somewhat underwhelming. In true Sennheiser form, they are gorgeous. The fit and finish are flawless, and despite being primarily all plastic, the material seems to be of reasonably high quality. The comfort is superb, and the cups are of a nearly perfect size and shape. They pivot in every direction and are lightweight. The cords supplied with them seem to me to be of somewhat inferior quality. I really dislike the proprietary connectors. What would be the downside of making both ends 3.5mm? None that I can see, considering that is where most failures occur. I didn't need these by any means. I missed the BF price on them last year and have since read mostly good reviews of them. I have the HD598, and like them well enough, despite their shortfalls on the low end. I know this is a trait of open backs and accept it as what it is. The reviews of the 599 have mostly said that is where they shine. It is both true and false. The mid-bass is somewhat more pronounced in them, but the sub-bass sends them into a nose dive. Try as they might to reproduce it, it sends them into a shudder that disrupts the entire spectrum with a single note. They would have been better off rolling them off at around 50 and leaving that to others that can handle it. I have a half dozen sets of lower impedance, open back, mid priced headphones ($100-$300). These are a real gem at the BF price, (half off). At full price, they would be going back. I do know that as they break in their performance may improve, but i really don't see them overcoming this limitation. That being said, 99% of the time, this will not be a problem, or even noticed. If you are interested in breaking into the world of the open back cans and can afford only one mid-priced pair, go for the Philips Fidelio X2HR. Even though they are somewhat clunky, not as streamlined, and considerably heavier, they are cheaper than these at full price, and outperform them at every turn. (I am by no means any kind of authority on this subject, and have not employed any testing methods other than my old, tired ears. This review is purely opinion, and only mine at that. Also note that I am running these on a stock sound card or portable device with a low priced portable amp and no DAC, but running only FLAC files.)

comment: I’m still relatively new to collecting headphones, but I do have a small collection for reference. I have used the Samson SR850s, SR860s with after market earpads, Moondrop Chu’s, Moondrop Chu II’s, Tanchjim Zeros, and both iterations of the AirPod Pros. These in short the HD599s are good enough that I can easily tell the difference in quality from listening to an MP3 on a iPod verses the same MP3 on my phone. So if you want these for listening to your old iPod you are overspending. I can also tell the difference in quality in certain FLAC files verses their MP3 counterparts, though I will admit the difference is slight to my untrained ears. I bough these on sale for ~$120 which I feel is more than a fair price for the product I received. Now for the compare and contrasting…In terms of audio quality the HD599s and the Chu II are my favorite sounding headphones. (If you want less bass and a more sparkly sound get the original Chus or the Zeros. Lofi, classical instruments, and female vocals in particular sounds amazing with them) They are both fairly balanced with a warmer bass. They both have a very different quality of sound thanks to these being an open back headphone and the Chu II’s having more of a passive noise cancelation. I can’t put it into words. Some say open backs sound fuller thanks to their open nature, but that word doesn't hit the spot for me. Needless to say, I find myself switching between both frequently to scratch the itch each of the qualities provide depending on my mood. The HD599s are naturally a harder to run so I have to crank the volume on my phone more, but they are still perfectly drivable without a dedicated DAC/AMP. The Chu II’s start at $20, but if you are cursed with small waxy ear canals, like myself, then you will have to replace the filters fairly frequently (every ~5 days) which would cost me around $4 a month with my average use case. That is a bit of a hassle and a hidden cost that is rarely mentioned. The HD599’s always sound good since they are not subject to the same moist conditions. Can you get competing sound for cheaper if you go the IEM (in ear monitor) route? Yes, but sometimes you just want over the ear headphones for the sake of comfort, lack of hassle, and sharability.If your not interested in IEMs like the Chu II’s then here is a comparison to the SR850s (the SR860s are basically identical, but have another color way and are usually more expensive). In terms of comfort the HD599’s are far more comfortable out of the box. The pads of the SR850’s touch my ears which felt fine until I experienced better, now I don't care for them and wouldn’t wear them for long periods of time. The HD599’s actually sit around my ears with the inner pads being deep enough that they don’t touch my ears. The ear cups also swivel to conform to my head which also improves the experience. Where things get interesting is if you splurge for after market velour pads for the SR850s which cost an additional ~$20 (I got mine from TRANSTEK). These increase the total cost to around $60 but feel equally comfortable (if not slightly more so) than the HD599s. I haven't seen any aftermarket pads that look as thick and soft for the HD599s yet, but if I do, I will definitely give them a try and update this review.The sound quality is a matter of preference between the two, I like the warmer and slightly fuller sound of the HD599s and I think the top end sounds slightly more crisp/accurate.In terms of sound leakage the HD599s are definitely worse. You don't want to use these if you don't want people to listen in to your content. With the SR850s you can tend to avoid people listening in if you’re at a moderate volume. If you are in a noisy house with children then both of these may not be right for you. You would want to look into closed back or IEMs. I personally like open backs because you can still hear the world around you when you’re working. You are not in your personal bubble.The removable cable is the greatest quality of life feature of the HD599s. It comes with two cables out of the box: a long boi with a chonky 6.3mm jack with a step down adapter to 3.5, and a reasonably sized 3.5mm cable. The SR850s in contrast have a non removable long 3.5mm cable with a step-up 6.3mm adapter. As a result the SR850’s don’t leave my desk and the cables stay cable managed underneath it. The HD599s offer way more flexibility. I use my short cable for around the house listening on my phone, handheld game consoles, and occasionally on my AMP/DAC on my PC while reserving the long cable for watching TV on my sofa or bed.If you’re looking for solid stationary desk headphones for work and general use with a flat sound get the SR850s with the aftermarket earpads are fantastic for the money and will beat pretty much any “gaming” headphone on the market in terms of sound quality. They also dont have much audio leakage so they may work well in an office setting as you can still hear what is going on around you. If you want convenience buds for daily use that you keep on you 24/7 get the AirPod Pros (the first gen had better connectivity and range but the second gen sound slightly better). If you want great affordable sound (with some maintenance) go the IEM route and snag the Chu’s or Zeros for a flat accurate sound or the Chu II’s for a warmer sound that maintains the accuracy on the top end. If you want excellent open backs that can be driven without an external DAC/AMP that are slightly warm then the HD599s are great.I don't think I would buy the HD599s at the retail cost of $250 considering the HD600s (the de facto benchmark for over 20 years) often drop down to $300 on sale or $250 in used like-new condition, but at $120 I think they are a fair price for what they offer as a package. They are versatile, comfortable, and accurate enough that you can hear the differences between good and bad mp3 playback and (depending on the file or the quality/accuracy of your hearing) the difference between a FLAC and MP3.Welcome to audiophile country, open your wallets and enjoy the process of nitpicking sound quality to justify your purchases. I hope you enjoy your descent.

overview_text: BLUF: One original pair, two replacements. They sound amazing...when they work.
comment: My issue doesn't seem to be isolated, so I'll explain.I first bought these headphones for office work. They worked fantastically for about 6 months. I started having major connectivity issues. The headphones would go into a never-ending loop of powering on and off. They would say they were connected to my phone, but they would have no audio. Then, as soon as I got audio, they would shut themselves off and start up again. For a while, they would still work with the Bose USB link on my laptop. Admittedly, when these headphones work, they sound phenomenal, and the noise cancelling is excellent.However, I have spent numerous hours on the phone with Bose. I bought the initial pair, but I had to pay $50 to replace them through the warranty. I am currently on either my third or fourth set, all replacements coming from the warranty or customer service. Customer service was good, and they even gave me slightly better set on the last time. However, I am experiencing the exact same issues.  Connection, but no sound. No connection, reboot cycle. Now I can't even connect to the Bose USB link. I thought maybe I was just on an unfortunate run, but after digging through numerous threads, there seem to be hundreds of people that have had similar issues, regardless of firmware updates. It appears that the best solution found so far is to delete any other Bluetooth apps from your device. I.e. if you use your Bose headphones for work but a set of Beats to workout, you must now delete the Beats app from your phone, because it interferes with your Bose headphones and sends them into the reboot cycle.I've always love Bose products, but this has most likely ended my experience with them. To continue charging close to $400 for a device with known issues for almost five years now is indicative of a very bad-faith company. I understand they have to make money, but I wish they would at least design a product worth having. Understand that when they work, they are awesome. However, you may go through a long, frustrating journey of dealing with a $400 set of ear muffs. Bose, do better.

comment: I have a few Bose, Sony, and Beats headphones. The Bose QuietComfort Ultra is a compact unit that is very portable and light weight compared to other units. It's quite well built, with a more minimalistic setup of just two buttons and a volume touch slide. The instructions are also digital, so the box contains just the carrying case and headphones. The overall physical build is nice, with swivelly ear pieces, smooth adjustable length, and a tight but not too tight headband. The only imperfection is some scuff marks on the ear pieces straight out of the box, which doesn't bode well for future use. The earpads are nice and soft. They fully cover and insulate, but you can still clearly hear any noise in your surroundings. That is, until you turn on the noise cancellation. There are several degrees of noise cancellation, but the immersion mode will omit nearly all ambient sound without sounding too staticky. It also has awareness mode which you can hear most ambient noise along with your music without having to excessively turn up the volume. It also doesn't leak much sound to your surroundings.The sound quality is quite good, with crisp highs and deep lows that are well balanced and not jarring. I use piano music with high octaves to test highs and it passed with flying colors, without any peaking or static. The bass is decently rich too, but not overpowering. However, it does amplify certain underlying notes to an unexpected degree. Some songs have this low, low bass thump that usually is not well transmitted through speakers or common headphones. However, these deliver that uncomfortable thump that's not "loud" per say but will make me grit my teeth whenever it happens, like I'm having a heart attack or something. Other than the unexpected random hits, it's a very nice overall listening experience.

comment: EDIT (1/8/2024): I discovered a workaround that is partially effective. In the Bose Music app, on the Modes tab, hit the + button to add a new mode. On this tab, you can access a Noise Cancellation level slider with 10 levels. Putting the slider about half way allows enough ambient sound to come through that you can hear yourself speak while still reducing distractions around you. It's not perfect, but it's better than nothing.ORIGINAL REVIEW:Number one thing you need to know: If you're using these for meetings or phone calls, wait. Right now, there is a bug where you cannot hear yourself speak (i.e. self voice / side tone doesn't work). It's as if you're conducting a meeting with ear plugs in. This is Bose firmware 1.5.4 (for those of you reading this in the future).I've tried this on two different headsets, one from Amazon, one from Walmart, different manufacturing dates. It flat out doesn't work - there is no difference between high self voice and off. I've also updated the Bose Music app - doesn't help. The good news is that this is probably a software bug as aware mode seems to work (can hear myself speak but also hear everything else in the room as well).Bottom line - I think this headset is nice, but I'm not sure about it being worth $420, and definitely not worth that amount when I have to switch to my older QC35s to conduct Teams meetings so I can hear myself speak.Also not a fan of the solid state volume slider. I much prefer the buttons on the QC35 series.Edit: On the Pro side: one not advertised feature is bluetooth range. This headset supports bluetooth 5.3 which is a significant upgrade from 4.x that the QC 35ii supports. With this headset, I can leave my phone in one corner of the house and walk all the way over to the other corner with no loss of signal. It's more than double the range of the older bluetooth protocols. The headset is backwards compatible with bluetooth 4 devices, but to get this benefit, make sure your phone / laptop / whatever supports bluetooth 5.On the negative side, another feature that annoys me on this set of headphones is the on-head detection. The way it's supposed to work is that when you take off your headphones, they automatically pause whatever is playing and go into a low power state. In theory...In practice, this is somewhat annoying for two reasons:1. It's not bullet proof. Maybe 1 out of 20 times I take off the headphones, it doesn't detect it and the music keeps playing. The benign case is when music is playing and you notice it and fix it. The treacherous case is when you've already paused the music, take off the headset, and then it doesn't go low power mode. Next time you wear them the battery will be dead. 2. If you take off the headphones, they don't disconnect from Bluetooth right away. It takes some time before it disconnects. So you end up having to manually disconnect anyway to use your phone / laptop speakers instead of the headset, and at that point you wonder why these don't simply have a slider on / off switch like the older models.

comment: At this price, you're going to be expecting a lot. Depending on what you prioritize, you are not going to be disappointed.First, let's get the bad out of the way, and why I'm docking a star. Bose heavily advertises the immersion mode for these. It's a form of surround sound, and while the head tracking and all that can be kind of fun, once the novelty wears off the sound quality in this mode is atrocious. It's tinny, with tons of reverb. Any immersion you get is as artificial as a $10 gaming headset promising the same features. I have bluetooth headphones and buds 1/3 the price with infinitely better simulated surround features. Your mileage may vary, but I can't see most people loving this.However, this is where my gripes end. The build quality is much improved, as well as appearance. They're extremely comfortable, have perfect clamp, and stay in place better than 99% of headphones I've tried. Setting up the connection is very easy, and connecting to multiple devices is a breeze. Sometimes my phone needs a reminder to connect, but once connected it is extremely stable. One of the biggest surprises for me was how great the range is, even when connected to my BT-W5 dongle with AptX Adaptive. I could get a good 10-20 feet further away than any other headphone I've ever owned before the connection would even think about dropping. Again, with the best codec connected AND multipoint enabled.Sound quality is not the best on the market, but the best on the market for sound quality would require paying more while sacrificing features. With the Bose, you get something that does great with everything, and best with noise cancelling. The noise canceling, as expected, is out of this world good. The sound leans kind of neutral, with a bit of bass emphasis. However, I like even more bass emphasis, especially when walking, and the app EQ allows me to add that with room to spare.If you value noise canceling, but want good or great performance with every other feature you can imagine, this is a great choice if you have the budget. Oh, and for small heads, this might be the best option out there bar none.

date_review: Reviewed in the United States on October 7, 2023
comment: Just received the Bose Quietcomfort Ultra headphones in black and I'll give you my impression. The box basically contains the case for the headphones, which looks exactly like the QC45 case from the outside. However, when you open it, this is a difference as the headphones cups site recessed in the case. The headphones resemble the QC45 with some noticeable differences. The headband is metal with comfortable faux leather cushioning as are the earpads.  In the box are the headphones a USB A charger cord and a cord to use to connect the headphones to a headphone jack (same as other Bose headphones)There are two buttons on the right earcup one to turn on the headphones and one to stop, advance or go back on the tracks you are listening to. There is a slider for the volume that works great and has a point on the slider that can be used to program anything the headphones can do. Default is battery strength. The slider took a few minutes to get used to but once that occurred it works really well. It's quite responsive and for me works better than the earpad controls on the Sony 1000XM5. The other button also controls the noise canceling features including the new immersive sound. Like the QC45 they pair to your device using the Bose Music APP. Similar the QC45, you have access to a very elementary equalizer that allows you to adjust bass, midrange and treble but does not allow you to adjust subbass, the bass roll off area or the very high end.My initial impression of these out of the box is the sound is similar to the QC45 but improved using the immersive audio. That is they have a very exaggerated upper end somewhere around 8-10K that dominates the sound scape. This is improved by significantly decreasing the treble on the EQ. Once that is done they sound similar to most Bose headphones but with a bigger sound stage using immersive audio (midrange forward but with extremely solid bass and tremble once adjusted)Otherwise the sound is quite solid. I compared these to my Focal Bathys and they don't have the tonal separation, clarity or timbre of the Bathys. They for me are as good as my Sony 1000XM5 headphones and I spent some time with them listening to a bunch of songs including  Pink Floyd Hey You, Portugal the Man  Feel It Still, Kings of Leon Wait For Me, or Halsey's Graveyard. The immersion audio does work as it does seem like the soundscape is in front of me and not directed from both ears; it is a definite upgrade from the sound heard using quiet or alert settings for noise cancelling. Finally, Bose states that battery strength is diminished by using immersion audio although I've not seen a big effect of that on battery strength so far. And like the QC45 cans there does not appear to be a way to listen to music without using ANC.The noise cancelling is as good as any set of cans I have but does not appear much different/better than the QC45. The microphones are much better both indoors and outside for calls than the QC45. I have not used these for computer games yet. And they are just a bit more comfortable than the Sony cans and way more comfortable than my Bathys which are quite heavy and difficult to wear all day.Finally, I'm not sure they are worth $429. Seems that these should be priced around $350 to maybe $400 but the decision to spend that type of money on headphones is clearly a personal one. And for me they are clearly for now my 1A or B daily headphones and on a par with the Sony 1000XM5 for sound, ANC and comfort but would not be ones I'd use for critical music listening where my Bathys or Celestee sound better.

date_review: Reviewed in the United States on March 22, 2024
overview_text: BOSE QUIET COMFORT ULTRA VS BOSE NC 700
comment: Bose Quiet Comfort Ultra HeadphonesSeveral years ago, I discovered Bose Quiet Comfort headphones.  My first pair wore the QC15 and I have owned every iteration since then.  Until now, the best of the best have been the Bose NC700 which are spectacular headphones.  Now, I find myself the proud owner of the company’s newest over-ear headset, the Bose Quiet Comfort Ultra.  After thorough comparison, I can confidently say that the new Ultra are an upgrade in every way.  There is especially one aspect which causes the Ultra to make them an absolutely must-have for music lovers.  I will get to that in a moment, but first here are my thoughts on how the NC700 and QC Ultra compare:COMFORTI am very happy to report that the Bose QC Ultra are more comfortable than the NC 700 headphones.  They are lighter, there is less clamping force and the headband distributes weight better on the top of your head.  I used to consider the NC 700 headphones as the second most comfortable pair of over-ear headphones second only to the QC45.  Well, the Ultra now take this 2nd place spot and they are almost as comfortable as the 45.  Very Great!NOISE CANCELINGYes, Bose has also improved the noise canceling.  When in quiet mode the headphones put you in a place where the world simply disappears.  Each iteration of Bose headphones through the years has improved upon the previous in this area.  The Ultra are no different.  In fact, when I was testing them out my wife was standing 3 feet from me and trying to talk to me.  I never even knew she was talking.  This has never happened with my older NC 700.SOUND QUALITYThe QC Ultra are more of a spiritual successor to the NC700 than they are the QC45.  The sound is much more similar to the NC700. What they retain is the excellent clarity and instrument separation.  The mids are just as perfectly present. Also the highs have a very pleasing ring without ever sounding harsh.  What was great on the 700 but even better on the Ultra is the bass.  Bose says that the new Ultra are now taking samples of sound inside the ear ups and then actively adjusts the bass to sound best dependent on the shape of ears, the seal of the pads, etc.  This really does make a difference.  I wear glass which compromises the acoustic seal.  The Ultra compensates for this and makes the bass sound deeper and have a greater punch than my NC700.  So, the sound signature overall is better and gets WAY better with immersive audio.  But, we are getting to that.IMMERSIVE AUDIOThis is the feature!  If you are a music lover then this is the feature which gives the biggest incentive to upgrade from the NC 700.  Music with immersive audio just sounds better.  I have several setups of actual stereo bookshelf speakers around my house.  I always preferred a good pair of music monitors over headphones.  Why?  Because you can hear and imagine the soundstage in front of you.  Good recordings place an orchestra or band members several feet from each-other as you listen.  With live listening you can hear the music spread throughout the venue and this is what immersive audio on the Quiet Comfort Headphones does.  It places the band a couple feet in front of you.  It feels like you can point to and reach out and touch the various vocalist and instruments.  It is so great!  It is exactly like advertised.  Immersive audio makes it sound like you are listening to a good pair of speakers in a room acoustically ideal for premium audio.  Now that I have heard it, I can never go back to regular headphones.CONCLUSIONThere is so much more good that I could say about the Bose Quiet Comfort Ultra headphones. The buttons are well placed and are useful - even the touch-sensitive volume slider works well enough!  The app also just works and all the needed settings are there to easily adjust.  The carrying case looks premium and is compact.  It is smaller than the NC700 case and even more compact than the QC45’s storage option.  There are some things I do not like about the headphones. For example, immersive audio for movies is still not as good or immersive as Spacial Audio on Apple’s AirPods Max when watching Dolby content. overview_text: Great Headphones but Not Quite Perfect
comment: This is a really well rounded and versatile pair of headphones, but they are still not perfect. The headphones themselves come with a short USB Type-A to C cable and an AUX 3.5mm to 3.5mm cable in the box, but interestingly, the pair I received also came with a 4ft USB-C to C fast charge cable that was in a separate box on its own.Design/Comfort:The headphones themselves are a bit on the smaller side, as they have a small plastic frame with medium sized cushioned ear cups and a reasonable amount of padding on the headband. The earcups have full vertical and horizontal swivel to get the best fit, and the headphones can be easily folded up and stored when not in use. The headphones have simple and easy to use multimedia buttons on the right side of the headphones which is also where you will find the headphone jack for wired playback and the USB-C port for charging. The headphones themselves are very light when wearing them for long periods of time, but I personally found that the earcups were a bit on the smaller side as they couldn't fully cover my ears and I would have to periodically adjust them to avoid ear strain. The padding on the top is very minimal as mentioned but it is still a reasonable amount due to the lighter weight of the frame. The headphones also have a good amount of adjustments in the headband, but I did have to adjust them quite a bit for my use, which is a bit of let down when my head is not very large and I don't have to make as much of an adjustment on some other headphones. However, the comfort was pretty good overall, and they are still comfortable to wear for long listening sessions.Bluetooth:When first powering them on, the headphones will immediately enter pairing mode, and it took me less than a minute to pair them to my iPhone and start playing music. However, the first thing I noticed is that I personally had to max out the volume of these over the Bluetooth connection as they are not very loud, at least in my opinion. Once maxed out, they are fairly adequate in terms of audio volume, and music sounds great- more on audio quality in a bit. The multimedia buttons work great in most of my apps in adjusting the volume and playing/pausing the music without any noticeable delay. Speaking of delay, the headphones do a great job at staying in sync when watching online content such as movies or videos with voices and audio staying in sync with what is playing on screen.Wired Mode:When using them wired with the 3.5mm cable, the headset does not have to be powered on and can be driven by the audio source such as your PC, Game Controller, or Mobile Device. Additionally, while the lower volume of the headset can still be a bit of an issue, I did find that I can get much more volume out of the headset over the wired connection versus Bluetooth when I have them connected to a sound card or DAC. The sound quality over the wired connection is virtually the same, but you will be able to get substantially louder audio depending on the device.Sound Quality:Now, let's talk about the audio. I do really enjoy using these headphones for music listening, or watching movies, but not so much for standard online videos with a lot of talking or for gaming. While the headset has an okay soundstage, I personally find the bass to be a bit more prominent than the mids and highs, and the mids and highs that are there sound a bit crushed. For example, action sequences in a movie are thumpy and immersive as well as drums in a rock song, but voices sometimes sound too raspy or sharp for my liking. The soundstage beyond the voices at this point are still a bit off, as higher frequency instruments can sound a bit tinny and not very natural. For video games, the unbalanced mids and highs can also make it harder to hear your surroundings as the bass of the action makes it difficult to know if an enemy is walking behind you. Aside from all of that, these are still good sounding headphones, but I think they are better for music listening or movie watching more than anything else. This is all just how I feel about them, and there are some who might find the audio to be perfect with these.Battery Life:The battery life on these headphones is probably one of the standout features. I rarely find headphones that can meet their advertised spec, but I was able to reach just a few hours short of this limit on the internal battery, but that is also probably due to the fact that I had to have the volume maxed out all the time when paired to my phone. As previously mentioned, you can also use them over a wired connection to conserve battery life or whenever the battery needs to be recharged. When it comes to charge times, they do charge extremely fast, but that was with using the 4ft fast charge cable that came with my pair.Aside from the few complaints I have about these, these headphones are still extremely solid, sound reasonably good, and are adequately comfortable. I am sure that most people would be more than happy with these overall, and I highly recommend them.

Now the possessed things are sitting in their box waiting to be returned, and I can still hear the muffled "power on" and "pairing mode" at random intervals.

date_review: Reviewed in the United States on October 24, 2023
overview_text: Missed potential. Are these just badly tuned or did I get a lemon?
comment: On paper these show so much promise. I'll get this out of the way right now: I don't care about ANC. I've owned one pair of ANC headphones and only found them helpful on airplanes. Otherwise it's not a feature I have ever prioritized. The ANC worked well enough for me on transit and I'm sure it would be helpful with the constant hum of a jet engine. I got these specifically so I ~wouldn't~ have to invest in ulta-lux ANC features like what Sony or Bose have to offer. All review and comparison sites indicated that these headphones offered good sound with absolutely no other frills, which is right up my alley.More on my needs and expectations: I have some premium cabled equipment that I use sitting at home or will commute with if it isn't raining. Otherwise, if I'm at the gym or the weather is wet, I will typically use my bluetooth gym earbuds - JBL Endurance Race. They are a party vibe and have enough clarity and separation. They don't distinctly excel in those realms. That's not why I bought them. I bought them to sweat and/or wake up for work, and my expectations of them are realistic. What I am looking for is a more mature, well-balanced sound from an over-hear headphone now that the weather is getting cold again and I have some long flights booked for next year. My Crusher Evos are extremely fun, but again I'm ready for something more refined that will treat bass as a place to find detail, not just as a place for energy. The Crushers also bleed WAY too much to use on commutes. I did not go into this expecting the same quality as my at-home-only open-backs.I make it a point to listen to new devices in the morning. I don't listen to any devices until I'm out the door and starting my commute. Too distracting, but this means my ears are not precooked with any particular sound profile and well rested from yesterday's adventures.7hz-40khz on neodymium magnets is always a promising foundation. They did indeed deliver on that promise. The bass was rather well textured and had a compelling amount of depth. Punchy in the right places, but not overdone. Good sub-bass rumble. The heartbeat drums at the beginning of Ascension by Big Wild had such good concussion in the ears. On the high end, these really shine with brilliance in the high treble regions. I was able to hear fine details at very high pitches on these headphones. These headphones accomplish this without sounding sibilant. These weren't "airy" at all, but where they excelled, their performance was more than fair. I was shocked by these qualities coming from such a modestly priced product.These headphones really flew off the rails at the mids. The vocal range is bloated and instrumentation is crowded. That effect where it sounds like the vocalist is singing into a box... it was especially boxy with KD Lang and Marisa Monte - the kinds of female vocals that are somewhat deeper and more resonant.  Even a sandy-textured voice like Adele had this weird timbre like she was singing through a foam cup. Jesse Rutherford was unlistenable. Look how they massacred my boy. I had to use the equalizer in the app to pull the 1khz slider down at least five decibels to reign in the boxy sound, but then when I moved on to Stevie Nicks and Ann Wilson, their vocals were shoved behind the energetic treble and bass. The upper and lower harmonics of the mids were however still present... it was just a pileup. I don't want to have to EQ between every song.The qualizer app is cool and useful, but it took a long time to create a profile could stand across multiple genres and sound like a train wreck in the mids. Not everyone has spent as much time as I have playing with these things. Less tech savvy users will rip these headphones off immediately and not look back. If it took me this long to find the right sound, there's not much hope for anyone less experienced than I am who had the same problem.Touch controls are simple and very effective. I had to get used to where I put my fingers when adjusting them or taking them on or off, but that comes with the territory of touch controls. The "hand over ear" gesture to temporarily allow for listening was a great addition. The fit is pretty comfortable. I am rather short and have a smaverage-sized head and smallish ears. I didn't find them tight but not exceptionally tight for such new headphones, but could understand why a larger person may find them uncomfortable. The cups fit completely around my ears. I think a person with a bigger head or ears than mine might have their ears pressed down by the padding. I don't know how that may influence their sound experience.I am ultimately disappointed. TAH8506s did the high and low ends with so much grace and detail, but the mids just... ruined the experience. Sad to see so much wasted potential from the high and low ends. Were these just tuned awkwardly or did I get a lemon? I soooo want to love them as an unglamorous underdog that punches above its weight on the high and low end, but the mids just don't cut it. Uuugh.

date_review: Reviewed in the United States on June 25, 2020
overview_text: Bluetooth headphone with a serious flaw
comment: The headphone is very good in terms of comfort, weight and design. It has Bluetooth 5.0 which is great but only supports SBC codec over Bluetooth. It does not support APTX or APTX-HD. So the audio bit-rate supported over Bluetooth is low. This headset does not support HI-Res audio over Bluetooth connectivity. There is some good rumbling sound it produces and the headphones vibrates on the ears.This headset have an overall satisfactory audio quality but it leaves a lot to be desired. The overall loudness at maximum volume is not "Too Loud" for anyone's ears. In spite of all that, there is a serious shortcoming on this headphones. This headphone cannot handle low frequency Bass at max or close to max volume. The sound distorts and crackles whenever there is a low bass sound in the mix if you are close to max volume. This can only be handled by bringing down the max volume by at least 3-4 clicks on your device. Bringing down the volume towards 60-70% looses details from the audio as these headphones are not too loud.Also, I don't understand what is the point of advertising this headphone as Hi-Res Audio compatible if it is not supported over Bluetooth. I cannot imagine a person who would buy Bluetooth headphones and uses it as a wired connection for better audio. These are certainly not studio quality. But apart from the issue described above, there is not much difference between wired or wireless connection to general ears.Lastly, the Noise cancellation is not very effective either. With 'ANC ON' I could still hear my AC noise, refrigerator noise etc. The Ambient mode seems to be working okay by lowering volume to about 20-30% and letting more surrounding sound to be entered.Overall, I am not satisfied with these headsets and the quest for "The One" needs to continued.

date_review: Reviewed in the United States on April 26, 2023
overview_text: Good headset for work and music
comment: The Philips TAH8507BK is a solid pair of ANC headphones with a few extra features that make it especially well-suited to working from home. There's room for improvement in the noise cancellation and custom EQ, but the headset is generally competent and versatile overall.Physically, the headphones are nicely built and feel sturdy. The headband offers a good range of adjustment, but its clamping force is somewhat higher than average. To get a comfortable fit, I ended up setting the band wider than I do with other headphones. These might be tight on people with larger heads.For music listening, the headphones present a crowd-pleasing sound with boosted bass and crisp treble. It works for most music genres but might not appeal to audiophiles (also, no aptX). The downloadable app offers audio presets and customization, but its equalizer isn’t very effective. The EQ graph shows ±10dB of adjustment, but the audible result seems barely a third of that.Noise cancellation works reasonably well, though not equal to that of the best ANC headphones out there. Most sounds are reduced to an unobtrusive level, but you won’t get complete isolation from the environment. An ambient awareness mode is available, but for whatever reason, I hear a constant low-frequency rumble while it’s turned on.Work-oriented features include a detachable microphone, in-call status lights (optional), and a wireless dongle for non-Bluetooth PCs. The boom mic is a noticeable improvement over the built-in one, allowing others on a call to hear your voice clearly. The headset’s voice assistant key doubles as a microphone mute button, although it doesn’t necessarily work for every app.All in all, the TAH8507 is a decent headset for both work and play. It may not be perfect, but there aren’t any major deal-breakers either.

comment: I am like different headphones for different kinds of music and have shied away from bluetooth type headphones because most of the ones I see are closed back. I miss the "wide open" sound that other phones reproduce. I really enjoy the fact I can move about the house and still hear my music. I love the capability of replaying or skipping a track from pushing a single button forward or back. I like being able to pause music when I take a phone call. I don't use or care about the noise cancellation capability of this set. I like to listen to my music but not be cut off from the rest of the world. They are very comfortable, light weight and don't clamp your head like a vise.  Even with the noise cancellation feature turned off they very much seem like quality closed back headphones.Now, the not so good: I really like being able to adjust the volume by running fingers up or down the right headphone, in fact, I think that is really a cool feature, however in my opinion I think it is very poorly implemented because 3 out of 4 times when I try to adjust the volume I get an audio message stating "the Google Assistant is Not Connected." In fact if you accidentally touch the right headphone that irritating message interrupts whatever you might be listening to. Seriously? Does Google have to be a part of everything?I really like these headphones, the price is decent and they sound pretty good but I would never recommend them because of the Google interruptions. I bought a different headset (Soundcore Q30) which are about as good sound-wise as the Phillips.

date_review: Reviewed in the United States on December 10, 2022
overview_text: The 802's are very good for what they are
comment: I had these in my wish list for awhile hoping the price would come down. I ended up purchasing a renewed pair (not on Amazon) for $30. These are not audiophile headphones. They are a decent set of Bluetooth cans that produce pretty good sound. Mainly used for classic rock, the sound at times can be a bit muddy. Not the cleanest of quality but not to bad. If you go into this purchase knowing you're not buying a $400 pair of headphones, you'll like these. If you think these are magically going to be the best kept secret on the market, you're going to be disappointed. There is a reason quality cost more. The build is good. Take care of them and they should last. Put them on a stand or on a shelf when not using. They are plastic (except the headband) and will break. The earpads are plush and comfortable. I've listened for 2 hours at a time, with no achy ears. The battery is strong. I can go 2 weeks in between charges. The look is sleek and aerodynamic. The matte black, coupled with the gloss black looks very rich and stealth like. They have decent weight, but not to heavy on the head. Back to the sound. Notes are distinct but can be muddy at times. Bass is very good and not over powering, but you can definitely feel it. Highs could be improved a bit. Mid range is where they sound best. They sound stage well, putting you in the center of the music. Vocals are clear. Joni Mitchell's "Blue" on vinyl sounds really nice and alive. Her vocals are clear and fall perfectly in line with the acoustic guitar.  The piano is rich and warm. Genesis "Abacab" is another album that surprisingly shines with these headphones. Bank's normally bright and powerful keyboards were not wearing or giving me ear fatigue. They did not work well with 80's metal for me. I needed a little more crystal and upper tone clarity.  The drums did sound good and bass notes were decent.  Other albums I enjoyed were The Cars "Heartbeat City", Rush "Hemispheres" and Eagles "Hell Freezes Over" live album.They are not noise cancelling, so remember that when purchasing. They are only noise isolating, and do a decent job.  The Bluetooth range is very good. I can walk from my music room to the kitchen (many walls) with no signal loss. About 50 feet. All and all, $30 is a great deal. $50 is a stretch. I definitely wouldn't pay any more. There are plenty of other options in that price range.The bottom line is Phillips, who has been in business for over 100 years has always been a name brand you can trust. But like anything, your going to get what you pay for and in that mix will be some bad eggs. I would gladly recomend these to a friend, but if you really want Phillips top of the line, try the Fidelio L3. But thats a review for another day.

overview_text: So many advanced features and OK sound at a fantastic value.
comment: On first impressions, the H8506 looks like it’s taking a page right out of some premium headsets out there in design and functionality. I can appreciate the sleek, matte black, plastic finish, but I did notice that the surface is a fingerprint magnet, so be prepared to clean them often. They also seem a bit flimsy and prone to scratching, so I would avoid dropping them. Also, I am not comfortable stretching the headband too much as it does creak a bit. While there is no full swiveling on the cups, the headsets do fold 90 degrees and can collapse -great for storing them in the included handy clam-shell case.However, the light build makes them quite comfortable. My ears fit snugly inside the cups and the leatherette pads are soft. There’s some clamping force to keep them in place but not enough to make them uncomfortable. I do wish there was a bit more padding on top, but I didn’t notice that until I wore them for a few hours. At that time, I also noticed that my ears did get a little bit hot.Featuring Bluetooth 5.0, these headsets paired easily with any device I tried them on. There were no noticeable lag or sync issues, and they reached decent distances without breaking up. By the way, I really appreciate multi-point pairing as I was able to switch back and forth between my tablet and my phone seamlessly. And just in case, the headset also sports a 3.5mm jack and cord when needed.The touch controls worked well for me as they are intuitive and responsive. I wish I could try them when it’s cold because other similar headsets have failed then. I guess we will see. I appreciate the feature of covering the right cup to stop the music and activate the ambient sound mode -just like those other much more expensive ones. Going from ambient mode to noise-canceling is easy by pressing an actual button and the same goes for muting the mic and powering on/off.Speaking of ANC, it’s good enough to block most lower sounds and rumblings. I could still hear a lot -especially traffic when not playing anything, but when the music is playing, this is not an issue at all.The call quality is what anyone would expect from any Bluetooth headset. I was heard loud and clear in different environments, albeit a bit tinny.At 60 hours per full charge and 45 with ANC on, this headset is a beast when it comes to battery life. It’s charged via USB-C and even has quick-charge capabilities.But how do they sound? I will say they are decent. This is an area where the difference between other premium (and more expensive) headphones is obvious, considering that they claim HI-RES (7-40KHz through wired mode). Out of the box, I found the 40mm drivers deliver a bass that is lacking some punch and a bit too loose for my taste. The mids and highs made the sound signature a bit too bright. The good news is that there is a companion app where you can select sound presets and mess around with an EQ. I found the bass boost the best preset overall. The bass was still a bit sloppy, but it gave the sound a warmer, fuller signature, while the midrange and treble were still noticeable and were not fully distorted, maintaining a good level of clarity. There was good channel separation and soundstage. Unfortunately, I found that the set did not respond as well to EQ changes as I would have liked. In the end, I found them good enough to listen to any genre, but definitely not for critical purposes.Featuring a sleek design, ANC functionality, decent comfort, instinctive controls, multi-point connection, and massive battery life, Philips has delivered a lot of value with the H8506. Although I am a little disappointed that they did not meet the HI-RES expectation in my opinion, for the asking price, I would still recommend them wholeheartedly.

date_review: Reviewed in the United States on June 12, 2022
overview_text: Great sound with some unique features and a wonky touch interface
comment: Phillips is a name brand for a reason.  They make quality equipment and have been doing so for a long time.  These headphones are definitely show that in their manufacture, with nice memory phone both on the ear pieces and the headband for added comfort.  The included hard case is well constructed and even the box it comes in is nicely designed and very thick and sturdy.The H8506 is a bit higher than then most of the "mid-budget" Bluetooth headphones possibly due to the Philips name brand, but in addition to that higher level of construction, we also get some added features you don't see on most in this price category.For one, there's an actual app you can download that helps you to make changes to the sound.  You can choose from presets, but there's a full equalizer built into the app if you are really particular about what you listen to.  I found using this was really helpful in getting the best quality both from music as well as spoken word podcasts, which is most of what I listen to these days.The app gives you access to a bunch of functionality that I don't believe you could otherwise do with the headphones themselves, including the equalizer that I mention above, but also setting the headphones to automatically turn off after a certain amount of time, I suppose helpful for when you are listening to something while napping on a plane and you want to preserve battery life?The app also has a digital version of the quick start guide which I've attached above, but also a more detailed manual.  While the app is very useful, I found that if I switched out of it for any reason, and then went back to it, often it had somehow disconnected from the headphones and I had to either wait for a while for it to reconnect, or in one case after waiting a long time I just force-stopped it and restarted it and it finally reconnected.In terms of the basic functionality of the headset, Philips has used a unique (in my experience) touch interface on the side of the right headset to control the volume, tracking, and pause and play.  It's a great idea but unfortunately the implementation leaves a bit to be desired.  This may be because I'm not used to a touchpad type interface on the side of my head to control such things, and maybe over time I'll get better, but for me personally, actual physical buttons are much more straightforward for my mind and fingers to figure out.  I find myself accidentally turning the volume all the way up or down before I can actually regulate it.  I have to actually look at my phone as a guide to see the volume going up or down, and if I have to do that, then I might as well just use my phone to control the volume.  The play and pause, though, are just double-taps, and those work well without any issues.  I've always changed tracks via controls in an app on my phone, so that functionality is not something I use, but if I'm trying to control the volume, the headphones occasionally interpret my swipe as a track command rather than a volume one, which is annoying.  The Philips app actually lets you turn off touchpad entirely, which is helpful if it doesn't work well for you, or if you are doing something that is important enough that you don't want to accidentally trigger something by mistake.When I used the headphone to make calls, the person on the other line said I sounded great, and they sounded good as well, so one can use these for phone calls without issues.The noise cancelling seems better than on most similar (and lower cost) headphones that I own, and the app actually allows you to choose from different levels of noise cancelling - or "noise control" as they call it.  You can choose high, low, wind reduction, "Awareness (full transparency)" which I guess is different from off?, Adaptive (which seems to detect whether you are moving and thus adapts to your environment), and off.The headphones are equipped with a 800mah battery which is apparently good for up to 60 hours of talk/listening time, although with noise cancelling it's 45 hours, but that's still the highest I've seen on a similarly priced headset.  It will require 2 hours for you to recharge them once they are depleted to zero though.While memory foam can be comfortable, I found that wearing these headphones for any decent length of time became a bit uncomfortable unfortunately.  I don't know if that's because they are heavier (made of more durable stuff), or because they are more snug and thus cause a bit more pressure over each ear, or perhaps both?  But even after wearing them for 45 minutes or so I was starting to feel the pressure.  Now, I don't think that it gets much worse, as I've worn them for up to 1.5 hours straight and part of this may be just getting used to wearing them.  I don't wear headphones every day anymore, so I'm not used to wearing them for extended periods, but I could see that doing so might allow you to acclimate to wearing ones that are a little tighter than others?One other nice feature is the ability to connect to a second device via the bluetooth connection - something you can also disable in the app if you wish.  While this can be useful in not having to re-pair with a new device each time, it wasn't as seamless as I would have hoped because it seems you can't actually have both devices playing audio through your headphones at the same time.  Not that I would want to listen to one thing on my phone and another on my PC simultaneously, but if I'm listening to something on my phone, it would be nice to at least hear notification sounds from my PC, and if I'm wearing the headphones, those notification sounds may go unheard due to the noise cancelling.  But maybe this is just a technical impossibility right now with Bluetooth devices, I'm not sure.One more feature that seems like it would be really useful is one that allows you to cup your hand over one of the earpieces in order to temporarily turn off noise cancellation so you can hear/talk to someone more easily.  However this didn't seem to work for me even though I confirmed that I had it enabled (you can enable/disable this in the app as well).  Optimally what would be great is if this feature not only turned off noise cancellation but temporarily lowered volume to a low level and/or paused the audio.  Hopefully I'll eventually get these feature to work and can determine if this actually does any of these things.In general, while there were some quibbles here and there, I do really like these headphones.  They are well-constructed, sound great (and the sound can really be customized well with the app), have a lot of advanced features to play with, and I'm even willing to give the touchpad a bit of a chance and try to get used to it.

comment: First things first: these are the best sounding headphones I personally have ever used. Some brands I've used include JBL, Apple, Taotronics, Jaybird, and Beats among a few others. These blow those out of the water, which is suprising, because I've never strongly associated Philips with sound technology. These headphones are very well balanced, and are pretty close to neutral sounding. Bass is clear and strong, but it doesn't drown out the highs and mids. All frequencies are quite clear. No frequency is competing with one another. The sound remains clear at all volume levels. For the sake of preserving my own hearing, I haven't cranked these up all the way, but I've gone up to about 75%,and they were very loud. I should also note that these sound best when wired to your device you're listening to with the included aux cord. In Bluetooth mode, there is a little more background fuzziness than what  you often hear with Bluetooth headphones. It's a tad distracting at first, but easy to ignore pretty quickly. Just thought I'd point that out. There's zero background noise in wired mode, however. The Bluetooth controls via a single button are handy. There's no active noise cancelling, but enough sound gets blocked out for my liking. I must also note that the comfort level of these headphones are phenomenal. The substantial padding on the top and on the ears make it to where hours of use will not make you sore. The build quality is sturdy, yet undeniably plastic-y, but that's to be expected at this price range. Overall, if you are just after amazing, mostly neutral, yet still slightly punchy sound, definitely give these a shot. I love them! I just docked 1 star because of the noticeable bluetooth background noise and the fact there's no controls on the aux cord.
