date_review: Reviewed in the United States on December 16, 2023
comment: There's A LOT to love about the Sony WH-1000XM5. I really wanted to write a rave review on them. Unfortunately I've also had a series of horrible problems that make them impossible to recommend.I'll start with the good. 1) These have the best ANC (active noise cancellation) on the consumer market right now. I also have Airpods Max and have compared with a freind's top of the line Bose QC Ultra. These put both to shame when it comes to ANC. It's incredible. Like so good it's almost dangerous.... I kinda worry I wouldn't hear a fire alarm going off while listening to music with these lol. I should note though, that to get this ANC performance you have to make sure there's nothing between the earpads and your head, like a hat or bunched up hair. My metal framed glasses don't make a difference, but my chunkier plastic frames let a bit more noise through  2) The battery life is amazing. I've been getting 24-28 hours of use with ANC on for each charge. They also charge fast - for me it's typically 45 minutes to go from zero to fully charged. For fast charging you do need a quality USB-C cable (I use Anker cables - they're excellent and very affordable). When I used a cheap crappy cable it took over 2 hours. 3) They're incredibly light-weight and very comfortable. I almost forget I'm wearing them. The ergonomics make them feel like they're custom made for my head and the ear pads and head band are the softest I've ever felt on headphones. The build is pretty plasticky, but they still feel well made / durable... and I think it's worth it for the weight reduction it allows. 4) Like any Bluetooth noise canceling headphones you're not getting hi-fi audio quality, but its better than most other bluetooth headphones. It's not as good as Airpods Max, but better than Bose and any of the cheaper bluetooth headphones I've tried. The most notable weakness is some muddiness in the lower frequencies, in my experience. 5) The case it comes with is awesome. It's a bit bulky, but it keeps the headphones very well protected and has a small compartment that you can keep a charging cable or 3.5mm audio cable in (which you can use for a wired connection if the battery dies, if the device you're using has a headphone jack). It's also very nice aesthetically. Overall the case puts Apple's Airpods Max case to absolute shame - that one barely covers half of the headphones, so it's worthless for protection. I'd honestly throw it away, but Apple is a dick and decided to make it so the headphones are always on and using battery unless you put them in their crappy case. 6) If you download the mobile app, there are tons of options to customize your experience. You can change the EQ, turn speak-to-chat on/off (disables ANC when it detects you're speaking to someone), choose your priority between sound quality vs. stable bluetooth connection, allow to connect to 2 devices simultaneously, integrate Siri or Amazon Alexa, customize controls, and a bunch of other things.Okay, now the problems. 1) A week after I bought them the speaker in the right ear started randomly making a loud buzzing/popping noise periodically. It's not all the time, but pretty frequent and very annoying. It happens for about 30 seconds a few times every hour of use. Sony claims it happens in places where ultrasonic waves are used to eliminate rodents and suggests you turn off ANC to prevent it... which is aggravating. ANC is the only thing that makes these worth such a high price tag and Sony is the only brand with that problem. Also, I'm 90% sure their explanation doesn't even apply to my environment. 2) Just two weeks after I bought them the touch controls started FREAKING OUT, detecting gestures when I wasn't even touching them. It rapidly flips between playing and pausing my music, skip songs, flip between enabling/disabling voice-to-chat, etc. all on its own, making them entirely unusable when that happens. It happens every hour or two, and once it starts it continues until I turn them off and back on. When I contacted Sony about this, they advised me to just disable gesture controls in the app. That prevents it from pausing or skipping my music, but it does not turn off the pinging sound the headphones make when a a tap/gesture id detected, so you still hear rapid random pinging  whenever it decides to bug out. SUPER annoying. 3) 4 weeks after I bought them they just turned off on their own suddenly 10 minutes after I finished charging them to 100% and would not turn back on. I tried a factory reset and they still wouldn't turn on. after repeatedly trying to turn them on, they finally did... for a second, but shut down right after connecting them to my device. I figured they were completely busted, but when I tried again a few hours later they started working again and were fine for a few day... then it happened again. No idea what the deal is, but it's happened 4 times now, so I need to send to Sony to see if they'll fix them. Based on past experience trying to use Sony's warranty for repairs on other products though, they're probably going to send them right back and claim nothing is wrong because it didn't happen during their 30-second inspection.To summarize, these are SO CLOSE to being the best wireless ANC headphones to buy right now IMO. I really love them when they work... whenever I have to use my much more expensive Airpods Max, they make me wish I were using the XM5s minus all the issues. When they work, I prefer almost everything about the XM5 over the airpods. Unfortunately they're ruined by a few really bad problems. I would recommend getting the WH-1000XM4 instead. They have the same noise cancelling performance and most of the other great qualities and haven't been plagued with bugs. They're slightly less comfortable, but the tighter fit makes them more secure, which can be a benefit for people who want to wear them while working out.

date_review: Reviewed in the United States on October 2, 2023
overview_text: I Can't Stand the Touch Controls!!
comment: I bought the xm5 to replace my pair of BOSE Quiet Comfort 35ii headphones, which I have used daily for over 3 years now. My first impression upon receiving the new Sony headphones was that they were quite bulky. Unlike the QCs, they are not foldable, which I really liked because they did not take up a ton of space in my bag.However, my biggest problem with these headphones involves the touch controls. Instead of physical buttons for volume, answering calls, etc., you control the Sony headphones by touch. Want to increase volume? Swipe up on headphone exterior. Answer call? Tap twice. Etc.Well I use my headphones every night to block out snoring, which means I use them while laying down. The touch controls are so sensitive that I could not lay on my right side at all, because anytime the pillow came into contact with the headphones, the music would either pause, skip forward or back, or get louder/quieter inadvertently. This also happened frequently while wearing them during the day if I raised my arm or moved my head a certain way. Each time anything came into contact with the headphones, my music would stop and I'd hear a beep, which got very annoying, very quickly.While the ANC in general is pretty great on the Sonys, I was not impressed by the Speak-to-Chat feature that automatically turns off noise cancelation when it detects you're having a conversation. I found that even the slightest sound was enough to trigger it, which was incredibly frustrating when trying to listen to a podcast or music. I could not yawn or sigh or clear my throat without the headphones turning off ANC and disrupting my listening with background noise that I was specifically trying to drown out. This was an issue even when I turned that specific feature off due to the sensitive touch controls, which would randomly turn the feature back on if headphones were touched a certain way.Finally, these were not nearly as comfy as my Bose headset. They seem fine for short-term use, but felt a bit tight after about an hour of wear. The ear cushions seem a bit firmer and not as breathable as I would have liked. Even when just wearing them around my neck, they felt awkward due to the inability to lay them flat on my chest instead of having the ear pad side exposed.Battery life is great, noise cancellation is amazing (when it's not interrupted), but neither is great enough to overcome the annoyances described above.Unfortunately, I'll be returning these in exchange for another pair of BOSE Qc35ii.

overview_text: Over valued headset - great, but not cheap - Extremely bad volume/pairing control
comment: This is another great product from Sony. If you want to pause to tap twice. But hold on there, that you need to tap in the right spot, otherwise does not work (you might find yourself tapping your headset while walking, and it is hard to aim for the same spot!). The same with volume up and down. For some design reasons, the volume works in phases, so if you want to lower fully, you cannot, you are only able to lower bit by bit, repeating the action several times to get to the right volume. It is ridiculous. Takes a hell of a time and keep you busy with the device instead of enjoying your music/sound.The issue is very similar than the smart watches that has digital (virtual) control over functions, instead of having a wheel that you can operate with your fingers any time, including while wearing gloves. If you have your hand wet or you are on the move, it is basically impossible to operate the device. The mechanical wheel is the answer. The same with this headset: why the hell Sony removed the volume and pairing buttons? I wont buy the next generation of headset if they carry on this way.The device (headset) has been thought in a engineering environment, by engineers, not users.  So it works precisely as the engineers defined, under the perfect conditions BUT life of the user is different. Try to volume up while entering a plane and having to carry your hand suitcase: impossible. Try to pair quickly with your rental car while on the go: impossible. The Sony headsets are a good piece of engineering but has huge challenges. My advise is to buy something alternative and not to spent so huge amount of money for a product that aim to re-invent the headset. Previous Sony headset did the job, was so hard to just improve on the comfort, the battery life and noise cancellation without the need of removing all switches in this new model? date_review: Reviewed in the United States on February 14, 2024
comment: I upgraded to the XM5 after owning the XM2 for many years. I used the XM2 for 6 to 8 hours per day most workdays over the last 4-5 years, and I've done the same with the XM5 over the past 2 months. I also occasionally wear them while traveling by plane.The XM5 is good, but it let me down in four notable areas:* Noise cancelation for the wearer: Sometimes these things can't make up their mind about which noise cancelation profile to use. This results in a noticeable and distracting changes in the background noise that I hear. The issue has occurred when I'm sitting in an airplane seat in very mild to negligible turbulence, and also occurs when I'm sitting in a slightly bouncy chair. This happens whether or not Adaptive Sound Control is enabled. I don't mind if the noise cancelation profile occasionally changes and I can hear it, but this sometimes happens maybe 2-3 times per minute. Noise cancelation of the XM5 is maybe a bit better than the XM2, but at least the XM2 was consistent.* Noise cancelation of the microphone: This was the main selling point that convinced me to upgrade from the XM2, but since switching to the XM5 I've had more occasions where the person on the other end of a call couldn't hear me well and I had to revert to my phone or laptop microphone. I can't tell if this is just correlation or causation.* Battery life: It's good, but surprisingly no better than what I was getting with my XM2 with its 4+ year old well used LiPo battery. I typically go 2-3 full workdays without charging them, and will get low battery warnings around 4 days.* The material used on the earmuffs is squeaky when rubbing against my glasses. This is not a problem if I'm perfectly still, but just the slightest motion of my head causes the squeak. This didn't happen with the XM2.On the plus side, USB-C charging is nice (though that existed since the XM3), they are a bit more comfortable than the XM2, and being able to simultaneously pair to two devices is nice. To my ears, the music sound quality is about the same between the XM2 and the XM5.Overall, I wouldn't say that either the XM2 or the XM5 is better than the other, but I'm giving it 3 out of 5 because I expected that the XM5 would be better than the XM2. None of the issues are deal breakers for me, but all together they make the XM5 border between underwhelming and disappointing.

The first day I received them, something really weird happened and the sound went completely muffled - like I was underwater. The sounds went back to normal the next day, but I was already skeptical about their performance.**Comfort (9/10): I think they were really comfortable. I wear plastic framed glasses, so headphones that work with them can be a mission. The Apple AirPods Max do not work with my glasses at all, they pinch my frames and move them around - I need to wear contacts with them. With the Sony WH-1000XM5, this really isn't an issue. I needed to adjust my glasses every once in a while, but maybe once in like 3 hours. I think they're one of the best fitting headphones for people with glasses. Also, when I went to adjust the headband portion to make them shorter/tighter, they would slip - they just would not stay adjusted to where I needed them (this could be because I bought them slightly used, so it could have just been from previous wear - but still an issue if they become loose over time).**Product Quality (6/10): The headphones themselves are cheap plastic and just feel flimsy. The case is nice and hard, and I personally think they store nicely and are easy to travel around with. I bought the beige ones (again, I bought them slightly used), but the case was dirty and it stains easily since it's made of cloth material. The foam on the ear part is very soft, so it's kind of just your preference there. I think they felt a little cheap, but I also think that they added to the comfort.**Battery Life (9/10): The battery life is fine, they last pretty long. Overall the sound just felt incredibly unbalanced and unsophisticated, kind of like it was playing underwater. Now, obviously take it with a grain of salt: the sound is probably fine - it's not like it's unlistenable. I instead bought the Sennheiser's HD 560S and couldn't be happier. overview_text: Great ANC, Passthrough, and Audio Quality, but less comfortable and missing previous features
comment: I'm no audiophile, just a bit more picky than most people, but you can find resources online with exact specifications about the audio quality. They're certainly the best sounding headphones I've ever gotten.I own both the previous models, the WH-1000XM3 & XM4, and the quality of the sound, noise cancelling, and passthrough mode has gotten better with each iteration. The passthrough on these compared to the XM4's now feels lile night and day, as these allow me to hear my surroundings far better.However, I have had a few small issues with these. The redesign of the headphone strap looks and feels more modern with a higher build quality than the previous versions, and they're slightly lighter, but they're a bit more uncomfortable to wear for long periods. The strap is thinner, so the pressure on the top of my head is spread out over a smaller area, which begins to hurt after a couple hours if I don't wear a hat or hood to spread out the weight a bit. This is also somewhat avoidable by simply adjusting their position on my head every once in a while.One advantage these have over previous models is the ability to seamlessly switch between two connected devices, but this has it's issues. I use a Samsung phone and a Windows PC, so results may vary, but often the computer will just take control of the headphones despite not playing anything. For example, I double tap the right ear cup to pause something playing on my phone, then a few seconds later, do the same to resume it. For some reason, the headphones often decide to switch control to the computer during that brief pause window, resuming whatever was playing on it, or just doing nothing at all if nothing was playing. This happens even if all the audio on the PC is muted, no programs are open, and no media is or was playing.The XM4's had a handy solution for switching devices: NFC. I could hold my phone up to the headphones to quickly connect & disconnect it, making switching between devices quick even though only one could be connected at a time. I always knew which device the headphones were currently controlling. However, much to my surprise, the XM5's completely lack any NFC functionality. This would be fine, if connecting to two devices at once didn't have this issue. It's not a dealbreaker, though, as I just have to remember to disconnect them from my PC when I get up, or spend a few extra seconds getting my phone out of my pocket every time I want to resume something I was listening to.If you get these, here's a tip: don't clip your nails in passthrough mode. Something about the sound of clipping nails causes the passthrough mode to make a loud, high-frequency noise and shut off for about a second. This also happens for some other loud sounds, but clipping nails consistently causes it.In conclusion, I do believe that the XM5's were a worthy upgrade for me from the 4's. The improvements in noise cancellation are a godsend when there's constant noise around the house, which is all the time. I do wish there were an option to turn off the weird adjustments the ANC makes sometimes to try to adapt to the environment, as occasionally it will try to adjust each ear individually, resulting in a weird pressure sensation in my head due to the uneven audio cancelling.

comment: I'll keep my review short. These headphones are a niche product, but I really think this design choice deserves more credit. The open back nature of these headphones add a really natural effect to sound. However it does come at the cost of base and treble response since an open back earbud naturally does not create a seal. BUT.... that lack of seal was the exact reason I purchased these. Normal earbuds with rubber plugs are very irritating to my ears. Especially when using the controls, having to constantly seal them back in my ear, or taking them in and out to talk to people. Call quality was amazing as the listener, although the mics I would say are "adequate at best". The added benefit of them not muffling outside noises was a HUGE plus for talking to people, commuting, and just overall being comfortable. These where my favorite earbuds ever until....These units started failing on me a little over the 1 year mark. The case often flashes orange when charging (indicating a charging issue), the right earbud rarely charges at all anymore and the left one has some kind of issue where the charge level is all over the place when in use and does not last very long. Even new though, the right bud would drain about 3x faster than the left one, but until recently was not an issue problematic enough for me to care about. I am not the type to abuse my tech, these never where exposed to water, I never left them in a hot car, etc.I contacted Sony about this 3 times in the span of the last 2 months. The first time they told me they would exchange it for a new pair but to contact them again in a week when they finished system repairs on their end to process it. The second time, they told me to do some trouble shooting steps first and then they would exchange it if it was still behaving weird. On the third time they told me I was outside of warranty and that they would not be exchanging it. They would not listen to me telling them the other 2 reps said they would exchange it, they did not care when I told them I had the chat transcripts to prove it. Only on the 3rd conversation did they tell me my device was purchased more than a year ago, then attempted to lie about the first 2 not knowing about that (even though that was the first question both of them asked) and then referred me to a repair center to pay it out of pocket myself. Which obviously, would cost more then the buds did themselves. Even explaining how the first 2 techs asked for purchase date as the first question did not phase them. I even had a case number, which I used to file a complaint and they still did not care. For anyone reading this, I am not upset my device was out of warranty. I am upset they doubled down on saying they would exchange it wasting weeks of my time to only at the end deny it like they where giving me the run around. Just stating the first time it was out of warranty would have been fine, and this review would be a lot better. To any Sony Rep thinking about sending the "Sorry you had a bad experience please contact us" copy/paste response to this, I am not interested, you have already shown how you communicate with existing customers and I am not interested in being lied to for a month again. Which is ashame considering how many Sony products I have purchased over the years.

overview_text: Wait until a new version comes out.
comment: Curb your enthusiasm.They are an open back tws which does allow you to here your environment very well, but music is almost completely lost in moderately noisy environment. Anything under 300 hz is not pleasant and almost missing without giving it a proper EQ. Even after the EQ you’re missing a lot of bass and all of the sub bass. Mids and highs are usable in quiet environments, but there’s nothing to write home about. Soundstage is unique, but how they sit in your ear has an enormous effect on what you hear and where you think you’re hearing it from.The provided wings/tips are under built and tend to lose their shape. I recommend using an over sized tip and dealing with the discomfort until it deforms and puts let’s pressure on your ear. If you use a tip that fits appropriately it will deform and over time the ear buds will fall out very easily, especial if your sweaty or in a humid environment. The part of the bud that enters your ear is also made out of a hard plastic that becomes pretty uncomfortable. If you typically use small earbud tips completely pass on these. Even if you have average sized ears you’ll experience the buds pressing to hard against cartilage.Battery life is pretty poor under normal circumstances, but it gets worse if you’re raising the volume to compensate for the lack of noise isolation. It gets even worse if you’re using the preprogrammed smart commands. The commands are not worth the hit on battery performance and I simply recommend not using them. The commands are frequently unresponsive or over active depending on what firmware update you’re using.The earbuds do frequently unpair from each other. Although they can typically recover pretty quickly it’s enough to mess a call up or have a negative effect on any music listening experience. I’ve found that simply placing your phone in your pocket, across multiple devices, is enough to break the connection.Overall I do not recommend these… at all. If you’re curious about how they sound try them first. I’m expecting that the next generation will have something more to offer than what we got here. After owning them for one year I can confidently say that you’re better off buying something like the the AirPods Pro 2, sennheiser momentum 3, or the moondrop Alice. date_review: Reviewed in the United States on March 2, 2023
overview_text: Great until they get dirty, then they're trash
comment: These open-air ear buds were initially a revelation to me.  They sounded so good and left me "connected" to the world around me rather than feeling isolated.  Phone calls and music were both great quality (though music a little lacking in bass as expected for an open earbud).Here's the problem -- you put these things in your ear, right?  There's ear wax in your ear, right?  That ear wax is going to get in the tiny little holes in these things.  It's very hard to clean those little holes out without accidentally pushing the ear wax inside the ear buds.  Once it's inside you will start to get really annoying buzzing sounds constantly as the wax interferes with the vibrating parts inside.  You cannot open these things up at all to clean that stuff out, nor does just soaking in something like isopropyl alcohol work (in my experience).  Sometimes you can dislodge or rearrange the wax temporarily by playing very loud bass-heavy music, but that's only temporary -- the buzzing will for sure come back.  Eventually that trick no longer works.So for me, these lasted only about 8 months before the sound quality became unacceptable, and that was even with me trying to very carefully clean them without pushing the wax further inside.  These things are way too expensive to last only 8 months.BTW, the most effective cleaning method I found was to get some blunt syringes (the kind sold for crafts and hobbies not for injections, usually sold as "injection syringes").  You can use these in reverse to suck stuff out of those little holes.  This is very laborious and doesn't always work.  Totally not worth it.

comment: My ears react badly to in-ear earbuds ever since I used the Samsung Galaxy Buds Pro and my doctor tells me to stop using tipped earbuds every time I have to go see him!  So, in my search for good irritant-free open earbuds, I tried the Sony Linkbuds - for about 15 minutes!.They are small!  I have the Sony WF-1000XM4 and thought these were similar in overall size, since there's some design similarity, but they seem tiny in comparison.  I have very large ears and wingtips never seem to work.  While the largest hoop did manage to hook into my concha, it was not a very solid fit and the buds could move around fairly easily, affecting the sound signature a lot.  Depending upon the angular position in my concha, the Linkbuds were either just OK or somewhat loose.  The hoop is not stiff at all and is only designed to stop the buds falling outwards, not to restrain it rotationally.  IMHO, they are very comfortable to wear because they aren't held in position that securely!  ☹.The donut speaker sat comfortably in my ear, but it was clearly at the wrong angle for any decent bass.  If I pressed firmly on the battery portion, the sound actually was pretty good, with a surprisingly substantial bass presence.  If they sounded that good all the time, I'd have kept them.  However, when I let go and the Linkbuds resumed their natural position in my ears, the sound went tinny and no better than $10 earbuds!  I just couldn't find a fit which gave a full, balanced sound worthy of the hefty price tag... and these are expensive for what they are..My wife and daughter tried them and the Linkbuds seemed to fit their smaller ears much better.  Not sure if they got a good sound as they aren't as audiophilic as me  😉 .  They did say they were fiddly to insert properly, with that hoop, and not worth the hassle..Disappointed, I returned these almost immediately for a refund.  My experience will be for my ears only.  I'm certainly not average when it comes to my ear shape.Each person's ears are unique, even left to right.  You may get a good fit, or you may not!  I'm just warning you that these are not a "one-size-donut fits all" set of earbuds, even with the different sizes of hoops, and that donut speaker positioning over the ear canal is critical for the sound.

The background noise is mild to nonexistent so I can hear my audiobooks easily while remaining aware of anything else going on around me, which is perfect. The sound quality is excellent (when there is no other competing noise). The wide area tap shortcuts are also great (and customizable to fit your needs).The biggest complaint I have is the battery life. I have yet been able to hit the 17.5 hours (which is already low) that Sony states the earbuds/case have. And if you're talking on the phone? That'll drain them VERY quickly. It's not a deal breaker for me - I only use them a few hours a day while walking. But keep it in mind if you're looking for an all-day pair because these won't last.So, if you're looking for earbuds that you only need for short periods of time in near silence while staying aware of your surroundings, these are for you! date_review: Reviewed in the United States on November 11, 2022
overview_text: Very niche product with a LOT of trade-offs
comment: The short version of this review is that I think this is a product that will make a very limited set of people happy that are looking for something very specific or don’t care about a lot of the trade-offs that come with making a product like this. It is tough to recommend for a general audience.  For that small group, maybe it is four stars, but for everyone else, I’d say it’s two stars, so three overall.  Let me get into the why…So to start, I’m big into music and headphones, and I own a total of 12 pairs.  Four of those are “consumer” headphones like AirPods Pro 2, AirPods Max, Sennheiser True Wireless 3, and all of the rest are true HiFi headphones like Audeze, Focal, Fostex, Denon, etc. and all of the accompanying amplifiers and DACs.  I generally enjoy lots of different genres of music - rock, alternative, R&B, hip-hop, pop, some classical.  I just point this out, to point out I do a LOT of detailed sound comparisons and appreciate lots of different types of music and how different headphones may impact the experience.So, with these, I think there are only a few specific reasons one should even consider these, as if you don’t fall into BOTH #1 AND at least one of the other reasons below, there are far better options for this price.#1 - you really don’t like the “closed” feeling of buds and want a more “open” sound (and as such don’t care at all about noise isolation - both from outside and others hearing your listen, which is standard for any open setup)#2 - you don’t care about sound quality much but want some wireless buds that are stable enough to do light workouts in or just want some really small/discrete buds#3 - you primarily listen to music like jazz and classicalNow onto the logic and trade-offs.First, with respect to the sound.  The tonal balance is extremely lacking in low end.  The reviews that have said that these are a “balanced sound” are simply wrong.  If you search around the net, you can see some sites have actually measured the frequency response of these, and not only is the bass very rolled off, it creeps up into the lower mids as well.  This results in a very hollow listen.  Music has nearly no low-end impact at all.  Even with every bass setting cranked all the way up, it makes almost no noticeable difference because the drivers and design simply can’t handle it (which I’ll get back to).  Further evidence of this, the EQ in the app only even goes down to 400Hz, which should be a sign, as most wouldn’t even consider it true “bass” until maybe 150Hz, and humans can hear down to 20Hz - yet the EQ doesn’t even let you adjust these frequencies.  To call this balanced is just wrong.  Good balanced headphones simply do not OVER-emphasize bass or let it bleed into the other frequencies - these lack bass, period.  This is a very big difference if you listen to basically any Top 40 type music - hip-hop, pop, R&B, EDM, even rock or alternative.  There will be no bass.  This CAN be ok, however, if you’re a classical music listener or jazz or music that doesn’t have a lot of low-end (including bass drums, bass guitar, etc.).  These would also be OK if you’re primarily going to use them for listening to voice stuff - podcasts, audiobooks, news, etc.The rest of the frequency response is overall just OK.  You can adjust the mids and upper frequencies to your liking, and those adjustments make more of a difference than the bass adjustment, as I mentioned.  So you can tone down or up the brightness to your liking, for example.  They do an OK job at brining out detail, about what I would expect for buds in this price range.  The semi-standout in the overall sound is the soundstage, or the way the music is presented in terms of position in space.  Because of the “open” design, they are somewhat more natural sounding in terms of airiness and don’t have that “dome in your head” kind of feeling.  That said, the stage itself is not hugely bigger than “regular” buds (goes ear to ear, maybe a tad outside the ear), it’s just a slightly more open stage.  Because the buds are still sitting in your ear, versus when an over-ear open headphone has a driver sitting outside your ear, i would call these only semi-open sounding.  The inside your head feeling is gone, but you still don’t get that great open naturalness of a true open-back headphone.  The positioning is also good, meaning, individual pieces of the mix are fairly separated and identifiable, for this price range.  The question is it worth the trade offs…Open back headphones of all types (buds, over-ear, etc.), all else equal, have less bass response than closed-backs.  This is because there’s less pressure build up and resonance for the bass to build (in simple terms).  So the tradeoff for losing that “in your head” feeling is less bass.  Bigger, over ear headphones can counter this by using bigger drivers that can pump more bass and by still creating somewhat of a seal around your ear with the pads.  in this case, these buds just sit in your ear, create no seal, and the drivers are tiny, so you get basically no bass.  This is the biggest trade off of these.  Whether that trade off is for you or not…your call.The other tradeoff is size.  Smaller size leads to smaller drivers, which as I discussed means less bass, and it also means - way small batteries.  Although the “up to” five hours of battery life may be accurate, there are some big issues with this.  First, you have to turn off all of the electronic conveniences to hit this target - automatic voice detection, automatic volume adjustment, wide area tap - which are all pretty cool.  Keep these on, and battery is more like two hours, which is FAR below, by more than half, what most buds get nowadays.Call performance is decent, and fit for me is also decent, though individual ears always vary with fit.  The smallest included piece is what got me the best fit, and they are stable in my ears.What these actually remind me of are the first AirPods that were released, then upgraded to the AirPods Pro.  The original AirPods also had a “sit in your ear” plastic design that was somewhat like this.  While they were wireless and packed with nice new apple “magic” features, many had a view that they really still sounded like the $30 wired buds that came with iPods/iPhones at the time, but they were wireless.  Then Apple released the AirPods Pro that claimed “far better sound”, and the biggest change was that they used a silicon tip to create a seal in the ear - and that added a way more appropriate low-end to the sound that was missing before, and NOW and AirPods Pro and Pro 2 are known as a mostly balanced set of buds.  These are the opposite - by having no seal, combined with tiny drivers, I would say these have the sound profile of a $50 or less pair of buds, but you are paying for the true wireless stuff and fancy features.  They MAY be worth it for you if you don’t mind the trade offs, but that’s not most.

overview_text: Unique design, but could use some work
comment: For context, the only other pair of wireless earbuds that I own are the Samsung Galaxy Buds+. I don't use transparency mode on my wireless earbuds and headphones, since it doesn't sound natural to me. But I think that's a given, since transparency mode reproduces outside sound with microphones. The LinkBuds fit my use case.Pros:- The sound is alright. Due to its design, it won't sound as detailed as in-ear earbuds, or as good as a pair of open-back headphones for around the same price, but I like it.- It sounds open. It still sounds a little bit like there's something covering the ears, but I can comfortably make phone calls or sing and hum along to music.- It feels very lightweight and is quite small, yet it doesn't fall out of my ears.But there are some cons that ultimately make me want to return them:- Mediocre battery life: Only rated for 5.5 hours on a single charge, less if you're using it with phone calls as well. I thought this wouldn't be a deal breaker for me, but it is.- The case: The hinge is floppy and loose. The case closes with a latch and button mechanism instead of being magnetic. You have to press the earbuds into the case until they click. Overall, it feels cheap.- I hate the color. Regardless of whether you pick gray or white, it's speckled, which makes it looks like there's dust and nicks on it.- Bluetooth issues: Sometimes I can hear a noticeable reduction in sound quality, or the sound becomes unbalanced between the left and right earpieces. I have this issue as well with my Galaxy Buds+, but it isn't as frequent as it is on the LinkBuds, and only happens when paired with my Macbook. I also sometimes get some sound distortion after a few minutes while watching YouTube videos, and one way to fix it is to pause and play the video. I've never encountered this with my other wireless headphones.Flaws, but not deal breakers:- No touch controls for volume control and going back to the previous track.- The "wide area tap" feature is nifty, but can be a bit sensitive. There were a few times where it skipped a track or paused the music while I was eating. I have this issue with the Galaxy Buds+ as well, but it only happens when I'm biting on something hard, like carrots.Overall, I really wanted to like it, but I think I'll wait and see if a future iteration of this product will fix the issues I mentioned above.

date_review: Reviewed in the United States on September 28, 2022
comment: If you want any noise cancellation (active or passive), this isn't for you. These earphones are great to wear on my commute, because I can still hear train announcements or the conductor coming through to check tickets. The sound is good, unless you raise the volume too high (these are small, after all), and don't have much bass. The open-backed sound you get is nice, compared to the over-ear noise cancelling headphones I'm used to.The real problem with these earphones is the way they're designed to stay in your ear. The wings do great in my right ear, but not my left. More annoyingly, they'll both work fine for a few hours, but at some point the left earphone just feels like it starts slipping out. Unlike in-ear earphones that make a seal by pressing the silicone tip into your ear canal, the way this stays in is a combination of where the wing makes contact with your ear (the rotation of the earphone matters here), and the way it sits just outside your ear canal. The former is far more finicky than the latter. The first day I got these I was eager to try them out, and actually ended up severely aggravating both ears because I was messing with the position so often (and boy did I have it wrong). I was unable to wear them for about a week after that due to the abrasions and inflammation that caused, but that's entirely on me. The fact is, however, that they're not easy or intuitive to wear from the start.Ultimately, I like them and use them, but I feel like this design won't last. That doesn't mean they never should have existed, though. I like that Sony tried something different. While it may not have a huge user base, I think it's better to experiment than to just release the same product with minor tweaks year after year.

However, these just have some of the dumbest hiccups I've ever encountered. As well, I was rocking the Sony WFs as my nicer non-activity earbuds but since they recently broke and I made the switch to Apple's Airpod Pros I cannot believe how much discomfort and lack of functionality I was opting in for. Seriously Sony, get it together!Oh not to mention I am frequently losing connection to my audio for split seconds, but it happens so reliably that it makes me rewind podcasts or throw me out of a good song. Had the same issue with my WFs and this must be something Sony is aware of.If you want a quality earbud that is extremely lightweight (I often forget their in when I pause my music/podcasts), lets in ambient noise, doesn't fatigue your ears, has nice call quality and more than decent music quality, this is it. As other reviews have mentioned, these are great, innovative open ear headphones and I hope they continue developing them to get rid of some of the problem areas. I'm giving these guys a 5/5 for the encouraging step forward, but it would probably be closer to a 4/5 if there were more earbuds with similar features.If you want noice cancelling, this isn't for you. These Linkbuds are specifically designed to allow in ambient noise, and they do this much better than bone conduction ever will. When I had Aftershokz, I would have to play my podcasts at 100% volume when outside to be able to understand 75% of what was being said. When conduction is at 100% volume, the volume is still too low but your face is vibrating like crazy and it's really irritating (and concerning). Aftershokz ships their headphones with earplugs, because when you plug your ears the noise no longer escapes and is instead amplified –– and yeah, that's really loud, but WAY too loud and I seriously don't know how that can be healthy. With Linkbuds, the sound is pointed at your ear so that you can still hear everything at moderate volume while retaining ambient awareness.LInkbuds also has a cool feature where you can tap your cheek for music playback and call controls, instead of blindly slapping at earbuds which can be a pain. date_review: Reviewed in the United States on January 19, 2024
overview_text: The Sony Linkbuds get a bad rap
comment: First off I want to say, I absolutely adore these earbuds. They are perfect for my use case, I work in an environment where I need to be able to hear and talk to people when needed but I also have some downtime where I like to enjoy some casual music listening. Speak-to-chat is the most useful feature on any earbud for me and is a must have when at work. So naturally, I gravitated toward these but not without trying others first. The first pair of two pair of earbuds I got with this feature were the Samsung Galaxy buds2 Pro and the Pixel buds Pro. Admittedly, the Samsung's implementation of said feature is better than these but the Linkbuds work well enough. The problem I ran into with the two buds mentioned before is that their transparency mode (and all other in-ear earbuds) gives this digital effect to voices and to me is quite unnatural sounding when having a conversation. So what better way to get around this issue than with an open-air design. I know this design doesn't work for everybody and causes a roll-off in both bass and treble. However, there is a market for this design and other companies have made open-air earbuds but no company has designed them in the way the Linkbuds are designed. Still being in the ear instead of hovering around the ear makes for a more enjoyable and comfortable experience. In addition, this keeps the earbuds size much smaller than others. Albeit, at the cost of battery life but you can't win them all.As mention above, I purchased the Pixel buds Pro. Mainly, because I own a Pixel phone and they had all the features I was looking for. However, I could never get the sound I wanted out of the buds, to me they always sounded muddy in the bass and congested in the mid-range. I can gladly say that the sound from the Linkbuds it much more suited to my liking. Even with some bass and treble roll-off due to the design, I typically listen at lower volume (got to protect your hearing) and at lower volumes the bass tones and treble detail become much harder to hear anyway meaning the roll-off isn't a large issue for me.Lastly, I want to talk about the negatives I have with the Linkbuds. First, is the battery life, other than Speak-to-Chat I have most other features turned off, no DSEE, no Google Assistant set to either earbud, no Spatial Audio, no Adapative Sound Control, and Multipoint. All of these features have a bad correlation with battery and the 5.5 hours advertised is most definitely with these features turned off. In addition, I tried to turn off Wide Area Tap but for some reason even toggled off in the app, Wide Area Tap stays on. Ironically though, it comes in handy when wearing a beanie. With the size of these earbuds, battery life was going to take a hit and I am more or less ok with that. My final issue is with price, at $180 these are a little too step. They most certainly are not a top seller for Sony, so I am not sure as to why they are still at full price. I think $100 would be much more appropriate for these buds.All-in-all, the Linkbuds have an innovative design and incredible comfort. If you're on the fence about purchasing a pair I urge you to go through the pros and cons and what decide if you're comfortable with giving up all the other feature of in-ear earbuds when buying these earbuds. Personally, they get 4 stars from me and full recommendation.

overview_text: The Most Unique Earbuds I've Ever Tried
comment: The Sony LinkBuds are the first "open" earbuds I've ever tried, and I love them. They allow you to hear outside noise while in use, similar to open headphones. The design is interesting; there's no earbud tip that sticks into your ear canal. Because of this, I can use them all day without any ear pain. They sit on the outside of the ear canal, rather than digging into it like most earbud designs. This also means they don't compact earwax into your ear and are less likely to get earwax on the earbud itself.The design to ensure the earbuds can't fall out is also one of the best. Standard earbud designs with the L stem tend to be wobbly, and they can potentially fall out with accidental hits or quick movements. The LinkBuds design hooks the earbud to your ear using the included silicone hook, preventing accidental dislodging. It's the most "fitted" earbud I've tried, and its smaller size makes the case slimmer and more compact. The flat earbuds also allow for comfortable use even while lying on a pillow, perfect for listening to meditation apps before sleeping.The software has a plethora of features that I immediately found useful. One of them is "wide area tap," allowing you to tap anywhere between your upper jawbone and under your earlobe for multi-touch controls. Other notable features include speak-to-chat, adaptive volume control, and simultaneous connections. The earbuds' ability to pause when you start speaking, adjust volume based on ambient sound, and seamlessly connect to multiple devices make them very convenient.However, there are some negatives to consider. The most obvious one is the lack of ANC (Active Noise Cancellation) due to the open earbud design. The firmware update is time-consuming, it took 2 hours for me. The app also lacks the ability to show the current battery percentage, updating only when the earbuds are reinserted into the case. Some touch controls cannot be fine-tuned or adjusted from their presets.Additionally, the charging case cannot be wirelessly charged, and there's no search function in the app to locate misplaced earbuds or the case, unlike Airpods. Achieving the perfect fit can be a bit challenging since they sit on the outside of the ear canal. While they are still comfortable to use, it's noticeable that there's a plastic donut outside the ear canal.Despite these flaws, the Sony LinkBuds have become my new favorite wireless earbuds. I appreciate the open design, which doesn't cause discomfort even after extended use. Unlike other earbuds, I can wear these all day without any major issues. It's a great product by Sony, although I do hope some of the mentioned negatives will be addressed in their next model.

date_review: Reviewed in the United States on September 14, 2022
overview_text: Great earbuds for very specific use cases
comment: Got these renewed a few days ago, since I didn't know whether I wanted to go full price considering they are an odd form factor and there are some mixed reviews. However, after a few days of adjustment period I really do love them. I bought them specifically for using when riding around on my bike (since I need ambient sound awareness when biking around traffic in the city) but I am finding out many other times that are perfect for using these and I gravitate towards them - around the office, when I am out and about walking the dog, when sitting at the airport waiting for my flight to start boarding, etc.  The ability to hear your surroundings is great, and if you pump up the volume you still can drown out most of the ambient noise if you choose to.The sound is great for the use we are talking about - it's a very pleasant sound signature, with clear and supple mids, and the highs rolled back a bit to match the fact that you will get a lower bass depth and punch than if you were using an in-ear with sound isolation. Let's be clear - if you want a set of earbuds that give you a meaty, thumpy bass these will be extremely disappointing. The bass is more or less hinted at, but not really very present - there's enough that the mix is not weird, but if you want that visceral thump of bass that hits in the chest, look elsewhere. But for casual listening while out and about, podcasts, pop, etc. they are really excellent. And like with any other set of headphones, once you start listening for a while and adjust to the sound, your brain fills in the rest. So you won't be missing much for casual listening.The fit takes a couple days to master. There's a tendency when you first get them to want to try to jam the speaker wheel closer to your ear canal to get more volume / bass, but that's not the way these go. Basically, keep the fin vertical at at 12 o'clock position and have them rest in front of the ear canal lightly. Once you get used to the fit, they are extremely comfortable, especially as you will not experience any of the "ear suck" common with in-ears.Battery life so far is good - after listening for an hour ad mid-volume I've lost about 12-14%, so that's more than adequate. The box is a bit fiddly, but I appreciate that the buds fit in securely with a noticeable clack, so you know they are charging and secure in their beds. The app works really well, I do recommend turning both Adaptive Volume Control (which dials up the volume to overcome ambient noise) and Wide Area Tap (which allows you to control the buds by tapping in front of the area). I also appreciate that there's a lot of configuration options for each earbuds gestures - I set mine up to control volume with the left bud, and playback with the right one and that works really well. Also, voice calls are excellent I am told.All in all, great little buds, and definitely fantastic for uses where you want to have some awareness of your surroundings...

date_review: Reviewed in the United States on July 26, 2022
overview_text: Good, balanced sound; tricky fitting; wind noise can be an issue
comment: I like to listen to music, audiobooks, and podcasts while out on my bicycle. After using a portable Bose bluetooth speaker strapped to my handlebars for a while, I realized not everyone on the bike path wanted to hear my stuff and some of it just wasn't appropriate for all audiences. I own a lot of wireless headphones and earbuds, but I needed something that would let me hear my surroundings along with my personal audio. After reading mixed reviews about transparency modes, I decided the Sony Linkbuds were likely my best solution. I was able to get these free through an incentive points system at work, so I went for them.People will say these don't have explosive bass, and that's true. With that said, they have a pretty balanced spectrum and I can generally pick out the highs, mids, and lows with no issue. The only time this isn't true is when I'm out on my bike, due to wind noise. You simply won't get the full spectrum on a bicycle with these. That's the tradeoff for the open design and the ability to hear your surroundings. For me the audio is good enough for my use case, and the main thing for me was being able to listen to stuff while remaining aware of what's going on around me. For this, the buds work great.My greatest challenge with these was finding a secure fit. All the ear models you see Sony using have ears that seem perfectly designed for an easy fit. I don't have the straight lines and deep ridges of the models, so it took me several days to find the right position. In my case, I have to rotate the buds forward so they catch a bit of the outer ridge of my ear. For a while they would fall out pretty regularly, which made me nervous about using them on a bike, but once I found my fit, they stopped falling out and are comfortable to wear. (Pro tip: a little Nerdwax on the wingtips makes them less likely to pop out as well)Battery life is another thing I wish was better with these. They don't get anywhere near the advertised 5 hours between charges (Last time I tested this, the left earbud died at around 3.5 hours with about 35% charge left in the right—uneven drain is another issue as well). I don't take super long bike rides and don't listen to music for hours on end at my work desk, so this overall isn't a practical problem for me, but I wish there was more range there in case I wanted to use them for more than a couple hours at a time.These buds are good for specific use cases like mine, but probably not for everyone.

date_review: Reviewed in the United States on April 9, 2022
overview_text: These are a game changer but I'm hoping the next generation will fix some flaws
comment: The good...First off, you should know these headphones have a very innovative design that makes them a really nice addition to my collection. The open space in the middle of the driver allows a lot of ambient sound to enter your hearing. In other words, these are the exact opposite of noise-cancelling headphones. I wear these headphones when I want a low-volume soundtrack to my life (like with overhead speakers in a department store). In particular I love wearing them to things like kids' sports events when I need to be able to hear if another part starts chatting. I also wear these around the house when others are home and I want to remain engaged with them. In that type of use the sound is good enough to bring a big smile to my face. Bass is decent if turned up all the way in the app and you have appropriate expectations of an open headphone design. Sub-bass is non-existent, but that's not a surprise given the design.The tap controls are fantastic and very reliable. You tap two or three times just forward of your ears. I have it set up so the volume is on one side (two taps for increase, three taps for decrease). On the other side I have track control (two for pause/play, three for next track).The not so good...I've read many reviews that say they have all-day comfort. I don't find that to be true for my ears. They press on some small structures in my ear and I have soreness after a few hours. Even so, I love the function I get when wearing them so I tolerate it. I seem to be adapting to them with time, but the jury is still out on that. Your mileage may vary as to comfort.The bad...The connection to the phone in my pocket sometimes gets really glitchy. When it happens it's really annoying. I've found it happens less if I take the left bud out of the case first, but I could be imagining that. I have set them to prioritize connection over sound quality and that helps (and sound quality is still very good), but even then the quality of the connection isn't up to par compared to the other Bluetooth headphones I've owned (including the cheapo ones). Disappointing at this price point. I'm hoping a firmware update improves that down the road.The final verdict...Would I recommend them? Depends. I thought about returning them, so I wouldn't recommend them to everyone. But I ultimately decided to keep them because they allow me to listen to music in situations where I never could before. If the open design is something you're looking for and you're willing to tolerate some first-generation shenanigans, go for it.

date_review: Reviewed in the United States on February 25, 2024
overview_text: I wasn’t sure at first but I absolutely love these.
comment: I really wasn’t sure if I was making the right choice with these at first. I hate the feeling of sound canceling earbuds. Pass through audio is disorienting to me. I wouldn’t be able to wear my buds multiple days in a row without my ears getting irritated and I always felt like my ears were wet. I basically hated everything about in-ear earbuds except the convenience of music and audio books at work whenever I needed to stay on task.These Sony earbuds have fixed almost all of those problems. These have to be some of the most secure feeling buds I have ever worn. It took a day or two to get used to where they sit in my ear. At first it felt like they were in the spot I would feel my in-ear earbuds being when they were slipping out. So that took some getting used to. I love that they are open, my ears don’t feel plugged anymore. I don’t get any irritation from wearing them everyday.  The case is really nice and has a beautiful fell and design. The buds click in to their spot in the case which feels more secure than just a magnet. The silicon bands for sizing are flexible and soft while being sturdy enough to hold the bud in my ear nicely.I really hope they keep this model available because I don’t ever want to go back to in-ear earbuds ever again.Things you might consider a con, but don’t bother me for what I’m am using them for. The battery life is not as long as my previous buds. I get 4-5 hrs, but I use one bud at a time so I always have the other ready to go. The sound that passes through is just as loud as if the bud wasn’t in, so if you are expecting it to block outside sound at all these won’t be for you. If you are an audiophile I don’t think these will be for you either. The sound is good quality and I don’t listen to a lot of bass heavy music, so for me the quality of the sound is great. It’s also really nice for audio books. If you are expecting highly dynamic sound though I doubt these will give you what you want. Sometimes they pause for no reason. I assume it has to do with the way you can tap the side of your cheek to start and stop. I chew gum a lot and it seems to happen if I’m eating lunch or if I cough. So I think it’s confusing a deep sound for a tap on my face.Other than that these are a great fit for me. I love the open feeling of the sound. I like that my coworkers can get my attention easily. They are comfortable for my ears and don’t leave them tender after a day of use through my work shift. These are my new favorite earbuds and I am very happy with my purchase.

date_review: Reviewed in the United States on January 11, 2024
overview_text: Great casual sports buds without the bulk
comment: As a solo skier I wanted to listen to music without blasting it on speaker, I have Galaxy Buds Live which works fine if I'm going on a short bike ride but it's huge bean shape isn't the most comfortable for long use. Not to mention passively it doesn't actually let in much ambient sounds as I'd like. Of course one could use the ambient mode but that cuts down on battery life so it's not the full proof solution.So LinkBuds solves that problem with a small hole and it's quite an engineering feat as most other "active" earbuds often resort to hovering the speaker around the ear or bone conduction. Which can be quite a hit or miss on sound quality when it comes to music. This also often leads to big cumbersome design that cuts down on comfort level especially for prolonged use. Though LinkBuds are not miles ahead in terms of comfort hard plastic meant that it was shaping my ear rather than the other way around which also means that it's prone to falling out if it didn't have a time to settle in. With that said the compact size at least meant that it wasn't fighting against my ear muffs or helmet for space and completely squishing my ear into hell.Despite those layers clothes you can still use gestures to skip track or activate Google Assistant, because instead of using touch or buttons you are asked to just tap around your ears. I thought this might lead to lot of false triggers but surprisingly it's very consistent. The only thing I wish was that the controls were more customizable. As it stands you are limited to preset taps locked into the type of functionality. This does lead to one small problem which is volume control. According to the app if you tap uncontrollably it supposed to lead to volume control but I've never been able to get it to work so your mileage will vary.Last note is on battery life on average I seem to be getting around 5 hours from buds alone for 95% music streaming on mid~high volume. Which is more than enough for my ski session and it could be charged up while I take a lunch or dinner break so it definitely will last long.Price is the awkward note though. I'm not sure that it's worth MSRP of $180. Especially with that build quality that leaves something to be desired. Recycled plastic is great but it feels hollow and could easily break if I accidentally banged it against a table. With that said it's a product that's been around long enough that you can find refurb models for $50, at which price it's pretty much no-brainer.

overview_text: These do what no other earbuds can
comment: The short and sweet of it is that if you want a pair of bluetooth wireless earbuds that are open-backed these are essentially your only option. Personally I prefer a neutral soundscape so the lack of bass doesn't bother me but don't me mistaken the bass is not completely absent, just much less than a closed-back earbud. They are still miles above bone conduction headphones for both sound quality and sound space. The battery life is also not great. I get between 2 and 6 hours of usage depending on what I'm doing and at what volume, and the case holds maybe 2 or 3 full charges before needing to be plugged in. As far as fit I have big ears with big ear canals, so the perfectly round shape of the speaker doesn't feel uncomfortable, but I do need to use the largest rubber stabilizer loops. Even then, if I shake my head violently or really open my mouth they can and do get loose or fall out.However, for all of those downsides, I absolutely love these headphones. They are true open-backed wireless earbuds. Thus, I am primarily comparing these to products that already cause me discomfort, so keep this in mind.I purchased a brand new pair of the Sony Linkbuds off eBay and have had them for just over a week now. The first thing I'll state is that, like everyone else, it took me some getting used to the odd layout of these earphones. They're just about the same size as other earbuds like the Galaxy Buds, with the added quirk that there's the 2 separated sections. I actually do really like the layout of these and find that the 'Large' sized silicone cups work great to keep these in my ears. I can swing my head around or run in place and they stay firmly seated where they are.Getting them in takes maybe a single second longer than normal earbuds, since you have to insert the lower ring into your ear, then push the silicone ring into the nook before resting the main body. That took a bit to figure out, but once you get it down it becomes second nature.The sound quality itself is surprisingly good. I'm not an audiophile at all, so perhaps I'm not as well-tuned to noticing the difference, but I get plenty of bass and the equalizer works well to tune it if needed. I leave the EQ off, though, as I like to prioritize battery life and the default sound is fine to me. Compared to my first-gen Galaxy Buds, these are significantly better sounding, but of course they don't have any noise cancelling at all, by design.As for battery life, it's rated at 5.5 hours and that's roughly what I get with all the extras turned off. Wide-area tap and adaptive volume seem to burn through the battery pretty quickly, and the equalizer can result in reduced battery life too. Still, it's long enough for any one session of use for me, so I'd say they're perfectly adequate in this regard.Speaking of wide-area tap, I wound up having to turn this off because chewing food resulted in it tripping some times - that got kinda annoying, and tapping the device itself is easy enough that it's no big loss.All told, I really like these things. overview_text: It's really too bad so many reviewers had the wrong expectations.
comment: These earbuds have a major problem. But the problem is not with Sony's design or implementation. The actual problem is with the way people review them and completely miss the intended, designed purpose of them. I find that to be a crying shame as it's likely to influence Sony's decision to iterate on the design in the future. In fact, the release of LinkBuds S tells me that they may have already given up on this idea. And that saddens me since they fill a need (admittedly a niche need, but one that I consider to be legitimate).If you read "mainstream" tech blog reviews on these earbuds, or watch video reviews on that big "Tube" site, you'll notice a common theme. That is, these "bloggers" who want to think of themselves as journalists review them using a cookie cutter template and don't consider what the designed purpose is. The most glaring fact is when the reviews complain about a lack of bass. Or the one that makes me literally laughing out loud is when they talk about how they don't seal to the ear. In case you didn't know, "open" and "sealed" are polar opposites. These buds are not intended to seal to your ear. They are intended to let you hear external sounds while they are being worn. You can't seriously review a Corvette and then complain about towing capacity. In that same vein, these earbuds are not designed with sound quality above all else (Sony has other earbuds aimed at that).So the main question is, do these earbuds accomplish their stated purpose? Yes. Absolutely they do. Secondary question is, do these earbuds accomplish that purpose well? Again, yes. They're not the most comfortable earbuds on the market, I'd say that distinction goes to the Samsung Galaxy Buds Live (another design that I'm sad to think may have been abandoned due to misguided reviews). But I can wear these for 2-3 hours at a time without noticing that they're in. In fact, the ability to be so aware of my surroundings really helps to reinforce that. And I occasionally will only remember I'm wearing them when I walk too far away from the device they're connected to and hear the tones telling me of that.The audio quality (again with the intended design in mind) is quite good. I don't often use them for music, but they sound perfectly acceptable in that regard. I do, however, use them often for video calls, or to watch videos/TV shows. They excel at video calls since you don't end up shouting into the room due to being able to hear your own voice clearly. For movies, I'd rather grab a good pair of over-the-ear headphones. Their primary goal of allowing you to hear your environment gets an A+ in my book. I can clearly hear the clicks of my keyboard as I'm typing this. Or the whispering whirr of the air purifier next to me. All the while, the podcast I have playing is crystal clear, just as if I were listening on speakers (except that the audio is 100% private to me).The only knock against these earbuds is the MSRP. I occasionally see sale pricing on these that bring them down around 30% off. If that sale pricing were the original MSRP, that would be about right. However, given how unique these are in the market (and the fact that there are no alternatives from established brands), I'd happily pay full price for them.I know the odds are astronomical, but if anyone at Sony happens to read this... Please don't give up on this design concept because misguided individuals went in with the wrong expectations. I sure would love to see LinkBuds 2 released in the next year or so.

date_review: Reviewed in the United States on January 15, 2024
comment: These headphones have changed the game for me for work, at home, at the gym, and... basically everywhere.They are incredibly comfortable to wear. I had previously been using a pair of very popular over-the-ear brand name headphones (rhymes with "heats") and I could only go an hour or so without them seriously irritating my ears and putting pressure on the top of my scalp. These are very lightweight and put almost no pressure on my ears, and I've NEVER felt them on the top of my head. I will regularly wear them on and off for 6+ hours for work. On that same note, the battery life is fantastic - I feel like I never have to charge them. I will routinely leave them on all day accidentally after leaving the house and when I come back the battery is still high - I have a feeling that they idle at barely no battery use. Probably 8+ hours of constant use in this battery, if not more (I haven't measured it.)The sound quality is superb, and one of my favorite features is the adjustability via cell phone app. I'm a musician, and I use these to listen to music while out walking and around the house. I can EQ and change levels, as well as turning ANC (active noise cancellation) on and off. The bass level is great and I get amazing definition.The ANC is good, but not the most high end I've used. I use these regularly at my gym and they play loud music over the speakers - it's enough to block out some sound so I can watch my show, but I can definitely still hear it through the headphones. I think my only complaint is that for a loud space like that, I don't seem to get enough volume to watch quiet points of my TV shows. I always want more volume. However, when I'm at home, the max volume is more than enough, and I don't ever go up more than 3/4ths of the way. If I'm listening to music at home with ANC on I will routinely not be able to hear my husband trying to talk to me!The mic raises and lowers and when lowered, it automatically accepts a call. When raised during a call, it will mute you, which is great for customer service purposes. I work from home and love this feature. Personally I kind of wish that the microphone had something to lock into on the headphones themselves so I don't feel super weird walking around with mic'd headphones at the gym, but I don't actually care what people think because these are SO comfy. I would rather wear unconventional headphones that actually function well than wear normal looking ones that hurt and don't work as well!The noise cancellation for speaking into the mic is decent. It blocks pretty well and keeps people from hearing light background noise, but for a noisy space or louder conversations in the background, they will be slightly audible. I do like that I have some active monitoring of my own voice when speaking into the mic. It seems to be intermittent - sometimes I will hear myself during the call, sometimes I won't. If I mute and unmute the mic, usually my voice monitoring will show up again.  It will block out environmental sound on my end for people that I am talking to remotely.I connect these to my cell to take work calls, so I can't speak to the connectivity of the USB dongle. However, with Bluetooth connection, they are very strong, and I have not had a call drop or disconnect once.I use these headphones every single day, and can't recommend them enough for work or play.

However, as the environmental sound gets loud, my voice will switch on and off as I speak abruptly and with increasing distortion as the headset try to remove the environmental sound. I would say it is effect in a low to medium noise environment like a quiet cafe. It will not work very well at an airport or a very busy restaurent.The ANC on my end, i.e. cutting out environmental noise for myself so that I can hear the remote speaker is fairly good. date_review: Reviewed in the United States on July 3, 2023
overview_text: Great bass focused budget buds let down by weak ANC
comment: tl;dr Bass focused buds deliver a fun sound and call quality is good, but the active noise canceling (ANC) struggles.Before we begin, ears are funny things and any review of headphones or earbuds is purely subjective. To cut down on variables I use the same sound sources and test tracks for all my reviews, but what sounds great to me might not sound as good to you.I've used a range of different JBL Bluetooth speakers over the years, but this is the first pair of earbuds from JBL that I've tried out. On unboxing, the first thing I noticed about the JBL Tune Buds was that the case was only flat on the bottom, all the other surfaces are carved which gave it a nice hand feel but meant it only stays safely on level surfaces in one orientation. Made of plastic it isn't a heavy case, but the bulk of it does make it larger than slimmer lozenge cases when carried in a front pocket.Inside the case the buds have an interesting shape, with the bulk of the earbud in the shell of the ear, but a slim protrusion coming forwards over the tragus (yes, I looked that up too). This forward protrusion helps balance the earbud in the ear, but in my experience it sticks out too far and acts as a hook for anything going past your ears. Every time I took off a t-shirt or necklace I would lose at least one earbud in the process. Compared to some earbuds I did feel these stuck out further because of this protrusion and that meant I had more moments of wondering if they would fall out than I am used to. The good news is that I never had one fall out in normal use.The box art for the JBL Tune Buds states "PURE BASS ... ZERO NOISE" and as far as the bass goes they are spot on. These earbuds are tuned for the bass fans with an obvious bass boost even the basic tuning of the buds even before using the "Bass" or "Extreme Bass" equalizer settings. The bass is deep and full, with a good sub-bass rumble that I could feel inside my head at higher volumes. Boosted as it was it didn't feel muddy, with good definition for earbuds meaning bass guitars and drums didn't blur into a throb of noise. JBL is a Harman company, and even with all that bass the Harman Curve is still apparent in the mid and higher frequencies. Both male and female vocals were clear with a nice organic warmth, and the high end was crisp and clear. My entire test track playlist sounded good just with a bit more bass than I am used to. The sound stage is good and they are definitely an easy listen, with no ear fatigue even after prolonged listening sessions. In fact the only complaint was from my wife who could hear high frequency leakage even at moderate volumes.Unfortunately the ANC seems to be the weak spot of the package. It works as one would expect but isn't particularly powerful so that even moderate noise items like a bathroom extractor fan were still loud enough to be noticeable with it enabled. It reduced the sound of a crowded supermarket, but I still needed to boost my listening volume above my normal range for it to be fully effective. Against louder sounds, such as a lawn mower there was only minimal difference between having it enabled or disabled. All this being said, it is good for this price point with many "budget" earbuds lacking ANC altogether or having very limited capabilities.In conclusion they are a good pair of everyday buds for general listening. The sound is very good for the price point, though unsurprisingly not as good as audiophile buds costing many times the price. Call quality is as expected, and the battery life is good too. The ANC does feel weak, and that's why I'm docking one star, but even then I'd be happy to keep them in my pocket if only the case was a bit smaller. 4 out of 5 stars.

comment: A lot of pros with one con.I didn’t think I had a lot of time for earbuds during the day, so I started off trying a cheap pair. They were $20 or something with 4.8 stars and reviews like, “I haven’t used my Airpods since buying these!” so I thought that sounded perfect.They sucked. The sound was harsh, they became painful after extended use, noise cancelling was barely noticeable, etc.  I can’t actually remember all of the problems at this point.  BUT they sold me on the functionality of wireless headphones.Fast-forward to a few months later - it’s Black Friday and I bite on these because they’re on sale.  I was a little hesitant because they had a lowly 4.2 stars.  Turns out average reviews aren’t everything.These are the polar opposite of the highly-reviewed, cheap headphones I tried: they’re comfortable, and the sound is amazing.  As the title implies, I master audio so this is not a hollow endorsement. The cheap ones had hyped bass, missing mids, and painful presence/treble.  These are very flat and well-performing by comparison, and can be EQ’d. The noise cancelling is also VERY respectable. I frequently work around loud sources and am sensitive to loud noises, and I have accidentally left these in when I intended to swap for earplugs, because the performance is similar.I love the app. Being able to select between audio quality vs. video sync’ing is awesome when I want to watch live musical performances where sync issues play with your mind. Being able to create custom EQ settings is  very important to me too.The con is that you have to take them out of the case to power them on. It’s not a huge deal - it’s easy to pop them in for a split second if they’ve timed out or something.  But there has been one occasion that I ran somewhere and forgot the case.  I intend to live my life without dependence on crap like headphones, so no big deal - take a break.I would normally give something like this 4 stars because that power-on function is a notable miscalculation on JBL’s part, but it deserves a much better average review than it has so I’m doing my part to raise it.  In everyday life it’s not that big of a deal unless you’re the kind of person who loves to find things to complain about.

Wasn't a sport model that I've liked.•BOSE: I love my QC35 over-the-ear headphones but have not paid the price tag to try Bose sport earbuds. Honestly, even if a higher end pair like Bose has a little more detail overall, I'm guessing the tiny nuances would be lost while exercising or doing yard work.•JBL: These are a happy replacement & update to my old JBL Endurance JUMP—easier connection, better sound, better waterproofing, individual earbuds. (But i did prefer the "swipe" up/down feature for volume on the old JUMP model.)Super-secure-but-comfortable fit. Punchy bass, deeper low end, no harsh highs, and clear sound at all volumes. date_review: Reviewed in the United States on July 31, 2023
comment: It pains me to say this as an exclusive Apple product user and shareholder, but you might as well save your time and aggravation and just flush a few hundred bucks down the toilet.
