Within a couple of days of use they began to occasionally drop the connection to my iPad Pro, even when device-switching wasn’t happening. They also occasionally struggled to reconnect when switching from my iPad to my iPhone and back, but I forgave that and was used to it from my Bose, but Apple SHOULD work better with other Apple products. Turning off the position recognition didn’t help either. As the problem got worse and reconnecting went from unreliable to impossible, I read that powering them down could help. So after searching at length for how the heck to do this (you hold down the Digital Crown AND adjacent noise cancelling button for far longer than the 15 seconds claimed), I force-powered down. That allowed me to reconnect them once. Then the problem got worse so I tried restoring them to factory settings, which no matter how long I held down the two buttons, didn’t work - not an uncommon problem as well, just Google it.After several attempts I was finally able to factory reset and re-pair. That made no difference either and the already worsening dropped connection issues got even worse, to the point of utter uselessness, disconnecting every 30 seconds or so, and suddenly the right earphone became inoperable.Out of curiosity (and frustration), I pulled the magnetic ear cups off (a neat Apple feature that I wouldn’t have discovered for a while if they worked properly) and was surprised to see droplets of condensation. I had been wearing them around my air conditioned house, nowhere near water. This is likely why one side shorted out. Google condensation and you’ll see this is a rampant issue, well known to Apple as it’s a common complaint noted in previous generations of the product. I even read that AppleCare blames users for issues by declaring that they’ve gotten the headphones wet. I can’t help but think this has to do with the tight fit and excellent padding to enhance the noise cancellation - that was exceptional, briefly, WHEN THEY WORKED.I went back to my hard-worn 3 year old Bose. The Apple sound quality and noise cancellation is better, when the things worked, which lasted about two days. Two weeks out of the box they are now useless and I’ll do everything I can to return these expensive paperweights.Shame on Apple for releasing such a flawed product. It turns out that my issues aren’t at all uncommon and at least some of the inventory shortages are due to the fact that these are constantly requiring replacement.  I’ll go back to Bose, noise cancelling headphones - very good, durable, reliable, and albeit pricey, less than half the cost of this dressed up garbage.

comment: I’ve had these for three years now, or perhaps more accurately I’d had three pairs of these for one year each. But Apple really missed the mark with the design. In a semi-humid climate like mine, condensation from wearing them normally, not even during exercise, has managed to kill two pairs of these already. It will start slowly, with random pops, screeches, and freezes where the headphones won’t respond. Eventually they stop connecting, or make horrific noises at all times. Apple’s “repair” for this is to send a new pair of headphones at ridiculous expense. So get AppleCare, because there’s a good chance you’ll need it.The other major problem is that the aluminum earcups makes these overly heavy for longer listening sessions, compared to other headphones using much more practical plastic bodies. And they don’t pack well at all for travel. Don’t even get me started on the atrocious case.Soundwise, they are pretty good, and I like the more neutral sounding response Apple targeted compared to some other big headphones that emphasize the bass. Transparency mode is also -very- impressive on these headphones, and it’s good enough that I practice guitar in these. Noise cancellation is also good, but surpassed by the AirPods Pro 2.Overall, I can only halfheartedly recommend them if you live in the more arid parts of the US. Otherwise these are too pricey for how limited their lifespan is.

date_review: Reviewed in the United States on September 1, 2022
comment: Updating my original review. I had to come back and throw some shade for the abysmal battery life. It appears to drain as much battery when idling as it does when playing music. I have to assume it has a stout battery in it. Most bluetooth headphones in the last few years claim 30, 40, even 50 hours of play time - which rings more or less true in most cases. Meaning, you can charge it up, play it for 2 hours, turn it off, and there are 28 or 38 hours of useful life left. If you assume these AirPods have 50 hours of battery life, you charge them up, leave them idle, then come back two days later to listen to them, and the battery is drained. In effect, the way I've had to manage the AirPod Max is to leave it charging at all times, and only take it off the wire when I want to listen. You simply cannot listen, put them down for a day or two, then listen again. They keep draining. I find this, for a $500 pair of headphones, completely and absolutely unacceptable. Whatever they needed to do to optimize battery life and reduce drain, they needed to do it before they were released.Don't go in for these. Just don't. Too many serious concessions, on sound quality and battery life. You can pick up some VERY good headsets from Bose or Sony for much less, or Bowers & Wilkins or Bang & Olufsen for the same money. Swing and a miss, Apple.--To set the context, I listen to many, many Bluetooth devices. Earbuds, over-ear headphones, wireless speakers. I love trying them with my favorite soundtrack and comparing the sound quality, the emotion.These Airpod Max’s are great in some ways, terrible in one other.What they do well:- Noise canceling. I have (and have tested) Sony, Bang & Olufsen, Bose, Bowers & Wilkins, and many, many others. This is as good as I’ve ever heard. The noise canceling is just astonishing, likely because it has four microphones and they are incredibly well-integrated into the software.- Comfort. They are brilliantly comfortable. However, Bose QuietComfort and Bang & Olufsen H9 are both also fantastic, well-engineered offerings that fit well to any size head and are also fantastically comfortable.- The volume knob. I love it. Maybe it’s like a steampunk version of modern Bluetooth headphones, but I love the knob. Maybe that can become my theme meme: “I love the knob.” No. Never mind. Hopefully not that. But, back to the headphones, they are a high-quality, well-engineered and well-manufactured device. That’s on point for Apple quality.What it does OK:- Style. It’s headphones. They’re round. The headband is nice. Yawn. Synthetic materials and oval-shaped cans. Meh. See Bang & Olufsen H9 for guidance. But like I said, the knob… distinguishing feature that I like a lot.What it doesn’t do well enough for the brand and price:- Bass. Sorry. Not adequate. It’s more of a studio monitor. Meaning, it gets loud and stays clear, but the bass is just not emphatic or articulate. It’s there, but well out of the way. With default settings, the headphones make deep bass that you have to squint and strain to hear. Obviously, it can make deep bass. I have begrudgingly jacked up the deep bass (60Hz) in Spotify and turned the bass levels way down in my car to compensate. Phone connects to Airpod Max, music sounds good. Phone connects to anything else, it’s bass-blurry. So I have to adapt. And I don’t want to. I spent $500 on these. Not a good customer experience.What it doesn’t do well at all:- Bass. There’s no way to adjust the equalizer trims for the headphones. Many others (Bose, B&O) offer apps (and software) that adjust the equalizer for the headphones themselves. Apple does not offer this. You take it as it comes. And as it comes, it isn’t acceptable. ESPECIALLY not at this price level. Like I have referenced many times, if you need how to do this properly, see the first-generation Bang & Olufsen H9.Overall, if you have software (an “app”) that lets you tweak the equalizer, you can make these sound as spectacularly good as you like.Were they worth the purchase price? No. I will gladly pay this much and more for a pair of headphones that does their job immaculately. I’ve found the Bose QuietComfort line also dim the low bass miserably, when noise-cancelling is engaged. Unacceptably so. I’ve never kept a pair of those even though they are also extremely comfortable and high-quality. If you would like pinnacle Bluetooth headphones, or if Apple should wish to learn how to make a pure, beautiful, mind-blowing pair of luxury headphones, reference the Bang & Olufsen H9 (original generation, NOT the H9x). The B&Os are also incredible for noise canceling, the best, bar none, for comfort, and the best, bar none, for balanced, pronounced, emphatic sound, at every frequency. If it’s in the music, you can hear it. With the H9x you have to use the app to adjust the equalizer, but at least you can do that in the headphones themselves, so everything you listen to has the trim you like.The bass, on these, is, by default, flaccid and depleted. I expect far better for this price. These are excellently designed and manufactured things, but I had to give it three stars instead of four, for the dismal, humble bass representation out of the box. I may even return them. I don’t need blaring, license plate-rattling idiot bass. I just want to hear every note clearly emphasized in my music, even if it’s under 50Hz. These can’t do that without a lot of help. So, let that help you locate your preferences with respect to the product.

overview_text: Great build quality and sound, but they also have flaws.
comment: I'd give these a 3.5 if Amazon did half-stars, but rounding down since there are plenty of glowing reviews and I think people should be aware of the downsides.In many ways these are great. The sound quality is among the best for bluetooth ANC headphones, the build quality is unrivaled, transparency mode is unrivaled, and in most ways they're super convenient if you're in the Apple ecosystem with iPhone and Mac. That said, they're far from perfect. Here are the biggest problems I have with these:1) If you wear for long stretches and/or live in a humid environment, condensation quickly collects in the ear cups, as shown in the attached photo, which shows the moisture collected after around 4 hours of wear time. These are not water/moisture resistant and Apple will not help you if this causes damage. It hasn't caused a major problem for me yet, but I expect it will eventually as it has for several other people I know. This happens with all closed back headphones, but it's far worse with these because these are mostly metal and metal is more prone to condensation than plastic.2) Once paired to an Apple device, you can only use these with devices that use the same Apple ID. If you want to share with multiple family members, you have to go through convoluted steps to remove them from you Apple account before someone else can use them with their device. Every single time. Apply claims it's a theft protection feature, but it's clearly also to force people to buy multiple pairs as they could easily just let you choose to turn this feature off if you want or let the primary owner add other Apply ID's to an approved list of users.Some less severe annoyances I have:1) These are the heaviest headphones I've ever used, and I work in pro audio, so I've probably used hundreds of different headphones over the years. That weight gets pretty uncomfortable after prolonged use and makes them prone to falling off when your head isn't upright - if you bend over to pick something up, for example.2) The ANC (noise cancellation) is just okay. Sony XM5's offer FAR better ANC performance, and some of the newer Bose perform better too. It's not terrible, don't get me wrong, just not as impressive as I'd expect from Apple and the crazy high price.3) The case is worthless for protection, but you still have to use it as putting the headphones in the case is the only way to conserve battery when they aren't in use - there's no way to turn them on/off.4) Very limited options for customizing the experience. You can choose which direction to turn the wheel for volume control, you can choose to press the button once or twice to end a call, and you can choose which modes to toggle through by pressing the button twice (transparency, noise cancelling, etc.). Thats just about it. Compare that to Sony, where you can customize the EQ (choose a preset, adjust the frequency bands manually, or go through a guided flow that helps you make a custom EQ preset based on your preferences) , decide whether or not to pause audio when you take the headphones off or away from your ear, decide if they automatically go into sleep mode when you aren't wearing or playing sound, enable/disable voice assistant, adjust / fine tune ANC/transparency performance, and a bunch of other things. I wish at the very least Apply would let me adjust EQ and turn off auto-pause when I move the headphones away from my ear.5) Like other Airpods models, they automatically switch to a different device you're using if it starts playing audio. I typically have these paired to my computer while I work, listening to music/podcasts on spotify or using them for zoom calls with coworkers. Every time I take a quick look at something on my phone and a video auto-plays (usually instagram) the headphones disconnect from my computer and switch over to my phone, interrupting whatever I was listening to. It's usually super aggravating. I really wish it instead triggered a popup asking if I want to switch the device the headphones are paired to... or just let me turn off automatic re-pairing altogether.

Why I can't have a standby switch or button and an update firmware option is beyond me.  And again, I'm a fanboy here.It's also pretty sad that the design allows the cans to bang together if not handled carefully, which will surely result in scratches at some point.Oh, and want to listen with a wire, enjoy buying that $35 proprietary cable from Apple. This is why people hate Apple.But despite these many very reasonable gripes, the bottom line here is that these sound better than every Bose pair I have owned, my Sony MX4s, and several Bang & Olufsen sets I've had. Unfortunately, after six months of use, it's hard to justify a five star rating.Background noise control is great, transparency mode is amazing, the sound quality is excellent. comment: Take my review with a grain of salt and or from a super picky perspective. These headphones are incredible. From the build quality, the feel, the fit, and the finish, they are worth the hefty price tag. The sound is bold with an open sound stage, medium bass at lower volumes and super punchy full bodied bass at higher volumes. The bass is not overwhelming and adds that “feel” to the music you are listening to without distortion. The issue I have is that these did not meet my expectations. I did not expect something BETTER, but I expected something DIFFERENT. I read reviews and heard feedback from some people I know and I created an expectation of my own as to what to expect with these headphones. Of course with them being Apple, they have to be great, which was true.From what I expected, the best way I can compare is when you go to an electronics store and see a super high quality QLED 4K LED Ultra HD tv in cinematic mode playing a movie and you can just tell that the scenes in the movie are on a stage or a set and you can see the layers to it, that is kind of what I expected from these headphones. I expected a super dynamic sound stage, I expected to hear each instrument and sound around me instead of layered, and to feel that I was in an open room. But that is what you’d expect from a different type of headphone. This is solely what I thought to expect, but not what I got. The takeaway from that is that my expectations were just different but I was not let down at all. I am returning them and going to do more research on what type of sound I am looking for.All in all, if you’re unlike me and my wild mind that doesn’t create images of things before you buy them, you will love these headphones. The aluminum is beautiful, the mesh on the headband feels like a cloud, and the sound and noice cancelling is spectacular. My only true gripe about the design is that when you take them off and want to put them on your neck, the bare aluminum might be uncomfortable on your collar bones. You might want to turn the ear cups and fold them flat, but they fold outward from your body and you have the whole metal body resting in your collar bones. I just wish they would fold in the other way so the ear cushions are resting on your body. And one last bit is since they fold that way, the aluminum ear cups, when folded will clank against each other and can cause scratches over time. Again, this is my extremely picky review on these headphones, but you’re probably a normal person and will love them, so please do buy them. You will not regret it!

Lightning charger on these now 2020 models . 6  loved them so much that after using a these black ones at work, bought a blue pair for home.  If Apple makes hearing aides that are true medical devices I’d say they would crush and own the market. These are that good with their technology.  I’m adding that after about a month of using them I finally got around to playing with Logic Pro for IPad.  These headphones have a noise cancelling feature that is unmatched. They are surprisingly comfy, even when worn for hours. They're a little less bulky and lighter weight than my Shures, and the comfort level for me is why I am giving them 4 stars instead of 3. I also LOVE the fact that the battery life is very long-lived, and you can charge these wirelessly. That said, you are only given a charge cord to charge them with, and there's no included protective case to store them in - not even a storage pouch, like most other earphones include.Overall, they're decent headphones, but I wish there were more features to them. comment: So long before this one I had another Pedal I bought that would get stuck occasionally but I had found a way around it when it did get stuck. date_review: Reviewed in the United States on June 6, 2019
overview_text: Does NOT have advertised half-pedal capabilities
comment: Regarding M-Audio SP-2 which I recently purchased . . .The description given on the Amazon site includes the following three phrases:1-  Designed to work and feel just like acoustic piano's sustain pedal. 2- . . . with expressive half-pedal capabilities. 3- Piano Style ActionI'm far from being an expert on this.  However, I know that this pedal is actually an ON-OFF switch with no gradation between those two states.  I find each of the three phrases above at least misleading.  Number 2 is simply incorrect.It cannot 'express' itself in a 'half-pedal' (or half-damper) state which I think means the digital equivalent of the acoustic piano's damper pedal which, when pressed, swings the damper cushions completely away from their normal position of pressing against the strings.  Doing this allows the sound of the strings to continue as the sound fades to silence naturally.  With the damper pedal at a so-called halfway point the pianist can cause the damper cushions to slightly touch the strings, slightly reducing the sustaining effect until the pedal is released to silence.  I'm used to an acoustic piano and was looking for more control than you get from a binary (instantly)ON to (instantly)OFF.  I found that marketing really pushes the envelope with 'works and feels like an acoustic' which simply means that the pedal,not the sound effect, "moves up and down with resistance similar to that of the acoustic pedal".  But "works" like anacoustic? Yeah.  And, since the dampers look to be part of the Piano's "ACTION" which is the series of levers and hammers that translate the press of a piano key to the sound that it makes by causing a hammer to hit a string or strings, I felt that saying it has "Piano Style Action" would only barely stand up in court.  This is a popular pedal, witha polarity switch which is a big assist in mating the pedal to the keyboard.  It's a beautiful looking thing and feels really nice underfoot.  Nothing wrong with the pedal - only with the description - plus, it's inexpensive.  Mine quickly developed an intermittent habit of cutting out while my foot held the pedal in the sustaining position, but it seems to have a good warranty and I could have it repaired, but I purchased it based on the promised half-damper effect whichis at best inaccurate.  Amazon is not being intentionally devious. I suppose not all technical writers are musicians.  I'm a very amateur piano player returning to the keyboard after many years without a piano to play.  My technical knowledge is limited and based upon several days of web-surfing vendors and musician forums.  I recently purchased the Roland DP-10 which really does have half-damper capability with a switch to toggle between ON-OFF  and half-Damper.  I just can't seem to get half-damper working on my Yamaha P-95 which I know is capable of it.  However, I find that its sustain effect is not as quick to get muddied as the M-audio SP-2.  Not such a big deal, maybe more of a personal preference - and the DP-10 is more expensive.

date_review: Reviewed in the United States on September 2, 2018
overview_text: Works fine, sturdy, no half damper pedal function
comment: This M-Gear SP-2 sustain pedal has a feel of being well-built, sturdy, and stays put on a smooth floor.  This is the second I've bought, this one for the purpose of engaging the push-to-talk (PTT) function on a ham radio, and it works fine for that.  It takes about 8 pounds of weight to fully depress which is a bit heavy, but not too bad.  It functions bascially as a momentary electrical on/off switch, and there is an switch on the bottom to change whether it opens or closes the circuit when depressed.  The resistance I measured for the closed position was between 1-10 ohms, but it was not continuous over the range of pedal motion, it just varied randomly across those values after depressing the pedal about 75% down.  So this is not a variable or 1/2 sustain pedal.  It's either on or off.  This is different from the first SP-2 pedal I bought 10 years ago, which I still use today on my Triton Extreme.  On that SP-2 the resistance varies continuously from 175 ohms 75% depressed to 80 ohms 100% depressed.  So it can be considered a variable or 1/2 sustain pedal.  A global setting on the Triton Extreme allows calibration for half damper which works for this older pedal, but not for the new one.  Only a few of more advanced sound patches make use of this feature.  I deduct 1 star for the change in design and function over the years for the same product model number, but otherwise a fine product (so far, but not so sure after reading some of the recent reports of the newer ones failing within a year).

date_review: Reviewed in the United States on July 7, 2019
overview_text: A good solution for those seeking a dongle-less wired listening experience
comment: When Apple removed the headphone jack from their phones many of us resented this act because it was not only inconvenient, but we saw it as a way for the company to push sales of Airpods. As a business strategy, time has shown this move it was genius. Airpods are a solid offering and a very good addition to the Apple Ecosystem. However, those of us who want to listen to music without worrying about whether we have a charged up Bluetooth listening device or have remembered to carry a dongle were left with a void.Belkin's RockStar Headphones are a godsend for us. Though small, the headset is well-constructed with a flat cable that has a lightning connector built right into it. This means there's no need to attach a dongle before listening to this wired headset. Now I can simply plug in my headset whenever I want to take a call or listen to something. My favorite feature of the build is found on the in-line controls. The volume buttons are circular with plus and minus buttons etched on each. This is a well-implemented solution I wish more headset manufacturers would adopt.While many have adopted a Bluetooth lifestyle and find wired listening devices antiquated I do not. I love being able to simply plug my headphones in and not have to worry about whether the additional battery drain I am placing on my phone will mean I can't listen to a podcast or take a call at the end of my workday. I don't have to worry about remembering or scheduling a separate charge cycle for these headphones, nor do I have to pair them or remove and re-pair them when the inevitable Bluetooth connectivity fails for one reason or another. And the best part for me is I don't have to deal with lag between the audio of whatever video I am watching. Those who use Bluetooth headsets have to either buy $300+ units which can still experience this issue, deal with it or unpair and re-pair their headsets to their phones to overcome this issue.This headset has no active noise cancellation but they do a very good job of isolating exterior sound. This is accomplished through the fit of the earbuds within your ear canals. Make sure to use the included tips to get the best fit for your ear size as this is crucial to your listening experience with this headset.As far as sound quality goes this headset produces a solid sound. Mids and highs are present but not necessarily emphasized or crisp. Bass is present and punchy, but that artificial deep bass found in some genres of music is not well reproduced. Spoken word podcasts are excellent and so are voice calls. Videos are a mixed bag depending on whatever content you are consuming. When watching action flix or anime I would call the experience passable. If watching a review, presentation or a story based drama I would say the sound is better than average.Grading this headset solely on its sound I would garner a score of 3.5 out of 5.0. However, the quality of the build and convenience of the offering are worth half a point. Belkin's RockStar Headphones earn a 4.0 out of 5.0 imho and are well worth a buy to those who want to enjoy a lag-free, wired listening experience from their iPhones or iPads.

date_review: Reviewed in the United States on May 3, 2023
comment: Sometimes people rate products for what an item is NOT rather than for what it IS. If you're excpecting an audiophile's dream, move on. I don't like blasting music or movies into my ears, I just want to hear it clearly, so these typically last me a good 7-8 hours on phone and pc.I have had these for 19 months & they're still going strong. NOTE: I use these every single day since the day I bought them, and I use them until they max out & need a recharge, every single day. They are now starting to show signs of degradation: the charge now creeps down to 90% when I go to use them after fully charging them the night before. If I charge them again real quick before use, I can get 100% again. Also, instead of 8 hours, they now last somewhere between 6 - 7 hours on a single charge. Still pretty darn good. 1 star off, since they're not good for calls bc the mic sucks, so if that's important to you ( it wasn't for me) it could be a deal breaker. Also, they're tethered to each other, so if you want to use them at the gym, they might annoy you with the cord flopping around your neck & maybe getting caught on clothing, etc. True wireless are probably better for the gym where you'll be moving around vigorously. They're just fine for biking though.The on/off button bothers some ppl but imo, it's fine bc you don't have to push it while it's in your ear -- just put the left earphone in, press the button on the right one until it turns on, then put in the right earphone. Easy peasy, no big deal. Same for turning them off, just take the right earbud off so you don't have to press it into your ear, if pressing the button while it's in your ear bothers you.And there you have it folks! For this price point you can't ask for much better! I'm very careful with reveiws & wait a long time before commenting to make sure a product is good. I do not hesitate to recommend these!TLDR: Although not good for calls bc the mic sucks & earphones are tethered to each other, these wireless phones are surprisingly good. Very good sound & volume, long battery life on a single charge, and solid quality -- still going strong for me after 19 months -- all at a dirt cheap price! Recommended!

The SoundCore's didn't have an IPX rating and most of the reviews said they didn't last long under stressful usage, so I was excited to see these not only having an IPX rating of 7 but also their price tag (I purchased them for $20)I bought them hoping they would suffice, and they came the next day. I have worn them to the gym a few times now and I can honestly say they're perfectly fine (for the price). Do they have amazing sound quality? But, then again, neither did the Shockz. In fact, my Amazon Echo 2 buds have more bass (and ANC) than these. At the gym, that doesn't matter to me since there's lots of clinking and clanking anyway. Plus, no ANC, which means I can hear around me when someone wants to whistle at my legs. Don't get me wrong, these aren't "tinny"' they're just bass-less, so, more treble. Kind of like my truck speakers ... but that's another story.The IPX7 rating also means I don't have to worry too much about them when I'm in the steam room or sitting in the spa. I don't swim or shower with them, though.The charge lasts far longer than either my OpenRuns or my Echo 2s, but these have significantly less features to drain the battery away.Earlier today I took a call while listening to music through these and the other end said I sounded fine, so that's a plus.These Optiums came with a small case, some ear pieces to adjust to your ears and a small clip you can use to clip the wire to your collar or headband, if you're that guy (don't be that guy).For $20 I couldn't be happier with a headset. overview_text: Good sound quality, medium comfort, and confusing controls.
comment: I've been a user of those old school wired earbuds for a long, long time and I'm just starting to dip my toes into the wireless bluetooth market.  I've owned a different cheaper pair of bluetooth earbuds in the $30 price range that I've been using for about the past year, but those were for sound only (no call functionality) and the sound quality for music is not great.  They lacked bass and music just didn't sound pure.  I will give them credit though, the part that went into the ear is comfortable and the controls are reliable and intuitive.Fast forward to these JBL earbuds.  The sound quality difference is immediately apparent.  I'm really happy with the sound quality on these earbuds for music which is what I use earbuds for most.  There's nice bass and the music is clear.  It's night and day compared to my $30 earbuds.  I'm a little indifferent towards them as far as call quality is concerned.  The people I talk to regularly tell me that they hear wind or that it's difficult to hear me if I'm outside.  If I'm inside and in a quiet environment they work well, but they aren't a substitute for just holding the phone up to your head if you're after max sound quality as far as I'm concerned.  I've been able to hear people ok on my end with them, but they're a little quieter than I'd like.Comfort wise, these aren't as comfortable as my $30 bluetooth earbuds or my old wired earbuds.  The plastic heads seem pretty standard size and do fit into my ears, but I don't know why people want such big bulbous plastic knobs in their ears when they could just have the smaller silicone part.  Maybe it's just me?  The old school little pea sized round silicone flexible caps are comfortable - what's with the hard plastic balls on higher end earbuds these days?  I don't think this is an issue specific to these earbuds, but I don't understand why people would prefer this style.  They're not as comfortable, they don't fit snugly, they don't create as nice of a seal in your ear to block out other noise, etc.Lastly, my biggest gripe with these is something that is probably learnable or fixable with just using them more over time, but the controls are wonky at best.  There aren't any actual buttons on them, but tapping on them does "do things".  It's a learning curve.  The instructions are confusing at best about this too.  Also, if I'm using them in both ears while listening to music and then I take a call but only want one earbud in, I will put one back in the case, but then I've had trouble reconnecting music to both earbuds once I'm done with my call.Overall I think I'm going to generously give these 4 stars for now and chalk the controls up to user error and just being new to understanding how the tapping system works.  If I still struggle with the controls down the road, I think they're more of a 3 star item for me.

date_review: Reviewed in the United States on January 15, 2024
comment: These headphones have changed the game for me for work, at home, at the gym, and... basically everywhere.They are incredibly comfortable to wear. These are very lightweight and put almost no pressure on my ears, and I've NEVER felt them on the top of my head. I will regularly wear them on and off for 6+ hours for work. On that same note, the battery life is fantastic - I feel like I never have to charge them. I will routinely leave them on all day accidentally after leaving the house and when I come back the battery is still high - I have a feeling that they idle at barely no battery use. Probably 8+ hours of constant use in this battery, if not more (I haven't measured it.)The sound quality is superb, and one of my favorite features is the adjustability via cell phone app. I'm a musician, and I use these to listen to music while out walking and around the house. I can EQ and change levels, as well as turning ANC (active noise cancellation) on and off. The bass level is great and I get amazing definition.The ANC is good, but not the most high end I've used. I use these regularly at my gym and they play loud music over the speakers - it's enough to block out some sound so I can watch my show, but I can definitely still hear it through the headphones. I think my only complaint is that for a loud space like that, I don't seem to get enough volume to watch quiet points of my TV shows. I always want more volume. However, when I'm at home, the max volume is more than enough, and I don't ever go up more than 3/4ths of the way. If I'm listening to music at home with ANC on I will routinely not be able to hear my husband trying to talk to me!The mic raises and lowers and when lowered, it automatically accepts a call. When raised during a call, it will mute you, which is great for customer service purposes. I work from home and love this feature. Personally I kind of wish that the microphone had something to lock into on the headphones themselves so I don't feel super weird walking around with mic'd headphones at the gym, but I don't actually care what people think because these are SO comfy. I would rather wear unconventional headphones that actually function well than wear normal looking ones that hurt and don't work as well!The noise cancellation for speaking into the mic is decent. It blocks pretty well and keeps people from hearing light background noise, but for a noisy space or louder conversations in the background, they will be slightly audible. I do like that I have some active monitoring of my own voice when speaking into the mic. It seems to be intermittent - sometimes I will hear myself during the call, sometimes I won't. If I mute and unmute the mic, usually my voice monitoring will show up again.  It will block out environmental sound on my end for people that I am talking to remotely.I connect these to my cell to take work calls, so I can't speak to the connectivity of the USB dongle. However, with Bluetooth connection, they are very strong, and I have not had a call drop or disconnect once.I use these headphones every single day, and can't recommend them enough for work or play.

I rarely use them though bc I find the controls to be hard to remember. I find the app to be quite handy.The headphones connect extremely quickly when you open the case. The first time I connected them it was SO quick and easy, I was shocked.For reference, I am not tech-savvy or a tech-snob. I have only ever used cheap products so my frame of reference is different. I've used the soundcore TWE by anker and the SkullCandy Evos and those were both just fine, but the Tone Free FP5 surpass them by many miles.I don't care much about noise  canceling because for me, when the music is playing I'm able to tune everything out. That said- with my previous TWE buds I would be able to hear things with my headphones any lower than 90% especially if they're louder sounds or closer to me. With these I don't notice that as much. If I focus hard I can hear my mom playing music in the car, the shouts of people at the park while I stroll, honking of cars while I ride my bike (I of course turn them down if I'm on the road) etc, but it's faint and very easy for me to tune out as long as I'm not having sensory overload. I don't find that turning on noise canceling makes all that much of a difference. Things do sound different when you turn it on, but not by a lot. I don't think it's worth the battery it uses. As other people have described, the noise canceling does create a sort of white noise sound. I can't hear it while my music is playing but inbetween songs or when I pause it I can. It's faint and easy to tune out for me, but if you're someone who is unable to isolate sounds and gets overloaded by sounds quickly this may be a problem for you, but I would still reccoment trying them and seeing.Ambient mode works well, but I don't find that the two settings (conversation vs whatever the other one is) make much of a difference. They do definitely sound different but I don't think they do what they say they do. Putting it on conversation mode won't actually let u hear conversations around you, at least not distinctly. Rather just a drowned out sort of chattering, like white noise I guess. To hear someone clearly you'd have to also adjust your volume rather low. I still use them when I'm on my bike paired eith 50% volume and it helps me being able to hear someone shouting or honking.I dont know the word but I'm not someone who is super picky about sound quality. I listen to a lot of different types of music, I like to listen to choral arrangements (music major), alot of rock/punk/emo/90s grunge, indie (?), and pop. Rock and indie are my two most listened to genres and rock has lots of electric guitar and drums, so the ONLY sound thing I'm picky on is that the guitars are distinguishable. They shouldn't sound like static or blend in with everything else. I want to be able to hear them. These earbuds do that perfectly. If you're someone that is picky about sound quality or has very specific things you're looking for then your experience might be different, but if you're just an everage Joe (jane) like me who has no real standards then I'd say this is a spot on observation.  There are different sound settings and lots of customization options in app, but since I don't know what most of it means or does, it's gone mostly untouched.The buds charge very quickly and hold a charge very well. I haven't measured how long in between charges but it's usually a ??? week. I use them probably averagely 8-15 hrs a week just depending and I don't charge them often enough to even definitively say how much.I find the volume to be well. No problems. Usually 100% volume is too loud for me and I listen at 70-80.The thing I absolutely HATE about these headphones is the feature that pauses them when you remove them. I'm aware most people like this, I HATE it. I'm a very itchy person so I usually itch the inside of my ear or near my ear about four times an hour when I'm wearing buds, which means they're removed often to itch. It pausing when I do this is INFURIATING. Now you caaan turn this feature off in the app but it doesn't really turn it off. It just changes how it works. It disconnects the bud temporarily and reconnects it when you put it back in. So the bud still in your ear continues to play while the removed one turns off. This is better, sure, but annoying because it can take 3-5 seconds for it to reconnect. This isn't all that long but it definitely puts a dent in my listening experience and is quite bizarre. To offset this, I cover the sensor as I take it out so that it still detects as in my ear.Once every 15ish uses it will randomly disconnect and then reconnect when you turn them on, or sometimes in the first four or five minutes of use. And occasionally you have to manually recconrct them, but both these occurrences are rare.I do feel a bit of ear fatigue when wearing these. They go far into my ears which I prefer. They don't fall out when I smile or run which is great, though when I smile or chew they do move and will have to be readjusted probably once in a five minute period. They protrude out at the bottom next to the stem which is what causes my ears to become sore. I beleive the shape of that part is what specifically helps keep them in your ear though,  so not much can be done on that. I have unusually small ears so this might not be a problem for anyone else. Every earbud I've used has given me this problem in different places. The sore-ness starts usually after an hour of use but sometimes sooner.I have worn these in the rain (granted not hard rain, usually misting or light rain. ) and have had 0 issues.Overall, i adore these and will purchase the next generation after these break!

All these things change in the immersive mode within the Tone Free app.The soundstage improves imensely, and has great width and to a degree, a nice height as well. mids are much more articulate, and treble finds a nice sweet spot, giving this a full sounding but bright presentation, with punchy bass that has improved texture and extention. At times it is still a bit uncontroled, but in my opinion, this mode brings out the strengths of the tuning for the FP8. if you wanted to make adjustments to the sound, I'd start with the immersive tuning and make changes here and there to match your preference.calls on the earbuds are great as well, and you can hold one earbud up to your mouth and whisper in to it, and the mics pick it up. nice feature when you need to say something on a call but need to say it at a lower less heard level. The person on the other end hears the whisper, almost as if you were in person speaking. It's amazing that the mics can be tuned to pick this level of noise up so well.The ANC is nothing to write home about. low level noises are reduced, but everything else is barely touched.The controls are mostly straight forward out of the box, but there is some redundantsy. Skipping to the next song for example, is done by 3 taps of either earbud by default, but you can change this in the app. I used a combination of changes but kept most default settings. Below are the settings i've customized.One tap on left to summon Assistant, one on right to play-pause. 2 on left to lower volume, 2 on right to raise volume. 3 taps on left to move to previous track, 3 taps on right for next track. toggling between ANC and Ambient is done by pressing and holding on either earbud. This setting can not be changed.As mentioned previously, there is wireless charging, they also charge via USB typeC.They have an IPX 4 rating.The UV cleaning system is activated only when the earbuds are charging wired or wirelessly. This does not work if the earbuds and case are not being charged.These are a great choice if sound quality is top priority with calls being second, but not wanting to spend more than $200. The compact size and great sound are big selling points and make these a compelling option.

date_review: Reviewed in the United States on December 6, 2021
overview_text: The best value pair of LG’s Tone Free 2021 Lineup
comment: This is essentially LG’s second generation of true wireless earbuds, they released the FN4-FN7 last year and they were a good first effort into the space but lacked key features like ANC until they released the FN7 later on after the first three pairs came out. These FP5 are the entry level of the lineup for this year, but they are also the best value that the essential features without any of what you probably don’t need. You get good battery life, active noise cancellation, good sound quality, and an easy to pocket charging case. The only things you miss out on are the UV Nano germ killing LEDs, wireless charging, and a built in bluetooth transmitter (only in the FB9). The battery life is slightly shorter compared to the other two models but it’s still quite respectable 8 hours per charge with another 22 from the charging case (compared to 10 and 24 hours respectively with the FB7 and FB9 models)I love the shape of these earbuds, they are really similar to the oblong like shape of the AirPods Pro, as well as having the same size stem. These use a touchpad at the top of the stem where it intersects with the bud, it’s one of the more accurate touch pads but some people struggle with these type of controls no matter how accurately it is implemented. There is an app that goes with these, you should definitely download it because it gives you a number of options and features that you can’t get without it (but it is not required).The biggest thing it gives you is 3D Audio, this will give you a surround sound like effect and it works the best when watching videos like shows or movies. This is actually not a regular thing to have on a pair of true wireless earbuds, only Samsung and Apple do this too (as far as I know), but each of those options requires that you have both a phone/tablet and earbuds from the same company.You can also change the control options for single/double/triple tap and what effect each action triggers. The app is the only way to update the firmware for the headphones, this might not seem like it’s worth it but it is. They are able to fix problems and improve certain features like ANC/Ambient mode or improve battery life. I owned a pair of the previous generation FN4 and I was impressed at how many different updates LG pushed out using the app, some of them really made a difference and improved the value.Now the sound quality, I think it’s really good for the $100 ish price they’re currently selling for with the discount. They have different EQ presets which also lets you create your own profile and adjust the sliders as you wish. This should suffice for anyone who has an issue with the default profile or just likes having different profiles for different types of music.The active noise cancellation is effective and the ambient passthrough mode sounds natural. Honestly, most pairs of true wireless earbuds are on the same page when it comes to products released in 2021. Almost all the brands have this technology figured out and the majority of them work about as well as the next one, up until you get to the $250-$300 price. There you will find Bose and Sony who have the strongest, most effective ANC using their own proprietary solution, rather than an off-the-shelf one made by Qualcomm or Mediatek or BESTechnic. Apple also uses a custom solution powered by H1, but it still isn’t quite as effective at blocking noise like what you get from Bose or Sony.Like I said before, this is the best version of the 2021 True Free earbuds because it has everything you need and is a lot more affordable than the higher end FB7 and FB9. You get a very good pair of comfortable, true wireless earbuds with ANC, 3D surround sound audio, a nice app, and good battery life.

date_review: Reviewed in the United States on September 10, 2022
overview_text: Best wireless headphones I've ever used.
comment: I picked these up after watching a review of the FP9s and almost buying those. I went with the FP5 instead because I didn't think the extra price was worth the extra features I didn't need and because I only planned on using these rarely around the house and sometimes when I'm out of the house. After getting them paired up with my iPhone (extremely quick and easy) I was shocked with how good they sounded immediately without any EQing. I installed the TONE app on iOS and changed the EQ settings to Immersive (Natural also sounds great) and I'm just blown away with how well they sound. I immediately paired them with my Android device and Windows PC and started using them as my daily drivers. I regret not getting the FP8 or FP9 headphones because those could only be better than these and were only about $50-$70 more when I was looking.They pair easily with all devices although I did have an issue with my Android phone where I had to pair and then put both earbuds back in the case to reset them because they kept reconnecting every 2-3 minutes, but after resetting them that issue stopped.Both the iOS and Android apps work great although updating the firmware on the earbuds with iOS was slow and mostly didn't work. I spent about 30 minutes trying to update the firmware on iOS and after it finally "worked" I thought I was good. After pairing with my Android phone the same firmware update was available so I had the Android app update both earbuds and it took less than 5 minutes. I'll be using Android to update the firmware going forward because of this one issue. I didn't notice any change after the firmware update so if I didn't have an Android device I wouldn't have missed out on anything so I didn't want to knock off a star for that reason.The comfort level is top notch, but they do not feel very secure with the included tips. I did test them and no matter how much I shook my head or moved around they were not going anywhere, they are definitely secured in place, they just don't feel like it with other earbuds I've used. They really feel like they're just floating in my ears which just adds to the comfort level for me.I had purchased some Etymotic Research ER3XR IEMs earlier this year for about the same price as the FP5 but the ER3XR were discounted from their $200 MSRP so I was told they were amazing, and they were great, the best pair I've owned in a long time, but the FP5 just sounds way better in terms of music. The ER3XR feel more comfortable and I can use them to monitor my microphone on my PC so I still use them, but the FP5 sound better and the wireless convenience has me using them more frequently than I had expected. I was also gifted a Audeze Mobius headset a while back which retailed for either $399 or $499 and, while it did sound really good for over the ear headphones, it didn't compare to the FP5's sound quality, comfort, and ease of use.The carrying case is great also, a lot smaller than I expected which was a great relief because I would rather keep it in my pocket than in a backpack. The biggest downside to both the earbuds and the case itself is that it collects lint, dust, and other particles very easily so I find myself cleaning them both every time I go to use them even if I cleaned them all off before I put them away. Not a huge deal, but a bit annoying.So to sum this review up: I really really like the FP5 earbuds, but I secretly wish I had a reason to upgrade to the FP9 model. After going through at least a dozen Bluetooth headsets, some I really liked but didn't last long, LG made me a fan for life with this product!

comment: To add to my previous review from December 2022, I still consider these very good headphones. They’ve lasted a year without losing sound quality or cushioning quality.The one thing I can’t stand is the feature where they turn off when you take them off. It’s too sensitive to movement. I can’t bend down, sort things, brush my teeth, or do anything that requires head movement without the music staggering pauses every three seconds. Quite the nuisance. Makes these more of a 3 star for limited mobility. Could use an update feature that turns that auto-off option off.….Before sticking with these headphones, I tried a few other pairs, including Bose 700, Bose 245, and a few Skullcandy varieties. My focus was on crisp treble that I could listen to without adjusting the headphones for every song.While Bose is probably still top of the line for their specialty, I didn’t notice that much difference between their headphones and Ankor for sound canceling; I could still hear the truck roar in the background, and the headphones didn’t mute conversations or a very loud parrot that lives on the same floor.  The base was good, but I listen to a variety of songs from Transiberian Orchestra to Thomas Burgeson and the quality of the treble was fuzzy under the weight of any added base. Every song had to be adjusted in the Bose app for adequate balance.To save myself the hassle of toggling with an app for every song, I tried the Ankor Life based on a friend’s recommendation.  The sound quality for TSO is phenomenal; every note is crisp and enunciated and you can definitely feel that surround sound without making any changes. They work for almost every genre of songs that I listen to. There is still some static on certain artists like Thomas Burgeson, which means I have to switch to earbuds; hence the four stars for sound quality.Volume control is easily adjusted on the headphone piece. I prefer buttons to touch control. My constant frustration with IPhone connection, however, is that earpieces don’t have their own volume outside of the phone. Everything I listen to is either one adjustment too loud or too soft. With these headphones (same with Bose), if it’s one adjustment too soft the sound quality is noticeably missing some notes.Battery life is great. I haven’t tried listening for up to 40 hours yet but it’s nice not to be reaching for a charger after a few hours.Side controls are easy to get used to and the headphones connect immediately. They don’t connect well in patchy service areas, though, which is weird. My $15 MPow earbuds work perfectly fine in the basement, while these randomly shut off.Fit is snug and comfortable, although they do tend to slip when I bend over. The headphones themselves are bulky, which is a minus because they are incredibly noticeable and look like a set of hubcaps sticking out. I can still wear them comfortably around the house, though. They nestle around my ears with no pinching whatsoever.Sound canceling is similar to my experience with Bose, at 1/3 the price. They don’t cancel piercing sounds like a parrot that can imitate the fire alarm, and they don’t mute rummaging sounds or conversations, but they do put an effective sphere of silence around you that makes the music seem like a part of the environment and not another distraction.They fold easily for stowing, and they come with a sturdy case. Also if you take them off they immediately pause whatever you’re listening to, which is fairly convenient.My phone automatically disconnects headphones during calls so I have no feedback on that aspect.Overall, compared with other headphones I’ve tried from higher priced companies, I’m  satisfied with these for daily listening. They have good treble, which is my preference, and the surround sound is a pleasant upgrade from my typical earbuds. They’re not the perfect headset, but for the price they’re decent and I enjoy using them for audiobooks and most of my music.

comment: So, my son has the Sony WH-1000XM5 headphones, and loves them.  I tried them out, and they are inded impressive.  But I wasn't about to spend $300+ on a set of bluetooth headphones.  So, after searching around for a bit, I came across these.  At a more attractive price, these seemed to offer much of the features that the Sony's did, so I figured I'd try them for less than 30 days, and see how it went.  The packaging is great, along with the included case, and accessories are pretty standard but fine.  They are about identical in design and construction to the Sony's.  I then listened, and they sound really good!  Music wise, they don't beat my Sennheisers, but they're studio grade and designed for that, so not gonna knock them for that.  But, as far as general music listening, they're not bad.  My main areas of focus, were YouTube, PlutoTV, and voice chatting/phone calls.  In these areas, they are very good.  The mic is nice and clear according to people on the other end.  For hearing conversations, including phone calls, YT, and PlutoTV for TV watching, these are amazing.  Keep in mind, I'm reviewing these without the use of the app.  This is straight out of the box.  I'm sure I could make them sound better for music and likely even better for my purposes, but I haven't felt the need to.  When it comes to human voice purposes, it's great out of the box.  I haven't felt the need for an app to modify the sound in any way.  The noise cancelling is very good as well.  When I'm listening to something with the NC enabled, I can't hear anything outside of what's being played through them.  One feature that I like better on these than the Sony's, is that on the Sony's, you have to hold your hand over the outside of one of the ear cups to disable the NC in order to hear people in the room.  On these, you merely have to hold your hand up to the cup for 2 seconds, and it disables it and you can remove your hand.  Repeat the process to enable it again.  That way you don't have to stand around with your hand stuck on the side of your headphones, looking like an idiot when you need to talk to someone.Between the sound (out of the box), construction, features, and all, this is more than worth the asking price.  Since using the app to make adjustments is going to be a subjective thing and determined by taste, I thought it'd be best to give an out of the box opinion.  Given that they sound this good to me for my purposes, I'm sure they could sound even better with the app, which I may eventually play around with.  But with what I use them for, I just haven't felt the need to.Solid headphones for the price, and definitely the way to go if you don't want to shell out $300 for the Sony's or equivalent.

Great choice if you need to be present somewhere but still want to listen to your media in high fidelity; very poor choice if you're trying to block the world out.Pretty comfortable to wear, with a few caveats. The headband is very unique and doesn't apply pressure to your whole head- as pictured, it essentially clamps on either side of your head above the ears. This is very odd at first but doesn't take long to acclimate to- also contributes to the "AIR"-ishness of the overall package. I do wonder about the longevity of these clamps as opposed to a traditional headband, but have owned the headphones for two plus years and haven't had issues so far. I think these run a bit warm in the earcups, but honestly that is probably more due to the comparative coolness on the rest of the head vs a traditional headband.Biggest issue with these is the absurdly long cable which is not interchangeable. Had to braid mine on itself to make it approximately 3ft long which is workable. Prior to doing that, I rarely used these headphones because of the excess cable. Wouldn't mind a long cable at all if I could replace it with a shorter one but it is "permanently" affixed, which is a problem. If your use case won't be affected by a long cable or requires one, this detail becomes moot.TL;DR - Great (balanced) sound, leaves the wearer more present in their environment, and is pretty comfortable to wear if you can tolerate or work aroind the very long cable. overview_text: Outstanding Mids and Highs - Not for Bass Heads.
comment: These are a fantastic pair of open-backs for anyone who appreciates high quality music but doesn't want to break the bank. I have four pairs of Audio Technica headphones now, but this was my first open-back pair. I did an extensive amount of research into 'hi fi' audiophile headphones before buying open-backs, and ultimately the reason I bought these was because they have amazing reviews, and anything above this price range suffers extensively from the law of diminishing return.All that said.. Audio performance:- Noise cancellation: These are open-back headphones. If you've done your research you know this is the opposite of what you're buying with open-backs.- Sound Quality: These headphones have absolutely incredible sound for mids and highs, and the sound stage is breathtaking - this line of headphones isn't called 'air' for nothing.. After dozens of hours listening to a broad range of genres, I can tell that acoustics and vocals is where these will provide the best experience. Rock, Country, Orchestra, classic, etc - these genres will absolutely blow your mind with sound quality, clarity, warmth, and realism. The first artist I listened to on these was Sam Smith, and they are still my favorite artist to listen to with these cans. If you've never cared much for bass, these headphones will not disappoint you.- Bass: If you've got this far, you've probably inferred that the bass isn't the best. I don't want to misrepresent here: the bass isn't bad... But if you primarily to listen to EDM, House, Dubstep, etc; I would suggest looking at closed back headphones. Audio Technicas ATH-M50X are universally considered one of the best mid-budget closed-back headphones on the market, and they will deliver a great bass experience. If EDM is only part of the deal for you here, you can always get an amplifier with bass boost, and that will easily take the cows home.- Comfort: These are very lightweight and comfortable, but I would put 2-3 hours as the max listening time before you'll start to notice them pressing into your skull. The loop design holding the two sides together makes for a somewhat slanted fit on your head, where (depending how big/small your head is) you will feel slightly more pressure under your ears than over. Over 2-3 hours, they will migrate down your head a little, eventually resting on the top of your ears. Because of this I have to readjust them every once in a while. In summary, they are comfortable, but not the best for hyper long listening experiences. They aren't the most comfortable headphones I've worn, but are certainly not bad.Summary:  If you want high quality headphones for any sound wave invented before the 1990's, these headphones will be highly satisfactory, and for a great price. These are amazing open-back headphones for $110~. Anything above this price range will deliver small and highly subjective improvements in sound quality, but there are better option out there if you're looking for a good bass experience.P.S. Audio is an extremely subjective sensory input, so every review will be different. If you can't decide because there are two many choices on the market, I recommend looking at 3 or 4 'Top 10' lists on google for the listening experience you want, then finding a brand on those lists that you already trust and matching it with your price range. Audiophilia is a deep, deep rabbit hole of subjectivity. I found myself spending too much time doing research, so I just decided to pull the trigger on something mid-budget (these) with a brand I trusted (Audio Technica), and I am not at all disappointed.

comment: This is a strange headphone, it uses a wing system instead of a conventional headband or suspension system. This makes it very light on the top of the head but also makes for barely any clamp which can be a problem for people with medium to small sized heads. There is a common "mod" that people do which is putting a rubber band in between the wings which essentially turns it into a suspension headband and increases the clamp. The earcups themselves also don't pivot at all so the bottom of the cups are more clamped than the top of them. Overall a weird fit which some people may find comfortable but others will not, this depends on the shape of your head. I find it decently comfortable but not as comfortable as my Sennheiser 58X or Beyerdynamic DT770.Now, the sound quality is quite unique, it has a fairly lean bass that's not completely absent, but is lacking in the sub-bass regions. comment: Let me start off by explaining that I have lost about 85% of the nerve sensitivity in my left ear due to Meniere's Disease. Conductive hearing is still about 80-85% though. My right ear has about 15% loss. I used to be able to hear well past 20 khz, but now there's significant drop off around 16 khz in both ears. The left ear hears sub 500 hz just fine, though I suspect there's bone conductivity at play. In the 1 khz to 5 khz range, which is where normal speech is located, the left ear only hears muffled sounds even at high volume. The right ear is good from 10 khz down.That background to let you understand the fact that while I could hear quite well even 10 years ago, I am hearing mostly through my right ear and through bone conductivity. I also have perfect pitch for whatever I can hear.In testing out these headphones, I listened to music I have listened to for 10-20 years. I know every nuance, every breath the artist takes when playing a wind instrument, the sound of fingers on strings, etc. I have Rokit studio monitors for my desk, and those are designed to be a totally flat response for music production. I can hear things with these headphones which I can't hear with the Rokit monitors. The bass is nuanced, not booming. The highs I can hear are crystal clear. The mid range is clean without a hint of muddiness. At the highest volume I can handle, there is no distortion whatsoever, and at low volume, the music is exactly how I remember and is perfectly reproduced without any loss of clarity.These are the first open headphones I've ever owned, and I can see why everyone recommends them for listening to music. I have been testing out a pair of the SteelSeries Arctis Pro Wireless headphones at the same time, and while the Arctis is quite superior for gaming compared to other headphones I've tried, these Audio-Technica beat just about everything hands down for music. I have a pair of Bose noise cancelling headphones, and for noise cancelling, that's the ones you want. These headphones don't compare because of the open design.I am sure professionals with perfect ears will point out all the things my ears are missing, but I can't imagine that audio monitor headphones would sound any better to me. These headphones are producing the sounds I can hear accurately and clearly with distortion or exaggeration.They also are extremely light. You can feel the difference even when they are in the box. I love the Arctis headband so much that I'm keeping those for gaming, but they are heavy in comparison. I stop feeling the AD700X a few seconds after I put them on my head. They stay where I want them too.I would recommend these as the starting point for any new purchase. I bought them on sale for $118, and at that price, you're going to have a hard time finding better sound quality even for ones which are  $200-300 higher. Remember, these are for listening to music. They'll work for gaming, but there are other headphones with built in microphones which would do better.

date_review: Reviewed in the United States on July 30, 2021
comment: So, I was in the market for some new headphones. A friend of mine had suggested the AudioTechnicaATH-M50x, but after perusing lots of extensive reviews on them I decided against them. The most important factor to me is comfort, and from what I had been reading about those, they weren't necessarily bad headphones, they just weren't very good ~$200 headphones. And apparently, they take "some getting used to" in terms of comfort. I was turned off by both of these sentiments and decided to look for something else. I figured open-back may be the way to go, and eventually settled on a pair of the ATH-AD700X's.In my opinion, the best things about these headphones are, ironically, things a lot of people have outlined in their own reviews here as being negatives.Let's start with the mechanism these use to stay on your head.You have likely seen many reviews here saying the mechanism these headphones use is "too loose". In my opinion, they are not too loose at all. They grip your head with a very light, feathery touch. At first it may feel like they could slip off if you just tilt your head the wrong way, but they will not. Unless you're thrashing your head to some VERY SERIOUS metal there is no way these are going to fall off, whether you're laying down in bed or sitting in a chair. Also, I have always had difficulty laying down in bed and using big headphones. More often than not, the cans just get shoved into strange, awkward positions, or the whole thing is really just gripping my head way too tight and it gets VERY uncomfortable VERY quickly. That is not the case with these headphones. They are extremely comfortable to wear in bed, and they sound great too.Next, let's go to the cable.I've seen SO MANY reviews saying they hate the cable for being "too long", and they hate how the cable "coils up." In my opinion, these are actually things worthy of praise. I would rather have a pair of headphones with a cable that is too long than a pair with a cable that is one inch too short. NOTHING is more frustrating than that. As for the cable "coiling up", when in use this is never a problem. The cable is so long that any coiling is going to occur pretty far away from your body. And the cable "coiling up" sounds like a bad thing at first, until you see HOW it is coiling up. This cable has a tendency to coil up into the shape it was originally packaged in. So if you put the headphones away somewhere, you can rest assured knowing the cable will VERY EASILY arrange itself back into a very space efficient form factor. This is a pro to me, because I do not have a dedicated microphone. So I will often switch between headphones when using my computer. Additionally, you will know the cable is also SAFE in these conditions. I have broken many headphones over the years because I have poorly maintained the cable. This cable going into the exact arrangement I need when I wish to store it somewhere, with very little effort on my part, is a godsend and I am totally cool with that.Now that these two are out of the way, let's move into some more pros. The sound is great. I'm not an audiophile, so I have no opinion on how "chocolatey" the mids are or how "minty" the treble is, or whatever buzzwords those people like to use to describe their sound equipment. But what I can tell you is, the sound is very clear and crisp and you will no doubt pick up on details in music that you never heard before, especially if you've spent your whole life using substandard, cheap headphones or "gaming" headsets. I play a digital piano through my DAW software, and immediately I could tell a massive difference in not just the overall quality, but also the clarity in the finer details of the various piano libraries I had been using for months --- details I previously did not even know were there. And this is straight, out of box performance. No EQ, not even hooked into an audio interface. Just plugging right into a line output on my computer case.So, how about audio clarity in a noisy environment?In my opinion, ambient background noises are only SLIGHTLY easier to hear through these, than my usual pair of closed-back headphones. I have a fan in my room that I run pretty much all the time on the lowest setting. Even with my usual pair of closed-back headphones, I can hear the fan. The only time I can't is if I barrage my ears with a constant stream of very loud noises. The same exact case applies with these headphones. If the sound is loud enough you will be completely tuned out to any external noises. I don't even need them that loud to reach a point that they overpower the sound of my whirring fan.Are there any cons I can think of? Not really. I guess they aren't quite as bassy as my usual headphones could get, but I prefer that. Sometimes stuff would just sound so...mixed up and muddied on my other headphones, and that was all due to their closed design. I'm sure someone with vastly superior background in audio equipment can find something to dislike about these headphones, but I'm a simple man. As that kind of person, I really can not find anything to dislike about these headphones. So far they have been a blast and I am loving them. If you are a relatively simple person too, and you just want to get something better than whatever dollar store headphones you've been using for years, these will definitely be good value to you. I will not be giving any rating towards "Noise Cancellation", because these are not noise cancelling headphones. Why that is even something I can rate on these doesn't really make any sense to me.

comment: I admit, I am an absolute sound snob. I am so picky it isn't funny. But these headphones... they check ALL the boxes.I knew I would be happy, Audio-Technica is such a respected name, but it goes beyond my expectations.To start, I don't go for bass heavy headphones. I prefer studio quality to hear all the sounds. Heavy bass cancels out some of the mid range.  So if your expecting ground shaking (or, I guess, ear shaking) bass, never buy studio quality. I simply use an equalizer on my computer to pop up the bass a bit (you should always use an equalizer or you miss out) . I listen to a lot of darkwave and aggrotech so you need a bit of bass on that.However, I did my first test in Valheim. My computer decided it was going to be a pain and not use my headset mic, regardless of what I told it, instead use my MXL condenser. Well, it is a good mic. Instead of fighting it, I just pushed my headset mic out of the way... and it would just get in my way (mostly sit right in front of my left eye), so it was time for headphones instead of a headset. My headset has some pretty good surround sound, so I knew what to listen for. But wow! Just on the game loading screen I was hearing sound effects I never noticed before.Once in game I was hearing what I can only think is the way the sound team intended the game to sound like. Footsteps sounded real now, birds I never noticed before, all the little chirps, wind, chittering of the MOBs, all totally more realistic.Tested the surround by hunting for some deer, and it exceeded expectations there too. I could accurately track the sounds of deer: right rear, left front, dead left, moving, I could hear the sounds moving naturally (which my headset did too, but the cans have a more vibrant sound).Then I loaded Spotify and put on a song by a band I've seen many times live. Now that.. was gorgeous as well. It sounded natural, like I was there live, hearing all the nuance and all the sound.As I mentioned, the huge bass isn't there, that's okay with me. The bass is very solid, not disappointing me at all. The human voice should not sound flat, and I was totally hearing all the range in the vocals. Just like being there. But the bass is good. I really love the bass I'm getting out of it (listening to some darkwave right now, so it's really got bass, I'm not disappointed).As for noise cancelling.... well, they are open back. That being said, I actually didn't hear much outside noise while playing music. And while in game, I pretended not to so to drive my kids crazy (it's a mother's job to driver her kids crazy). But yes, in game I heard outside noise pretty well. In my situation, though, it's not a big deal. I have a fairly quiet office space where I play, and well, when I'm in the living room, being able to hear outside noises is usually good, I'm down there to be around the fam, after all.But if you want no outside noise, I recommend a closed back headphone. As I mentioned, when the music was on, I wasn't hearing much, even when the kids started talking. They could hear my music pretty well, but I couldn't really hear them.The comfort level... that too is great. I was hesitant of the way the headband was designed. However, it fits great. I got spoiled by self adjusting headbands as it always seems I can't find the right click on other ones. This one self adjusted perfectly.At first it felt loose, I shook my head quite a bit and they stayed perfectly in place. The ear pieces fit well over the ear, I put on my glasses and they felt great with the glasses on. The "looseness" really seems to help with not feeling squished while wearing glasses. I've been wearing them for a couple hours now (once headphones on, its hard to get them off of me) and it's not hot and sticky, still feel comfortable, and I don't feel like my head is in a vice. I could totally wear them all day if I had to.I would totally, 100%, recommend these headphones for anyone who want quality sound. Of course I'm a person who thinks ear buds should be outlawed on the basis they deliver inferior sound (I told you I am sound snob).They are ..worth.every.penny.Totally worth it.
